exp20v2-aivocab.sampling:
Temperature and Sampling

AI Vocabulary for Product Managers. A case-style explainer on why "temperature zero" does not mean "same answer, always right".

1. A reply that would not reproduce

On Tuesday 8 September 2026, Wamika Khosla, head of product at Kaumudi Support Systems in Pune, sat down with her engineering lead, Kishore Wagle, and her head of customer operations, Kalyani Wadhwa. Kaumudi sold a drafting assistant to Kunjal Insurance Services, which used it to answer about 12,000 policyholder emails a day about claim status. The contract was worth ₹1.8 crore a year. Two weeks earlier, Kunjal's compliance team had asked Kaumudi to reproduce a reply sent on 19 August, which a policyholder had disputed. Kishore re-ran the identical input; the text that came back was not the text that had been sent.

The deployment used a "temperature" setting of 0.7. Kishore argued that setting it to zero would make the model deterministic and the audit problem would disappear. Kwame Asante, the quality analyst in Kaumudi's Accra office, had already tested that. He sent one claim-status prompt 500 times at temperature zero. In 458 runs the output was word-for-word identical, which is 91.6 per cent. In the other 42 it was not, which is 8.4 per cent, and the differences appeared mostly in the first few words.

Wamika faced a decision with real money attached. If she promised Kunjal "identical output on replay" and could not deliver, the ₹1.8 crore renewal was at risk. If she set temperature to zero and told the business the model would now be correct, she would be promising something no setting can provide. The rest of this page builds the vocabulary she needed, and ends with what she decided.

2. The idea

A large language model (a program trained on vast amounts of text to predict what text comes next) does not write a reply in one piece. It writes one token at a time. A token is a chunk of text, often a word or part of a word. At each step the model produces a score for every token in its vocabulary, which may be over 100,000 entries. These raw scores are called logits. A logit is an unnormalised preference: higher means the model considers that token a better continuation, but the numbers are not yet probabilities.

Two further steps turn scores into a choice. First, a function called softmax converts the logits into probabilities that are positive and sum to one. Second, a sampling step picks one token from that distribution. Temperature is a number that rescales the logits before softmax. Low temperature sharpens the distribution so the leading token takes nearly all the weight. High temperature flattens it so unlikely tokens get a real chance.

The idea is borrowed from physics. Ludwig Boltzmann described in the 1870s how particles distribute across energy states as a function of heat; the same mathematical form reappeared in the 1980s in neural network research, including work by Geoffrey Hinton and colleagues, and in his 2015 work on model distillation. Its purpose here is practical: always taking the likeliest word yields dull, repetitive text, while free sampling drifts into nonsense. Temperature is a dial between those failures.

The sentence Wamika could repeat in a meeting: "The model produces odds for every possible next word, and temperature decides how strictly we follow the favourite, but it never tells us whether the favourite is true."

Temperature is applied at inference, when the model is running, not in training. The same model at 0.2 and 1.5 has identical knowledge; only the selection rule differs.

3. How it actually works

Figure 1 shows the loop. The model reads the context, meaning the prompt plus every token generated so far, and emits logits. The temperature step divides every logit by T. Softmax then exponentiates each result and divides by the total, so each probability is the exponential of one scaled logit over the sum of all the exponentials. Because the division happens before the exponential, a small T stretches the gaps between logits and a large T shrinks them.

The truncation step, which practitioners often leave implicit, removes tokens before the draw. Top-k keeps only the k highest-probability tokens. Top-p, also called nucleus sampling and proposed by Ari Holtzman and colleagues in 2019, keeps the smallest set of tokens whose probabilities add to at least p. After truncation the survivors are renormalised so they sum to one again. Only then does the draw happen: the system picks a random number and selects the token whose slice of the distribution contains it. The chosen token is appended to the context and the whole loop repeats for the next position. A 120-token reply involves 120 draws, and an early unlucky draw changes every probability that follows.

Temperature zero is a special case. Dividing by zero is undefined, so providers implement it as "always take the highest-scoring token", known as greedy decoding. There is no draw at all. That is the source of the belief that zero is deterministic, which is only half right.

4. A worked example

Take the first word of Kunjal's status sentence. Suppose the model scores four candidates: "Approved" 4.0, "Pending" 3.0, "Partly" 2.0, and "Declined" 1.0. These four logits are invented for illustration; real models score tens of thousands of tokens. At T = 1, divide each logit by 1 (no change) and exponentiate: e4 = 54.598, e3 = 20.086, e2 = 7.389, e1 = 2.718. The sum is 84.791. Each probability is its exponential over 84.791.

Table 1. Softmax at three temperatures for the same four logits

Table 1 lays out the arithmetic for all three settings. At T = 1 the probabilities are 64.4, 23.7, 8.7 and 3.2 per cent, which total 100.0. For the second pass, change one input: halve T to 0.5. The scaled logits become 8, 6, 4 and 2, and the exponentials become 2,980.958, 403.429, 54.598 and 7.389, summing to 3,446.374. "Approved" now carries 86.5 per cent and "Declined" only 0.2 per cent. Doubling T to 2 has the reverse effect: the exponentials are 7.389, 4.482, 2.718 and 1.649, summing to 16.238, and "Approved" falls to 45.5 per cent while "Declined" rises to 10.2.

Figure 2 draws Table 1 as bars, grouped by token. Read the "Approved" group: the bar shrinks from 86.5 to 64.4 to 45.5 per cent as T rises, while the "Declined" bars grow from 0.2 to 3.2 to 10.2. Temperature does not add or remove any candidate; it moves weight between them. Now scale up. Of 12,000 daily replies at T = 1, about 7,728 would open with "Approved", 2,844 with "Pending", 1,044 with "Partly" and 384 with "Declined", which sums to 12,000. At T = 0.5 the "Declined" count would fall to about 26. If the claim is actually pending, "Approved" is still the wrong opening, and it wins at every temperature, including zero, where it wins every time.

Top-p adds one more wrinkle. At T = 1 with p = 0.9, the running total is 64.4, then 88.1, which is still under 90, so a third token joins to reach 96.8. "Declined" is cut. The survivors renormalise to 66.5, 24.5 and 9.0 per cent, totalling 100.0. Truncation removed a rare option and shifted the remaining odds upward.

5. Nuances a learner must become aware of

Zero is not the same as deterministic

Greedy decoding removes the random draw, but the scores themselves can vary between runs. Graphics processors add floating-point numbers in orders that depend on how requests are batched together, and addition of decimals is not perfectly associative. Two logits that are almost tied can swap places, and a different first token changes everything afterwards. That is how Kwame's 42 differing runs arose.

Zero is not the same as correct

Greedy decoding returns the model's favourite, not the truth. If the favourite is wrong, it is wrong reliably. In Table 1 the most likely word might be "Approved" for a claim that is pending; lowering T makes that mistake more consistent, not rarer.

Temperature is not creativity

Higher temperature does not make the model smarter or more inventive; it makes it willing to pick lower-ranked tokens, which are sometimes fresher and sometimes simply wrong.

Settings apply per token, not per answer

A 5 per cent chance of an odd word at each of 100 positions is not a 5 per cent chance of one odd answer. The chance that every position avoids the odd word is 0.95 to the power 100, roughly 0.6 per cent, so some wobble is almost certain.

Some providers fix or hide the dial

Certain reasoning-oriented models ignore or restrict temperature. Check the documentation, and ask whether a seed parameter exists: it fixes the random draw but not hardware variation.

It cannot fix a bad prompt or bad knowledge

Sampling operates only on what the model already computed. It cannot add missing facts, and it has no access to whether a claim was actually approved. That knowledge must come from the retrieved data placed in the prompt.

Ask first: what does variation cost here?

Ask whether the real requirement is identical text or merely identical meaning.

6. How the setting differs across products

Table 2. Typical stance on sampling by context
ContextUsual priorityTypical stance
Consumer (brainstorming, chat companion)Variety and delightModerate to high temperature; users expect different answers on retry.
B2B (claims, contracts, support)Consistency and auditabilityLow temperature, structured output, stored logs of what was actually sent.
Marketplace (listings, buyer-seller messages)Fairness across many partiesLow temperature for facts; some variety for descriptions to avoid duplicate-looking listings.

In consumer products variation is often the point: someone asking twice for gift ideas wants different ideas. In B2B work such as Kaumudi's, the buyer must explain what was said, so consistency and records matter more than novelty. Marketplaces sit between: facts stay stable while descriptions benefit from variety. A startup can check informally; a larger company such as Kunjal treats settings as versioned configuration with a test suite before any change ships.

7. Common mistakes

Believing zero guarantees replay. The symptom is an audit where the same input yields a different reply. The misunderstanding is conflating "no random draw" with "no variation". The cheapest diagnostic is Kwame's: run one prompt 500 times and count distinct outputs.

Treating low temperature as an accuracy control. The symptom is a confidently wrong answer that is also consistent across retries. The misunderstanding is that sampling governs truth. The diagnostic is to score a fixed set of known-answer questions at two temperatures and see whether accuracy moved; usually it barely does.

Tuning by anecdote. The symptom is a setting changed after one bad reply. A single draw says little about a distribution; sample the same prompt at least 100 times before and after.

Ignoring the record. The symptom is an inability to reproduce what was sent. The misunderstanding is that replay is the only route to auditability. The diagnostic is to ask whether the exact sent text, prompt and settings were stored.

8. What good looks like

A well-run team begins with the requirement, not the dial. It separates three needs: the facts must be right, the wording may vary, and compliance must see exactly what was sent. It sets low temperature for the status sentence, verifies status against the claims system, logs the final text with prompt and settings, and runs a weekly 500-run check. It can tell a regulator such as IRDAI, in one sentence, what is fixed, what varies and what is recorded.

9. The decision, and what to study next

Wamika did not promise identical replay. She proposed three changes to Kunjal: lower temperature to 0.2 for the status sentence; have the system insert the claim status directly from Kunjal's records as a fixed field, so the model never chooses between "Approved" and "Pending"; and store every sent reply with its prompt and settings, so a disputed message is retrieved, not regenerated. Kishore would set up Kwame's 500-run test as a weekly check. Wamika's reasoning was that the dial could reduce variation but could not guarantee either sameness or correctness, so the two guarantees Kunjal actually needed had to come from the data and the archive.

The natural next topics are structured output and function calling, which constrain what a model may emit and so narrow what sampling can choose from, and hallucination, which explains why the model's favourite can be fluent and wrong. Two questions to sit with. First, in a product you know, which outputs must be identical, which only equivalent, and who decided? Second, if the most likely token is wrong at T = 0, where in your system would you catch it?
exp40v2-aivocab.sampling:
Temperature and Sampling

AI & Data Products › AI Vocabulary & Primer for PMs. A near-expert treatment of the two beliefs about temperature that are both wrong.

1. Two rooms, eighteen days apart

On Thursday 6 August 2026, in an operations room in Hyderabad, Tejaswini Ambekar was shown two discharge summaries that ought to have been the same document. Ambekar was vice-president of product at Chikitsa Coding Systems, whose clinical documentation assistant drafted the free-text impression at the foot of each summary for Tridhara Hospitals Network, a seventeen-hospital chain across Telangana. The contract was worth ₹6.4 crore a year.

Tridhara put 1,80,000 encounters through the system each month, of which 40,500 needed a written impression rather than a template, or 22.5 per cent. Tanuja Wankhede, its head of clinical quality, had pulled two encounters with identical structured inputs from the same ward on the same afternoon. One said the patient was discharged in a stable condition; the other said satisfactory. An audit before a NABH accreditation visit flagged the pair. Chandrakant Bhosale, Chikitsa's principal engineer for inference, offered the answer offered in every such room: set temperature to zero and the problem goes away.

Eighteen days later, on Monday 24 August 2026, Chirayu Mahadevan read the opposite result in Mumbai. Mahadevan co-founded Titli Story Labs, which generated illustrated bedtime stories in eight Indian languages for 4,10,000 monthly active accounts, producing 24,60,000 stories a month, an average of 6.0 each. Charulata Sabnis, who ran growth, had just closed a fourteen-day temperature experiment: the warmer arm retained better and produced more content the safety classifier disliked. The dial Bhosale wanted to turn down was the one Sabnis wanted to turn up. Both were asking one question from opposite ends: what does this setting control, and what does it leave untouched?

2. The idea, and who disagrees about it

A language model does not produce text. At each position it produces a vector of real-valued scores, one per vocabulary entry, called logits. A logit is an unnormalised preference: larger means more favoured, but the numbers are not yet probabilities. The softmax exponentiates each logit and divides by the sum of all the exponentials, giving positive numbers that sum to one, and sampling then draws one token from that distribution. Temperature is a positive number T by which every logit is divided before the exponential is taken. Because the division sits inside the exponential, T below 1 concentrates weight on the leader and T above 1 spreads it outward.

The form is borrowed: it is the Boltzmann distribution from statistical mechanics, where temperature governs how often a system occupies a higher-energy state. It reached computing through simulated annealing and Boltzmann machines in the 1980s, and modern practice through Geoffrey Hinton's 2015 work on distillation. The problem it solves was documented by Ari Holtzman and colleagues in 2019: a model trained to maximise the likelihood of human text, then decoded by always taking its likeliest token, produces prose that is bland and collapses into repetition. Human text is not the most likely text.

Three positions are held by competent practitioners and are not reconcilable. The control school will sign that for any output a third party relies on, temperature should be as low as the provider allows and every other source of variation moved somewhere auditable; it will not sign that zero produces reproducible output. The distributional school holds that the distribution is the model's real product and one sample discards nearly all of it; it will sign that several samples aggregated beat one, and will not sign that a single low-temperature output safely summarises what the model believes. The nuisance-parameter school holds that the dial is cosmetic and that almost every problem attacked with it is better solved by changing the prompt, the evidence or the schema; it will sign that temperature deserves a default and no more, and will not sign that a task has an optimal value.

3. Mechanics, worked through

Take the position in Chikitsa's draft where the condition at discharge is chosen, and suppose the five leading candidates carry logits of 3.5, 3.0, 1.9, 1.2 and 0.5. At T = 1.0 they pass through unchanged.

The runner-up carries 31.0 per cent: nearly a third of the mass sits on a word a clinician reads as a different clinical statement. Now rescale. At T = 0.7 the logits become 5.000, 4.286, 2.714, 1.714 and 0.714, whose exponentials sum to 243.7568; at T = 1.5 they become 2.333, 2.000, 1.267, 0.800 and 0.333, with exponentials summing to 24.8715.

Temperature redistributes from head to tail rather than flattening uniformly, so a team reading it as "how sure the model is" will be wrong about the cases that matter. The formal measure of spread is entropy: 1.387 bits at T = 0.7, 1.711 at T = 1.0 and 1.992 at T = 1.5, giving branching factors of 2.615, 3.274 and 3.979.

The step usually left implicit: truncation

Between the softmax and the draw sits a filter. Top-k keeps the k highest-probability tokens; top-p, or nucleus sampling, keeps the smallest set whose probabilities reach p. Survivors are renormalised to sum to one, and only then is a random number drawn against the slices.

The nucleus holds 92.3 per cent of the mass, so each survivor is divided by 0.923: 51.1 becomes 55.3, 31.0 becomes 33.5 and 10.3 becomes 11.2, summing to 100.0. How many tokens a given p retains depends on the temperature applied before it. At T = 0.7 the cumulative reaches 90.7 per cent by the second token, so p = 0.90 keeps two candidates; at T = 1.0 three; at T = 1.5 it is 85.4 after three and 94.4 after four, so four. Top-p partly cancels temperature, which is why teams that move both report findings that will not replicate.

Temperature zero, and why it is not determinism

Division by zero is undefined, so providers implement T = 0 as greedy decoding: take the highest logit, no draw at all. That removes the sampler, not the variation. Logits come from summing very large numbers of floating-point products on a graphics processor, and floating-point addition is not associative. The order in which partial sums accumulate depends on how many requests were batched together at that instant, and so on other customers' traffic. Where two logits are close the ordering can flip; on mixture-of-experts architectures batch composition can also change which expert a token is routed to.

Catalina Restrepo, Chikitsa's evaluation lead in Lisbon, measured it. On Tuesday 18 August 2026, twelve days after Wankhede's escalation, she sent one fixed encounter through the production endpoint 2,000 times at T = 0. Of those runs, 1,874 returned a byte-identical impression, or 93.7 per cent; the remaining 126, or 6.3 per cent, produced eight further variants. The impressions averaged 240 tokens. If each position flips independently with probability q, identity needs 240 consecutive non-flips, so one minus q, raised to the power 240, equals 0.937, giving q of 0.0271 per cent: about one position in 3,689.

Figure 2 carries the consequence that surprises executives: reproducibility is a property of the setting and the length. At 60 tokens the same endpoint reproduces 98.4 per cent of the time; at 960 tokens, 77.1 per cent. A pilot on short answers looks deterministic and production on long ones does not, with no change in between.

4. When the idea applies, stated as testable claims

Lowering temperature reduces output variance. True, and testable by sending one prompt many times and counting distinct outputs. Lowering temperature raises accuracy. Not generally. Score a fixed set with known answers at two temperatures; for Chikitsa's code suggestions the difference sat inside noise, because the favourite code was the same at every temperature, so lowering T made right and wrong answers more consistent by the same mechanism. T = 0 makes a past output reproducible. False, as Restrepo's 6.3 per cent shows; what a hospital or a regulator wants is retrieval from an archive.

Variance is a cost. True for Chikitsa, where two clinically different words for one state creates an audit finding. False for Titli, where variance is the product: the cooler arm's users tapped "tell it differently" on 38,880 of the 1,80,000 stories generated, or 21.6 per cent, against 26,100 in the warmer arm. They were asking the cooler model for the variety it had been configured not to give.

The idea becomes actively misleading in three situations. When the defect is factual, temperature is the wrong lever: a model cannot sample its way to a fact that was never in its context. When the output is constrained to a small enumerated set, the distribution is so peaked that no usable temperature changes the choice. And when the variation comes from the prompt rather than the sampler — an injected timestamp, a re-ranked retrieval set, a rotated model version — lowering temperature changes nothing and the team wrongly concludes the model is unstable.

5. Hard edge cases and the organisational seams

The setting rarely lives where the product manager thinks it does. In multi-product companies one gateway serves several surfaces, and temperature is a field in a deployment file owned by a backend team. The commonest real incident is not a bad temperature; it is one that changed and nobody knew. Two-sided products face a sharper version: at Chaturanga Retail Exchange, a marketplace with 4,80,000 active listings, variety that made a seller's catalogue look less duplicated made two listings of one item read as two different items to a buyer. The parties want opposite settings on the same string.

In regulated contexts the resolution is architectural rather than numerical. Chinar Insurance Services, asked to reproduce a policyholder communication, could not do so by rerunning anything; it stored the rendered text, the prompt, the model version and the settings, and retrieved them. Tridhara's NABH exposure has the same shape. Hardware adds a layer: Tulaa Instruments Works ran a quantised assistant on 2,700 weighbridge controllers, and two controllers on different firmware builds resolved near-ties differently at T = 0, so determinism there is per-build, not per-setting. What mature companies do, rather than what they say, is stop promising sameness. They promise a recorded artefact and a bounded distribution: this is the text we sent, this is the configuration that produced it, this is the weekly measurement showing no drift. Tarasetu Payments Network declined to expose temperature to partner developers at all, since a parameter a partner can set is one the platform supports forever.

6. Nine distinctions that separate an expert from a competent practitioner

Zero is argmax, not determinism. The tell-tale sign is a reproduction failure rate in the low single digits, concentrated where two candidates are close. The obvious reading, that the system is broken, is wrong: this is hardware behaving as designed, and no product setting removes it.

Zero does not make the answer true; it makes the error consistent. The tell-tale sign is a wrong output that reproduces perfectly and so acquires an unearned air of verification. If stable is the favourite for a patient who was guarded, greedy decoding returns it every time, and reviewers read that as confirmation.

Temperature and truncation are not independent. The tell-tale sign is a team reporting a temperature result without its top-p, then failing to reproduce it a month later. As Table 3 shows, p = 0.90 keeps two, three or four candidates at T = 0.7, 1.0 and 1.5: the dial you moved was not the only one that moved.

Most observed variance is not sampling variance. The tell-tale sign is a distinct-output count at T = 0 far above the hardware noise floor. Diff the prompts, not the settings: injected timestamps, re-ranked retrieval and silent model upgrades produce more variation than the sampler does.

The setting applies per token, and the effect compounds. The tell-tale sign is a guarantee that held in a short-form pilot and failed in long-form production, as in Figure 2. A reproduction rate quoted without an output length is incomplete.

A seed fixes the draw, not the logits. A seed makes the pseudo-random sequence repeatable and does nothing about batching-dependent arithmetic. The tell-tale sign is a team that has set one, still sees divergence, and concludes it is being ignored.

Sampling many times is not a free accuracy upgrade. Suppose five samples are drawn at T = 0.7 and the plurality wins. Using the T = 0.7 column, the leading token takes an outright plurality 71.2 per cent of the time, ties 10.9 per cent and loses 17.9 per cent, whereas greedy decoding selects it every time. Voting is a noisier argmax; self-consistency pays only where the modal answer across whole reasoning paths differs from the greedy path's.

Token probability is not claim probability. The tell-tale sign is a product surfacing the top token's probability as a confidence score. Stable at 51.1 per cent does not mean the model is 51.1 per cent sure the patient was stable; among the phrasings it might write, that word took half the weight. A single proposition spread across three synonyms looks uncertain and is not.

Constraining the output space beats reweighting it. The tell-tale sign of maturity is a team that answers a sampling complaint by changing the schema. If the condition at discharge must be one of five values pulled from the chart, the model is not choosing between stable and satisfactory. Structured output removes positions from the sampler's reach; temperature reweights only those that remain.

7. How this differs by product type and stage

The mechanics are identical everywhere, and most claimed differences between product types are differences in who pays for variance rather than in how sampling works. In consumer products variance is often the feature; a user who asks twice and gets the same answer feels the product is broken. In business software the buyer must explain the output to someone else, so the premium is on recorded consistency. Enterprise adds procurement: the setting becomes a contractual term, and product managers should refuse to let "deterministic" enter that document. Marketplaces have two customers with opposite preferences on one string; hardware makes it a firmware property. Stage changes governance, not physics: a seed-stage team sets one default and moves on, a Series B team gives the setting an owner and a regression suite, and at scale it needs change control, because moving Titli to the warmer setting changes 24,60,000 stories a month.

8. Three worked examples

Chikitsa: the cheaper option was not the safer one

Titli: the arm that retained was the arm that flagged

The warmer arm retained 26,880 accounts against 24,900, a relative improvement of 7.95 per cent on the 41.5 per cent baseline. It also tripled the flag rate, which at Titli's volume of 24,60,000 stories means 3,690 flagged stories a month instead of 1,230, an increase of 2,460. At ninety seconds each, 3,690 flags consume 5,535 minutes, or 92.25 hours. That is what the setting actually buys: a staffing decision disguised as a configuration value.

Chaturanga: where the approach failed

Chaturanga reached for temperature to fix the wrong problem. Buyers complained that descriptions stated specifications the item did not have. At T = 1.1, 31,200 of the 4,80,000 listings, or 6.5 per cent, carried at least one unsupported specification, and 1,404 of those 31,200 — 4.5 per cent — produced an item-not-as-described return at ₹410 each, or ₹5,75,640 a month. The team cut temperature to 0.4 and the problem barely moved: the specifications were not in the prompt at all, so the model was filling a gap, and a colder model fills it with the same confident invention.

The recovery was structural. Chaturanga split the description into a specification block rendered from the catalogue with no model involved, and a prose blurb generated at T = 0.9 instructed to reference only that block. Unsupported specifications fell to 0.5 per cent, or 2,400 listings; returns fell to 108 a month, costing ₹44,280, a saving of ₹5,31,360. Temperature ended up higher than the panic setting and the defect fell by more than ninety per cent, the most instructive fact in the case.

9. Failure modes, with their early warnings

Promising replay. The early warning is the word "deterministic" in a contract draft or security questionnaire. The diagnostic: if a customer disputes a message six months from now, do we retrieve it or regenerate it? Caught late, it is a breach found during an audit.

Tuning by anecdote. The early warning is a configuration change traceable to one screenshot in a chat channel. The diagnostic: how many samples were compared before and after? One draw says nothing about a distribution.

Unowned configuration. The early warning is that nobody present can state the current value from memory. The diagnostic is to ask for the value, the date it last changed and who approved it. Caught late, an unannounced change produces a regression nobody thinks to trace there.

Under-sampled evaluation. The early warning is a suite that runs each item once. Above zero, one run measures one draw, so a suite reporting 94 per cent may describe a system scoring between 88 and 98. The diagnostic is whether it reports variance.

10. Where experts genuinely disagree

The first disagreement is whether nondeterminism at T = 0 should be engineered away. One camp argues it can and should: batch-invariant kernels exist, the cost is a modest throughput penalty, and a provider offering bitwise reproducibility would win regulated business outright. It rests on the variation being a batching artefact rather than anything fundamental, and is wrong if the penalty is large enough that no provider will bear it. The other camp calls the demand misconceived: customers asking for bitwise identity almost always need retrievability, which an archive delivers more cheaply. It is wrong if regulators begin requiring regeneration rather than retrieval.

The second concerns whether temperature has a defensible optimum. The tuning camp points to measurable differences in human preference scores across settings and treats the dial as a product surface. The nuisance camp observes that an optimum found on one model version rarely transfers to the next, so teams re-tune after every upgrade without recovering the cost. It would be wrong if optima proved stable across generations, which they have not.

The third concerns what sampling does to a post-trained model. Alignment sharpens the output distribution, so 0.7 on an instruction-tuned model is a different intervention from 0.7 on a base model. One view holds that this makes published temperature advice worthless across model families; the other, that the qualitative direction survives. Public evidence is thin, and serious people hold both.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has internalised this starts from the guarantee, not the dial. Asked to make outputs consistent, they first ask which of four things is wanted: byte-identical text, the same decision, the same meaning, or a retrievable record of what was sent. Only the last is cheap and certain. They quote reproduction rates with an output length attached, treat a temperature value as configuration with an owner and a change log, and ask for the scored set when someone proposes lowering it to raise accuracy. And when a distribution genuinely matters — a confidence display, a routing decision, a safety gate — they read all of it, not the sampled token.

12. The decisions

On Wednesday 9 September 2026, twenty-two days after Restrepo's measurement, Ambekar made four commitments to Tridhara. Chikitsa would run configuration B for narrative text. The condition at discharge would become an enumerated field populated from the chart, removing the position at which stable and satisfactory competed. Every sent summary would be archived with its prompt, model version and settings. And the contract would say "retrievable" rather than "reproducible", a word Ambekar defended twice to Tridhara's lawyers. Her reasoning: the dial could narrow the distribution but guarantee neither sameness nor correctness, so both guarantees had to be built elsewhere.

On Friday 11 September 2026, eighteen days after the readout, Mahadevan shipped the warmer setting with two conditions. The child's name, age and any named real-world entity moved out of the sampled text into rendered slots, and moderation was funded for 92.25 hours a month. He declined to run it on the eight-and-under band until the flag rate there had been measured separately.

Three questions. Ambekar bought consistency by removing a choice from the model rather than reweighting it: where else in a product you know is a sampled decision being made that ought to be a rendered field? Configuration D costs 1.32 per cent of contract value and nearly halves the amendment rate: who may make that trade, and on what evidence? And Mahadevan accepted 2,460 more flagged stories a month for a 7.95 per cent relative retention gain: if the flag rate tripled again at the same gain, where would you stop?

13. Going deeper

What a large language model actually is supplies the object that produces the distribution, and tokens and tokenisation explains why the choice happens at sub-word level, which makes the compounding in Figure 2 inevitable. Inference versus training establishes that these settings change nothing about the model, and structured output and function calling is the direct sequel: it removes positions from the sampler entirely. Hallucination and confabulation explains why the favourite token can be fluent and false. The context window governs how much evidence shapes the logits; the transformer and attention explains where they come from. Embeddings and vector search and similarity determine what evidence reaches the prompt, which moves the distribution far more than any temperature change. Pre-training, post-training and fine-tuning and RLHF and alignment explain why the distribution arrives already sharpened, and so why a temperature suiting one family misleads on another.
case40v1-aivocab.sampling:
Hastakshar Systems: Clause 9.4

An ambiguous case for discussion. Pune, October 2026.

1. Sunday night, Baner

At a quarter past eleven on the night of Sunday 18 October 2026, Jahnavi Hardikar sat at the dining table of her flat in Baner, Pune, with three tabs open. The first was a nine-page audit note dated 22 September from the internal audit department of Hiranya Finance Services, Hastakshar's largest client. The second was a spreadsheet from Rashika Hegde in Hyderabad showing that the most accurate configuration of the product was also its least repeatable. The third was a slide titled Recommendation, empty under the heading.

At 9:30 the next morning, Monday 19 October, she would join a board sub-committee call to recommend how the company's credit-memo engine, Jaanch, should be configured. On Thursday 22 October the thirty-day cure period Hiranya had invoked under Clause 9.4 of the master services agreement would expire. Hiranya's festive lending peak ran from 19 October to 15 November, straddling Diwali on 8 November, and with it a change-control freeze: no production change could reach Hiranya's environment until 16 November.

The contract was worth ₹11.04 crore a year, 12.0 per cent of Hastakshar's FY26 revenue of ₹92 crore, and Hiranya was the reference client named in three bank tenders Jitendra Hiremath's team had to answer by 30 October. Jahnavi had written four options on paper and crossed out two of them twice. In February 2025 she had herself written “deterministic, reproducible output” into the Hiranya response document, on Rohan Jhaveri's assurance; the board has never been told.

2. The company, and a decision made in March 2025

Hastakshar Systems was founded in Pune in 2018 by Jyotsna Hattangadi, formerly a credit-risk head at a mid-sized NBFC, and Rohan Jhaveri, an engineer from a Bengaluru outsourcing firm. Its first product, which the team still called Jaanch 1, read a borrower's bank statements and GST returns and produced a structured set of figures — net monthly income, average balance, existing EMI obligations, turnover trend, bounce count — for the lender's policy engine. It was a rule-based parser with machine-learned classifiers around the edges: brittle on scans, slow to extend, entirely deterministic. The same file produced the same numbers in 2019 and in 2023.

By 2024 lenders wanted the memo, not the fields. In November 2024 Hastakshar rebuilt the product around a hosted large language model from an American vendor. Jaanch 3 read the whole bundle, produced twelve structured fields, then wrote eight to twelve sentences referring to them. Underwriting time at pilot clients fell from about 40 minutes a file to about 11. The rule engine was retired during 2025 and nobody has maintained the parser since March 2026.

The decision that shaped October 2026 was taken on 15 March 2025, when Hastakshar signed its master services agreement with Hiranya Finance Services, a Mumbai lender with a book across personal loans, loan against property and MSME working capital. Hiranya's legal team, advised by an auditor preparing it for Reserve Bank of India scrutiny, inserted Clause 9.4 — “Outputs of the Service shall be reproducible. Re-processing of an identical input bundle shall yield identical extracted field values and identical memo text. The Supplier shall retain for seven years the capability to reproduce any memo furnished under this Agreement.”

Rohan read it, set temperature to zero and signed off: zero makes the model pick its highest-probability token at every step, so output is deterministic and the clause is satisfied by construction. Clause 11.2, from Hiranya's information-security team, required that borrower data be processed within India, so Hastakshar deployed against the vendor's Mumbai region. Both clauses were accepted that afternoon, by different people, and nobody has read them beside each other since.

3. The industry

Lending technology in India in 2026 was crowded and heavily supervised. The Account Aggregator framework, with Sahamati as its industry body, had made consented bank-statement data cheap to fetch; the GST Network made turnover verifiable; TransUnion CIBIL supplied scores. Perfios, Signzy and Yubi had built businesses on parts of the stack, and lenders such as Bajaj Finance and HDFC Bank ran in-house teams. Hastakshar's claim was narrower: it did not score the borrower, it wrote the memo.

The RBI's digital lending guidelines and its directions on outsourcing of IT services oblige a regulated entity to remain accountable for decisions taken with a vendor's software and to produce, on demand, the basis of any credit decision; the Digital Personal Data Protection Act added the obligations Hiranya turned into Clause 11.2. None of these instruments mentions sampling, temperature or model versions. Their language is about records and reproducibility — words auditors had applied to deterministic systems for thirty years without rewriting them for systems that draw from a probability distribution.

Exposure was not only Indian. In January 2026 Hastakshar signed Jawhara Finance House LLC of Muscat, a ₹1.2 crore a year contract with go-live in December 2026, requiring memos in Arabic and English and an explanation trail acceptable to the Central Bank of Oman. Rehema Juma, customer success lead, worked from Nairobi; Joost Haverkamp, the only staff inference engineer, from Amsterdam.

4. What happened, and what has turned out to be wrong

Jaanch 3 went live at Hiranya on 1 May 2025 and by mid-2026 was producing about 46,000 memos a month there, just over a quarter of Hastakshar's platform volume of 1,80,000 memos a month. Hiranya paid ₹200 a memo; across the book, usage fees of ₹41.4 crore in FY26 on 21,60,000 memos came to about ₹192 a memo, licences and other modules making up the remaining ₹50.6 crore. For fourteen months nobody raised reproducibility.

Then, in order. On Wednesday 22 July 2026 the vendor moved its Mumbai-region endpoint to the next minor model version; the change appeared in a changelog, no notice was due, and nobody at Hastakshar registered it. On 1 September Harpreet Jaggi, Hiranya's chief information officer, said the RBI had indicated an inspection window and internal audit would test the vendor chain first. On Monday 14 September the audit team drew 300 memos produced between 2 June and 31 August, re-submitted them and compared output byte for byte. Exhibit 1 is their result: in 34 of the 300 cases, 11.3 per cent, at least one of the twelve figures differed; in 70 cases, 23.3 per cent, the memo text differed. The note of 22 September found the service “not reproducible within the meaning of Clause 9.4” and gave thirty days to cure.

Rohan's response on 23 September was that the test must be wrong, because temperature had been zero since 2025. Joost, joining from Amsterdam at the end of his day, said two things the minutes record and nobody followed up. First, zero does not make a hosted endpoint deterministic: the sampler takes the highest-probability token, but on shared accelerators the arithmetic producing those probabilities depends on how requests are batched, and where two candidates are nearly tied a difference in the twelfth decimal place can flip which is highest. Second, a version change makes the question moot, because the probabilities themselves are different.

Rashika's team then ran two studies. The first, on 26 September, measured accuracy rather than repeatability: 480 bundles with human-verified values for all twelve fields, 5,760 field values, under five configurations. Greedy decoding at temperature zero got 5,472 of 5,760 fields right, 95.0 per cent. Five samples at temperature 0.7, majority value per field, got 5,587 right, 97.0 per cent — 115 fewer wrong fields, 39.9 per cent of greedy's errors. Nine samples got 5,616 right, 97.5 per cent, exactly half the errors of greedy. The configuration Hiranya's auditor would most readily accept was the least accurate available, and the most accurate drew its answers at random.

The second study, on 29 September, re-ran 200 bundles five times each at temperature zero against one pinned endpoint within a single hour: 1,000 runs. Six, 0.6 per cent, differed in at least one figure; 41, 4.1 per cent, differed in memo text, and Exhibit 2 shows the failures rising with bundle length. The gap between Exhibit 1 and Exhibit 2 — 11.3 per cent against 0.6 per cent — is the most-argued number in the company. Splitting the audit sample by date narrows it: memos produced before 22 July failed at 16.7 per cent, those produced after it at 4.5 per cent. The version change explains most of the audit finding; nothing in evidence explains the remainder.

Exhibit 6, from Hiranya's workbench, shows underwriters logging 1,784 figure corrections across 1,81,500 memos reviewed between June and September, 9.8 per 1,000 memos. If 5.0 per cent of all twelve fields are wrong, the expected rate is 600 per 1,000; counting only the three fields underwriters must verify, on which Jaanch scored 99.1 per cent, it is 27.1 per 1,000. Either the benchmark is harsher than production, or underwriters are not catching what it catches, or not logging what they catch.

5. The people

Jahnavi Hardikar, 34, director of product, Pune. Position: stop arguing about temperature and decide what the company is promising. Incentive: a product line that must pass an audit and win three tenders in one month.

Rohan Jhaveri, co-founder and chief technology officer, Bengaluru. Position: a version-control problem, not a sampling problem — pin the version, keep temperature at zero, Clause 9.4 holds. Incentive: a Series C in which gross margin, 68.0 per cent in FY26, is the headline metric; five-sample voting takes it to 66.3 per cent, nine-sample to 64.7 per cent. Not saying: on 4 September he told Harpreet the pipeline was “deterministic end to end”.

Rashika Hegde, head of applied machine learning, Hyderabad. Position: the five-sample vote should ship, the only change that measurably reduces wrong numbers reaching an underwriter. Incentive: a team of nine whose value is easiest to show through accuracy. Not saying: 192 of the 480 benchmark bundles were labelled from a Jaanch memo, and she does not know which way that cuts.

Joost Haverkamp, staff inference engineer, Amsterdam. Position: only self-hosting an open-weights model with a fixed seed and fixed batch configuration can make the word “identical” honest, and then only while the serving stack is unchanged. Incentive: a two-year argument for owning inference. Not saying: his ten-week estimate assumes he does nothing else, and he has interviewed twice this quarter.

Hiren Rathod, head of risk and compliance, Mumbai. Position: reproducibility is the wrong control — an auditor needs the retained artefact, the bundle, version, settings and exact output stored immutably. Incentive: avoiding an inspection finding that names Hastakshar. Not saying: he has not asked whether the auditor would accept artefact retention, because asking would reveal that Hastakshar cannot re-run.

Jitendra Hiremath, vice-president of enterprise sales, Gurugram. Position: nothing changes before 30 October, because three tenders worth ₹14 crore of annual recurring revenue cite Hiranya and ask whether outputs are “auditable and repeatable”. Incentive: a quota closing in March. Not saying: in two responses he has already written that outputs are “deterministic, and therefore verifiable and accurate”.

Rehema Juma, customer success lead, Nairobi. Position: memo quality, not byte-identity, is what underwriters notice — in a blind comparison of 40 memos rated by eight Jawhara underwriters, the sampled version scored 4.3 out of 5 against 3.6 for greedy; her underwriters read memos and never re-run them. Incentive: a December go-live in Muscat. Not saying: each rated only five memos, and Pune has not been told.

Harpreet Jaggi, chief information officer, Hiranya, Mumbai. Position, in writing: Clause 9.4 means what it says. Incentive: an inspection at which he would rather show a vendor defect than a gap of his own. Not saying: his audit team added a quality-control incentive for underwriters in August 2026, which may be why logged corrections rose from 7.7 per 1,000 memos in July to 13.3 in September.

6. Exhibits

7. Voices

“Temperature is zero. Zero means the top token, every time. If the audit got two different answers, somebody changed something underneath us. That is a procurement problem.”

Rohan Jhaveri, engineering call, 23 September

“Zero means you always take the most likely next token. It does not mean the most likely token is always the same token, because the numbers that decide ‘most likely’ are computed in a batch with other people's requests, and on a 50,000-token bundle there are thousands of near-ties. Nothing about zero makes the top token correct. We have been selling the wrong property of the wrong dial.”

Joost Haverkamp, same thread, 19:10 CEST

“Look at Exhibit 3 before we spend ten weeks making a worse model repeatable. Five samples and a vote removes 115 wrong fields out of 288, and nobody here has put a rupee value on that.”

Rashika Hegde, email to Jahnavi, 27 September

“115 fields on a benchmark where two-fifths of the labels were corrected versions of our own output. I would not put that in front of an auditor.”

Hiren Rathod, comment on the same email

“Clause 9.4 is there because my auditor asked how I would answer the RBI if a borrower disputes a memo. If your answer is that you kept the file, the version and the settings and can show exactly what was produced, put that in writing and let me take it to him. Do not tell me again that it is deterministic.”

Harpreet Jaggi, call with Jahnavi, 14 October

8. The options as Jahnavi sees them

Option one: pin the version, keep temperature at zero. Rohan's proposal. The vendor offers version pinning and reduced batching variance on a dedicated tier at a minimum of ₹2.6 crore a year, about two and a half times today's ₹1.03 crore of token spend. Accuracy stays at 95.0 per cent. The difficulty, which surfaced only on 12 October, is that pinning is offered in the vendor's United States and European regions, not in Mumbai, which runs rolling versions: honouring Clause 9.4 this way would breach Clause 11.2.

Option two: ship the five-sample vote and renegotiate the clause. Rashika's proposal. Field accuracy rises to 97.0 per cent, cost by ₹12,83,040 a month, ₹1.54 crore a year, taking gross margin from 68.0 per cent to 66.3 per cent; p95 latency of 26.1 seconds stays inside the 30-second ceiling. Memo text becomes irreproducible in principle: Exhibit 5 puts text reproduction at 7.8 per cent. Clause 9.4 would have to be rewritten to cover figures only, and even then 96.4 per cent is not “identical”. Jahnavi would be asking Harpreet, three days before the cure expires, to weaken his auditor's clause.

Option three: self-host an open-weights model. Joost's proposal. A fixed seed and pinned batch configuration delivered 100.0 per cent figure reproduction and 99.8 per cent text reproduction on the test cluster, in India, satisfying both clauses literally. Field accuracy falls to 90.0 per cent — 576 wrong fields against 288 today — and the migration is estimated at ten weeks, landing after 30 October and after 16 November.

Option four: split the memo. Rehema's instinct, and increasingly Jahnavi's. Generate the twelve figures one way and the prose another: a five-sample vote on the short structured extraction, where sampling is cheap and the vote is auditable, and a greedy pass for the narrative. Nobody has costed it, or tested whether prose generated from voted figures reproduces at all.

Jyotsna Hattangadi's note for Monday asks for one sentence the company can defend in an inspection, not four engineering options. Each option above answers the question “what temperature and sampling scheme should Jaanch use?”, and it is not obvious that this is the question. Hiren's point — that an auditor wants a retained artefact, not a re-runnable one — would dissolve Clause 9.4 without touching an inference setting, if the auditor accepted it. Exhibit 3 says nine of the twelve fields are the weak ones, and those nine are what the retired Jaanch 1 parser read deterministically at 97.8 per cent. And Exhibit 6, read sceptically, raises the possibility that the production error rate is far below 5.0 per cent — in which case option two rests on a benchmark that does not describe production.

9. The deadline and the hard constraints

The cure period expires on Thursday 22 October. Hiranya's freeze runs from 19 October to 15 November, so no code change reaches its production environment before 16 November; only a contractual or documentary response is available this week. The three tenders close on 30 October, asking whether outputs are repeatable and auditable, and Jawhara's Muscat go-live is in December.

Money: inference at the current configuration costs ₹1.03 crore a year against FY26 revenue of ₹92 crore; the five-sample vote adds ₹1.54 crore a year, the nine-sample vote ₹3.08 crore. Reserved self-hosted capacity costs ₹1.90 crore a year whether volume arrives or not; the dedicated tier ₹2.6 crore. Hastakshar has ₹38 crore of cash and a Series C in which gross margin is read first.

People: Joost is one person in Amsterdam, and his estimate assumes he does nothing else for ten weeks. The four engineers who understood the Jaanch 1 parser moved on in March 2026 and two have left. Rashika's nine are on the Arabic model until end-November.

Regulation and contract: Clause 9.4 requires identical outputs on re-processing and a seven-year capability to reproduce; Clause 11.2 requires in-country processing. The RBI's outsourcing directions make Hiranya accountable for Jaanch's output whatever the contract says. Termination under Clause 9.4 carries ninety days' notice and would remove ₹11.04 crore of ₹92 crore of revenue.

10. Questions for discussion

  1. What does setting temperature to zero do to the output, and what does it leave untouched? Using Exhibit 2, explain why 6 of 1,000 re-runs differed at all, and why the failures concentrate in the longest bundles.
  2. Rohan's position rests on two claims: that zero makes output identical, and that it makes output correct. Which exhibits bear on each, and what would you need to measure before accepting either?
  3. Exhibit 1 reports 11.3 per cent figure mismatch, Exhibit 2 reports 0.6 per cent. Reconcile them as far as the evidence allows and state what remains unexplained. Which would you put in front of Hiranya's auditor?
  4. Exhibit 3 says the most accurate configuration samples at temperature 0.7; Exhibit 6 implies a far lower error rate. If you believe Exhibit 6, what happens to the case for sampling? If you believe Exhibit 3, what happens to the case for Clause 9.4?
  5. Clause 9.4 asks for reproducibility, Clause 11.2 for localisation, and no configuration delivers both with the best accuracy. Which would you give up, who pays for it, and what would you have done differently in March 2025?
  6. It is 9:30 on Monday 19 October. What do you do, in order — what do you say to Harpreet Jaggi before Thursday, what goes into the tender responses by 30 October, and what single sentence do you give the board describing what Jaanch's output can be relied upon to be?

At half past midnight Jahnavi closed the audit note and picked up the sheet of paper. Two options were crossed out twice; the other two she had not been able to cross out at all. At the bottom she wrote what are we actually promising?, and under it figures or words?, and capped the pen. The board call was in nine hours. The slide was still empty.
case20v1-aivocab.sampling:
Pallav Payments Network: The Zero Setting

A decision case on temperature and sampling

1. Opening

On Monday 12 October 2026, Meghna Pillai sat in a glass-walled meeting room on the fourth floor of Pallav Payments Network's Pune office, with two printouts in front of her and a deadline on her calendar. On Thursday 15 October she would tell the leadership team how the company's new merchant assistant should be configured for the Diwali season. Engineering needed her answer by then, because the code freeze was set for Monday 26 October, and Diwali fell on Sunday 8 November.

The first was a message from Gautam Pandey, her engineering lead in Bengaluru: "Set temperature to zero. Same question, same answer, problem closed." The second was a spreadsheet from the data scientist in London that suggested the problem was not closed at all. Meghna, vice-president of product, had to decide what the assistant would promise merchants, and she had three days to decide it.

2. Company Background

Pallav Payments Network, founded in Pune in 2017, supplies UPI QR codes, voice soundboxes and a settlement app to small merchants: tea stalls, pharmacies, kirana stores, salons. It serves about 6,20,000 active merchants and reported revenue of ₹312 crore for FY26. Its founders modelled the business on the pattern that PhonePe and Paytm had proved, namely cheap hardware, free UPI acceptance and money made on lending, insurance and value-added services. Its edge was service in Hindi, Marathi, Tamil and Kannada.

The regulatory ground was firm. NPCI governs UPI flows, and the RBI's payment aggregator rules and grievance-redress expectations require that a merchant who disputes a deduction receives an accurate, traceable response. Razorpay, PhonePe and Paytm each offered merchants chat help, and Pallav's founders believed a better assistant could cut support cost.

In June 2026 Pallav launched the assistant, built on a hosted large language model, inside the settlement app. Merchants could ask why a payout was short, or what the fee was on a ₹1,500 card payment. The assistant read the merchant's ledger through an internal service, then composed an answer.

3. The Situation

Within weeks, Prakash Mehta's support team in Chennai noticed a pattern. Merchants pasted screenshots of two different answers to the same question, asked minutes apart, and demanded to know which one was true. Agents could not tell. Escalations to human agents, which cost Pallav ₹38 each, ran at 14 per cent of the assistant's fee and settlement queries.

Gautam's diagnosis was that the model was "random". The vendor's default temperature, which Pallav had left untouched, was 0.8. His reasoning was that temperature zero would remove the randomness, make every answer repeatable, and, he added, make wrong answers unlikely, since the model would always pick its best choice.

Gayatri Menon, the data scientist in London, who worked four and a half hours behind Pune until the clocks changed on 25 October, tested the claim. During the week of 5 October she took the 40 hardest fee and settlement questions from the support logs and ran each one ten times at three settings, 400 runs per setting. Her results appear in Exhibit 1 and Exhibit 3.

The mechanism behind her result is simple. A language model does not retrieve an answer. At each step it produces a probability distribution over possible next tokens, which are word fragments, and a sampling step picks one. Temperature reshapes that distribution. At a high setting, less likely tokens get more weight, so wording varies. At zero, the sampler always takes the single most probable token. That makes the output close to repeatable, but only close: the hosted service batches requests on shared hardware, and tiny numerical differences can flip a near-tie. It also cannot make the most probable token correct: a wrong top choice is wrong every time. Temperature is an inference-time setting; it changes nothing the model has learned.

4. The People

Gautam Pandey, engineering lead, Bengaluru, wants a quick, shippable fix before the freeze.

Gayatri Menon, data scientist, London, wants the team to measure before it promises. She is worried that "deterministic" will end up in a merchant-facing message and then in a complaint to the RBI's ombudsman.

Prakash Mehta, head of merchant support, Chennai, wants fewer contradictory screenshots and fewer escalations during the festival peak, when his agents work double shifts.

Preeti Gokhale, head of compliance, Mumbai, wants every figure the assistant quotes to be traceable to a ledger line, and wants to avoid a published claim that Pallav's assistant is "always accurate".

6. The Options

Option A: set temperature to zero for everything and say so. It takes an afternoon of work and gives Gautam the repeatability he wants. Its cost is the ₹37,80,000 of monthly dispute cost from confidently repeated wrong figures, and the risk of calling the answers "consistent and accurate" when only the first is largely true.

Option B: keep 0.8 and add a disclaimer. Nothing needs building, and the conversational tone suits merchants who write in Hinglish. The cost is the highest figure in Exhibit 2.

Option C: split the assistant by task. Questions that quote money (fees, payouts, settlement dates) would call the ledger service for the figures, run at a low temperature of about 0.2, and show the ledger line they used. Explanatory and drafting replies, such as a polite note about a delayed payout, could keep a higher setting. Output for figure-bearing replies would be validated against the ledger before display. It costs ₹18,00,000 of one-time engineering, a harness that reruns the 40 questions on every change, and a hold on the Diwali launch of one new feature. Its upside is the lowest monthly total in Exhibit 2.

7. Questions for Discussion

1. Using Exhibit 1, what does a temperature of zero change, and what does it leave unchanged? Why can 24 of 400 runs differ at zero?

2. Gautam says wrong answers become unlikely at zero. Which row of Exhibit 1 contradicts him, and why does consistency make some errors worse for support?

3. In Exhibit 2, which cost lines does temperature move, and which does it not? What does the ledger lookup in Option C do that no sampling setting can?

4. Which option would you take to Thursday's meeting, and what would you tell merchants and Preeti's compliance team the assistant guarantees?

8. A Note for the Learner

The lens. A model outputs a probability distribution, and sampling picks a token from it, one token at a time. Temperature controls how much weight less likely tokens get. It is an inference-time dial, not a quality dial. Two common beliefs fail the test in this case: that zero guarantees identical outputs (here 94.0 per cent matched, not 100), and that zero removes wrong answers (here 7.5 per cent of runs were wrong, some of them every time).

One defensible path: Option C, in its smallest form. Use a low temperature for figure-bearing answers because repeatability is a genuine benefit when the same merchant asks twice, and keep wording flexibility where nothing is at stake. But rely on grounding in the ledger, not on temperature, for accuracy. The numbers support this: moving from B to C saves ₹58,39,200 a month, and against Option A it saves ₹27,02,400 a month, repaying the ₹18,00,000 build in under a month.

Reasoning and caveats. Option C's rates are estimates from one week, so Meghna should present them as a range, ship the ledger-grounded path for fee and settlement queries first, with the harness as the release gate before the 26 October freeze. She should instruct that merchant-facing language promise "figures taken from your settlement ledger" rather than "always accurate", which satisfies Preeti. Option A is defensible only as a disclosed stopgap; Option B fails on cost and trust.
exp40v2-aivocab.rag.architecture:
Retrieval-Augmented Generation as an Architecture

A two-stage system, an identity that decomposes its quality, and why "we added RAG" answers none of the questions a manager needs answered

1. Two decisions, five weeks apart

On Monday 7 September 2026, nine weeks to the day after the pilot opened on Monday 6 July, Pallavi Bhatkande sat with a tabulation she had twice requested. She is vice-president of product at Bhandaar Exchange, a Pune marketplace for industrial spare parts: 3,100 sellers, 47,000 buying organisations, ₹1,860 crore of gross merchandise value in the year to March 2026 at a 4.2 per cent take rate, or ₹78.12 crore of revenue. Its pilot, Bhandaar Assist, is a fitment adviser: an engineer names a machine and a part, and it says whether the part fits.

The tabulation covered 400 questions from real buyer chats, each with an answer verified by Bhandaar's parts desk; the assistant got 240 right, 60.0 per cent. Commercial wanted general release on Thursday 1 October, before the festive peak. Bhairavi Pethe, who runs catalogue operations, noted that orders following an assistant answer drew "does not fit" returns 5.4 per cent against 2.1 per cent after a parts-desk chat. Prasoon Bandodkar, the search lead, wanted budget for a larger model.

In Rajkot, Prachi Balsekar closed a different pilot on Monday 3 August, ninety-one days after it opened on Monday 4 May. She directs digital services at Pinaak Industries, which builds packaging machinery: ₹640 crore of FY26 revenue, of which ₹96 crore — 15.0 per cent — is service contracts across 6,800 installed machines. Pinaak Assist runs on a technician's phone over 2,900 manuals, 41,000 fault-code entries and twelve years of field reports.

Her tabulation was stranger. Across 250 verified technician questions, retrieval put a passage containing the correct answer before the model 220 times — 88.0 per cent, a figure any search team would like — yet only 165 answers were right: 66.0 per cent. Balwant Padhye, head of service, put it plainly: the assistant had told a technician in Vadodara to torque a clamp to a revision that plant never owned. Both products "used RAG"; the phrase told neither manager anything actionable.

2. The idea, and the schools that disagree about it

A large language model generates text by predicting continuations from patterns learned in training, and consults nothing at inference time. So it cannot know Bhandaar's catalogue or Pinaak's service bulletins, and the context window — the span of text, in tokens, a model reads in one request — is finite. Bhandaar's corpus is 11,400 OEM manuals averaging 20,000 tokens, or 22.8 crore tokens, plus 8,60,000 listings averaging 120 tokens, or 10.32 crore: 33.12 crore in all, 1,656 times a 200,000-token window.

Retrieval-augmented generation answers both constraints in two stages. Stage one searches the corpus for relevant passages; stage two places them in the window beside the question and instructs the model to answer from them. Nothing about generation changes; only the contents of the window differ.

The lineage explains the confusion. The name comes from a 2020 paper by Patrick Lewis and colleagues at Facebook AI Research, University College London and New York University; REALM and Dense Passage Retrieval, its contemporaries, shared the premise that a parametric model should consult a non-parametric store. The retrieval half is older still: the probabilistic ranking work of Stephen Robertson and Karen Spärck Jones, and van Rijsbergen's cluster hypothesis, are 1970s scholarship. After 2023 the acronym came to mean any pipeline where a vector database returns top-k chunks pasted into a prompt — Pallavi's problem, because a wiring diagram has no quality level.

Four schools disagree about what follows. The retrieval-first school holds that RAG quality is information-retrieval quality, and would sign that most production failures are ordinary search failures, addressable with hybrid lexical-plus-dense matching, rerankers and metadata filters; it would not sign that retrieval quality alone bounds answer quality, which Prachi's 88.0 per cent recall against 66.0 per cent accuracy refutes. The long-context school holds retrieval to be a cost optimisation that falling token prices will erode; it would sign that any retrieval step is a lossy filter, and not that the filter is free of judgement. The agentic school rejects single-shot top-k retrieval: the model should query, read and re-query. The structured-data school makes the sharpest anti-RAG case — where the answer lives in a relation rather than a passage, a query interface beats any retriever — but would not sign that structured interfaces cover the tacit knowledge in service bulletins.

3. Mechanics, and the identity that decomposes them

Build time is where practitioners leave most implicit. Documents are cut into chunks — Bhandaar used 400 tokens with 20 per cent overlap, a stride of 320, giving 7,12,500 chunks from the manuals plus one per listing, 15,72,500 in all. Embedding all 38.82 crore tokens at ₹12 per million costs ₹4,658. Indexing is nearly free; the expensive part is judgement about what belongs in the corpus and what supersedes what.

The formal treatment is one decomposition. Define recall@k as the share of questions for which at least one retrieved passage contains the verified answer, a as accuracy given that, and b as accuracy when it has not happened. Then accuracy = R·a + (1−R)·b. At Bhandaar, R was 300 of 400, or 75.0 per cent, and a was 240 of 300, or 80.0 per cent; a fitment question cannot be answered from general knowledge, so b was effectively zero. The identity gives 0.75 × 0.80 = 60.0 per cent, exactly what the tabulation said.

The obvious lever is k. Bhandaar measured three settings at ₹180 per million input tokens and ₹720 per million output, with 500 tokens of instructions, a 60-token question, a 260-token answer and 3,20,000 questions a month.

Here is the second-order effect that separates people who have run one of these from people who have read about them: a is not a constant. It fell from 85.0 to 80.0 to 75.0 per cent as k rose, because every extra passage is one the model must ignore. Had a held at 85.0 per cent, k = 8 would have delivered 0.75 × 0.85 = 63.75 per cent rather than 60.00, and k = 16 would have given 70.55 rather than 62.25. Those gaps — 3.75 and 8.30 points — are the distraction cost.

The marginal arithmetic settles it. Moving from k = 8 to k = 16 costs ₹4,60,800 − ₹2,76,480 = ₹1,84,320 a month for 2.25 points of accuracy, which across 3,20,000 questions is 7,200 additional correct answers: ₹25.60 each. From k = 4 to k = 8 costs ₹92,160 for 15,200 more, ₹6.06 each. The lever works, then stops, and never touches the 26 corpus-hygiene failures.

4. When the architecture applies, and when it misleads

Four conditions state as testable claims. First: the answer exists in a corpus you control, as text a person could point to. At Bhandaar that holds for manual-derived fitment rules and fails for the tacit knowledge in a parts-desk agent's head; at Pinaak it holds for 2,900 manuals and fails for the eight machine families never digitised, eight of Prachi's thirty retrieval misses. Second: the question can be turned into a query that finds that text — where both pilots broke. Third: the corpus is governed. Fourth: a passage is the right shape for the answer. That last is where the structured-data school draws blood: "does this bearing fit a 2019 Pinaak PX-40" is a lookup against a relation, and dressing it as semantic search is an architectural error, not a tuning problem.

It actively misleads in three situations. When the question requires aggregation — "how many of our 8,60,000 listings are duplicates" — retrieval returns eight passages and the model confabulates a count. When the corpus holds the disagreement rather than the answer, as with two conflicting service bulletins, retrieval supplies both and the model averages them; seven of Prachi's failures were this. And when no answer exists, retrieval still returns its k nearest neighbours, so the default posture is to answer. Abstention must be engineered.

5. Hard edges and organisational seams

Bhandaar is two-sided, which moves the ownership of quality. The corpus is written by 3,100 sellers with no shared schema, in English, Hindi and Gujarati, with part numbers rendered six ways. Bhandaar cannot instruct sellers to write better, only normalise, dedupe and tag afterwards. On a marketplace, retrieval quality is a supply-operations problem in an engineering costume.

Pinaak is hardware plus software, and its edge is versioning. One model number exists in seven hardware revisions whose manual passages are near-identical prose. Embedding similarity is the wrong instrument for telling them apart, because they are semantically similar. The fix is not a better embedder but a filter applied before ranking, restricting candidates to the revision implied by the serial number.

Regulation adds its own seam. Bhaav Services, a Mumbai discount broker, could not let its research assistant summarise a note into anything a SEBI-registered adviser would call personalised advice, so the retrieval layer became the compliance boundary, filtering by document class before ranking. Under the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, a retriever that can see a document a user may not is a disclosure waiting to happen. Firms say the assistant "respects permissions"; what works is running retrieval under the user's identity.

6. Eight things experts see that competent practitioners miss

The word names a pipeline, not a quality level. The tell is a roadmap line reading "add RAG" with a completion date. Two RAG systems differ as much as two search engines; nothing in the acronym constrains chunking, ranking, freshness or abstention. The obvious reading — that using your documents means grounded — is wrong: grounding is a claim that the answer follows from the passages, which no architecture guarantees.

Recall must be defined against the answer, not the document. The tell is a team quoting retrieval above 90 per cent while accuracy sits near 70. Whether a chunk from the right chapter was retrieved is easy to measure and nearly useless; whether it contains the verified answer span is laborious and decisive. The two can differ by thirty points.

The model's own knowledge hides retrieval failure. The term b is rarely zero outside narrow domains: in a general-knowledge product the model answers correctly from training even when retrieval brings nothing, so accuracy flatters a broken retriever. Run the test set with retrieval off; whatever it still gets right is b, and invisible to your retrieval evaluation.

Similarity is the wrong tool for identity. Dense embeddings encode meaning, but part numbers, clause references and revision letters are identifiers: two that differ by one character mean different things while embedding to nearly the same place. The tell is failures clustered on questions containing codes. The fix is lexical matching alongside dense, and metadata filters before ranking.

Conditional accuracy decays with k. The tell is a team that raised k, saw recall improve, and saw accuracy improve less. Passages compete for attention, and position matters — the finding called "lost in the middle" is that material in the centre of a long input is used less reliably than material at either end. Reranking usually beats retrieving more.

Chunk boundaries are a product decision. Fixed-length windows are chosen by infrastructure teams because they are trivial. But a chunk that severs a worked solution from its problem statement, or a torque table from the revision heading above it, destroys the answer before retrieval runs. The tell is passages that are topically right and informationally incomplete.

The corpus is a product surface with a lifecycle. Retrieval returns what the corpus says, including what it said two years ago. Nothing in a vector index knows a wording was superseded unless someone recorded effective dates and retired the predecessor. The tell is answers that were correct last year. That is an operations role, and in most companies nobody holds it.

Citations show provenance, not faithfulness, and refusal is a tunable. A citation says which passage was supplied, not that the sentence above it follows from it; the tell is a reviewer who checks that citations exist rather than that they support. And a system that answers everything trades a known escalation cost for an unknown wrong-answer cost. At Bodhini Learning Network, an exam-preparation service in Indore, 2,40,000 doubts arrive monthly; the assistant attempts 2,04,000, or 85.0 per cent, escalating 36,000 — 15.0 per cent — to tutors. That 85 is a chosen point on a curve.

7. How it differs by product type and stage

In consumer products the corpus is often public, b is large, latency is felt, and errors are cheap individually and expensive in aggregate. In enterprise and B2B the corpus is private, b is near zero, permissions are load-bearing, and one wrong answer can become a contractual dispute — which is why Bhandaar's abstention threshold should sit higher than Bodhini's. On platforms and marketplaces the corpus comes from third parties, so normalisation and deduplication dominate. In hardware plus software, versioning and offline operation dominate: Pinaak technicians work in plants with no connectivity, which forces a cached subset of the index onto the device and turns freshness into a synchronisation problem.

Where the difference is not real it is worth saying so. The identity holds everywhere, as does the decomposition into search, corpus, window and generation, and the finding that most failures are search failures; only the values differ. In an AI-native product the difference is ambition rather than kind: retrieval becomes a tool the model calls, several times, making cost and latency variable per question. Stage changes what is affordable, not what is true. A seed-stage team can hand-verify 200 questions in a week and should. A company at Bhandaar's scale has the opposite problem — several teams, several corpora, no owner of freshness — and the seam is where quality goes.

8. Three worked outcomes

Bhandaar: the cheap fix beat the expensive one. Rather than raise k, Prasoon added lexical matching for part numbers alongside dense retrieval and re-ran the 400 questions at k = 8. Recall rose from 300 to 345 — 86.25 per cent — with conditional accuracy unchanged at 80.0 per cent: 276 correct, or 69.0 per cent, at the same ₹2,76,480 a month. Bhairavi then retired 1,12,000 superseded and duplicate listings, 13.0 per cent of the catalogue, leaving 7,48,000 active and 14,60,500 chunks. A third run returned recall of 350, conditional accuracy of 84.0 per cent, and 294 correct: 73.5 per cent. Nine points came from search, four and a half from housekeeping.

Table 3. Correct answers are recall × a: 300 × 0.80 = 240, 345 × 0.80 = 276, 350 × 0.84 = 294. Inference cost stayed ₹2,76,480 a month.

Pinaak: filtering beat ranking. Purnima Bhide's team tagged all 96,000 chunks with model and revision. Path rules covered 84,000; the other 12,000 took 2.5 minutes each of adjudication — 500 hours at ₹900, or ₹4,50,000. Retrieval then ran only over chunks matching the serial number's revision. Across the same 250 questions, recall rose from 220 to 225 — 90.0 per cent — and conditional accuracy from 75.0 to 88.0 per cent: 198 correct, 79.2 per cent, up from 66.0. Revision mismatches fell from 39 to 6. Repeat visits on 1,200 quarterly service calls fell from 22.0 to 17.5 per cent, 264 to 210; at ₹18,400 an avoidable visit that is ₹9,93,600 a quarter, or ₹39,74,400 a year, against a one-time ₹4,50,000 — recovered in about six weeks.

Bodhini: five months on the wrong half. Bodhini's doubt solver serves 7,40,000 monthly learners. Its dashboard reported recall of 92 per cent and accuracy of 71.0 per cent — 355 of a 500-question audit — so the team judged the model to be the constraint and spent ₹38 lakh over five months on fine-tuning. Accuracy did not move. The error was definitional: recall had been scored as "a chunk from the correct chapter was retrieved". Re-scored as "a chunk containing the verified answer", it was 320 of 500, or 64.0 per cent. Of those 320 the assistant answered 284 correctly, so a was 88.75 per cent; of the 180 it missed it still answered 71 correctly from training, so b was 39.4 per cent. The identity reproduces the audit: 284 + 71 = 355, or 71.0 per cent. A large b had concealed a broken retriever.
