Teaching case · AI & Data Products

Ishara Works: Teaching the Model Our Business

1. Opening

On Tuesday, 6 October 2026, Indrani Chitale carried a printed results sheet into a glass-walled meeting room on the fourth floor of Ishara Works' office in Baner, Pune. As vice president of product, she had until Friday, 16 October to tell her chief executive and the board how the company's insurance-support assistant would be built for its largest client. The client wanted the new version live by 3 November, five days before Diwali, when enquiries rise.

The chief executive, Lokanath Pattanaik, had already voiced his preference in the corridor. “We have six thousand policy documents,” he had said. “Let us fine-tune the model on them, so it simply knows our business. Then nobody can copy us by pasting a PDF into a prompt.” The sheet in Indrani's hand suggested otherwise.

2. Company background

Ishara Works, founded in 2019, sells a support copilot to health-insurance brokers and third-party administrators. A customer-service agent types or speaks a policyholder's question, and the copilot drafts a reply in the broker's house format, citing the relevant clause. Forty-one clients use it, and annual recurring revenue stands at ₹38 crore. It handles about 3,00,000 queries a month.

The market is crowded at both ends. Insurers such as Star Health and aggregators such as Policybazaar run large service desks. Freshworks and Zoho sell general helpdesk tools with an AI layer. Ishara's defence is depth: it knows the vocabulary of waiting periods, sub-limits, room-rent caps and cashless pre-authorisation. Its replies follow IRDAI rules and handle personal data under the Digital Personal Data Protection Act.

Until now the product has run on a hosted general-purpose model, steered by a long set of written instructions.

3. The situation

Mahanagar Health Brokers, Ishara's biggest client, accounts for ₹2.4 crore of annual revenue and is up for renewal. Its operations head wants the copilot to answer in a strict six-part template, refuse to give medical advice and quote the correct clause.

Indrani asked Bartosz Wrona, the data scientist in Warsaw, to test the options on a held-out set of 400 questions from real tickets, plus a separate set of 40 questions about clauses that Mahanagar had amended during the pilot. Bartosz opened his write-up with a vocabulary correction. Pre-training, he wrote, is how a model such as the one Ishara rents learned language, from a vast corpus. Post-training is how its maker then shaped its manners, style and refusals on curated examples. Fine-tuning is Ishara's own, much smaller adaptation of a model that has already been through both. All three adjust the weights of the same network. What they change is different: fine-tuning moves behaviour and format reliably, but facts only patchily. (See Exhibit 1.)

Meanwhile, from Manchester, Ishara's customer-success lead, Mallika Raghuvanshi, relayed what clients actually complained about. It was rarely wrong facts; it was replies that wandered off the template. From Austin, the sales head, Sanjog Bhalla, warned that an answer of “we are using retrieval” sounds unfashionable to buyers who have read that rivals are “training their own models”.

4. The people

Indrani Chitale, vice president of product in Pune, owns the recommendation and the customer relationship. She wants a decision she can defend to the board with evidence, and to protect the Diwali date.

Lokanath Pattanaik, chief executive in Pune, wants a defensible technical moat.

Bartosz Wrona, data scientist in Warsaw, wants the pilot read carefully.

Sanjog Bhalla, sales head in Austin, wants a story that wins deals. Mallika Raghuvanshi, customer-success lead in Manchester, wants fewer complaints and no surprises when policy wording changes.

5. The evidence

Bartosz tested four set-ups on the same questions. The first used the current instructions only. The second added retrieval, in which the system looks up the relevant clauses from Ishara's document store at question time and places them in the prompt. The third fine-tuned an open-weight model on the 6,200 documents, with no retrieval. The fourth combined retrieval with a light fine-tune on 2,500 curated example replies, to teach template and refusals but not facts. Exhibit 2 gives the results.

The document-tuned model gained on format (84.0 per cent against 62.0 for instructions alone), which is what fine-tuning is good at. Its facts improved from 28.4 to 59.2 per cent but stayed well behind retrieval's 82.0. And on the amended clauses it scored 9 of 40, because the old wording was still in its weights. Retrieval simply read the new document.

The cost comparison is in Exhibit 3. It assumes 3,00,000 queries a month. Per-query token cost is input tokens times the input price plus output tokens times the output price, priced per million tokens.

Option B looks cheaper per month than A, ₹6.20 lakh against ₹7.20 lakh, but its ₹18 lakh build and quarterly retrains make year one ₹92.40 lakh against ₹90.40 lakh. Option C costs ₹34.94 lakh in year one, but Bartosz cautioned that a fair rival to C would be A on the same small model, untested.

6. The options

Option A: retrieval on the hosted model. Keep the current approach, improve the instructions and the document store. The upside is speed: the system can be live well before 3 November, and new policy wording is available the moment it is indexed. The cost is the highest monthly bill and template compliance of only 66.0 per cent.

Option B: fine-tune on the documents. Train an open-weight model on all 6,200 documents and serve it from Ishara's own GPUs. The upside is the story Lokanath wants, a model no competitor can copy, and a lower token bill. The cost is the largest build, retrains every quarter, stale answers between retrains and a factual score of only 59.2 per cent.

Option C: retrieval plus a behaviour fine-tune. Keep retrieval as the source of facts, and fine-tune a smaller model on 2,500 curated replies so that it learns the template and the refusals. The upside is the best score on all three tests and the lowest year-one cost. The cost is a ₹7 lakh build, a new evaluation routine and a tight schedule before Diwali.

7. Questions for discussion

  1. What does each of pre-training, post-training and fine-tuning change, and which has Ishara done?
  2. Using Exhibit 2, which problem does fine-tuning solve well for Ishara, and which does it solve poorly? What does the 9-of-40 result tell you about when the facts change?
  3. Using Exhibit 3, why is Option B not decisively cheaper than Option A, and how much of Option C's saving comes from fine-tuning itself?
  4. If you were Indrani, what would you tell Lokanath on 16 October about the claim that Ishara must have “its own model”, and what test would you run before go-live?

8. A note for the learner

How the topic frames the decision. The request “make the model know our documents” sounds like one problem but is two. Facts that live in documents and change are a knowledge problem. The house template, tone and refusals are a behaviour problem. Fine-tuning teaches behaviour and format far more reliably than facts, which is why it is usually the wrong answer to “the model does not know our data”. Retrieval keeps facts outside the weights, where they can be cited, updated and deleted.

One defensible path: Option C, staged. Use retrieval for all policy facts and fine-tune only for behaviour. The evidence supports it: 87.2 per cent on facts, 94.0 on format and refusal, and 92.5 on amended clauses, the best on every test. Year one costs ₹34.94 lakh against ₹90.40 lakh for A and ₹92.40 lakh for B.

The honest caveats. Most of C's saving comes from the smaller model, so before committing, run Option A on that same small model to separate the two effects. Make a go-live gate of 90 per cent on the 150 format questions, and keep A as the fallback for 3 November if C misses it.

What to tell Lokanath. The moat is not the weights. It is the curated 2,500 replies, the 6,200 documents indexed cleanly, and the evaluation set that tells Ishara whether a change helped. Those belong to Ishara whichever model it rents or tunes.
exp20v2-aivocab.training.stages:
Pre-training, post-training and fine-tuning: what each one changes, and what none of them can do

1. The Tuesday meeting

On Tuesday 6 October 2026, Geetika Raghunathan, head of product at Gandiva Labs, sat down with her machine-learning lead, Girish Kamath, and a one-line request from the company's largest customer. Gandiva sells a claims-assistant to general insurers: an adjuster pastes in a claim, and the assistant drafts a reply that cites the right policy clause. The customer, a large general insurer operating under IRDAI rules, had 40,000 policy and circular documents and wanted a pilot live on 2 November. Its sentence was: "Fine-tune the model on our documents so it knows our business."

Girish had a quote from a cloud vendor and a view. Geetika had a decision due to the customer on Friday 16 October, a pilot worth ₹3.6 crore over the year, and a worry. If the assistant cited a withdrawn clause, an adjuster might reject a valid claim, and the insurer's ombudsman cases would trace back to Gandiva. If she refused the request, the customer might read her as unable to do what competitors advertised.

She needed three things: to know what "fine-tune" would actually change inside the model, to see the evidence before choosing, and to be able to say no, or yes, in one sentence the customer's chief technology officer would accept.

2. The idea: three stages, one function

A large language model is a mathematical function that, given text so far, assigns a probability to every possible next token (a token is a word fragment, roughly three-quarters of an English word). Its behaviour is fixed by billions of numbers called weights. Training means adjusting the weights so the function predicts better. The phrase "training a model" hides three different operations, done by different people, on different data, for different purposes.

Pre-training is the first and by far the largest. The developer feeds the network trillions of tokens of web pages, books and code, and adjusts the weights so the model predicts each next token. The technique matured with the transformer architecture (2017) and the GPT models of 2018 to 2020. The problem it solved was labelled data: hand-labelling is expensive, while raw text is plentiful and supplies its own answer, the next word. The result is a base model: fluent, broadly knowledgeable, and poorly behaved, since it continues text rather than answering questions.

Post-training is the developer's second stage. On curated examples of good conversations, and on human or automated judgements of which of two answers is better, the developer reshapes the base model into an assistant that follows instructions, adopts a tone, and refuses some requests. OpenAI's InstructGPT (2022) made the approach famous. Fine-tuning is the same kind of adjustment performed by you, on your data, on a model someone else has released.

The sentence Geetika could repeat without sounding glib: "Pre-training gives the model its knowledge, post-training gives it its manners, and fine-tuning lets us adjust the manners, but it is a poor way to add knowledge."

StageWho does itDataMainly changes
Pre-trainingModel developerTrillions of raw tokensKnowledge and fluency
Post-trainingModel developerCurated examples, preference judgementsBehaviour, style, refusals
Fine-tuningYouYour examples, from thousands of tokens to hundreds of millionsFormat, tone, narrow skills

The figure shows the continuity. There is no separate "knowledge module" that fine-tuning plugs into. Each stage nudges the same numbers, which is why a later stage can overwrite or distort what an earlier one left.

3. How it works, step by step

Take Gandiva's case. Step one is the gradient update, the core of every stage. The model reads a passage, predicts the next token, and is scored by a loss, a number that is high when the true token was given low probability. Calculus tells the training system which direction to nudge each weight to lower the loss; it nudges all of them slightly; it repeats across billions of passages.

Step two, often left implicit, is that the nudge is small and diffuse. Nothing is written to a location, the way a record is written to a database row. A fact becomes a faint statistical tendency spread across many weights, reinforced only if it is seen often and in varied wording. A clause seen three times in a fine-tuning run is a weak tendency, not an entry.

Step three is that the stages differ in what they show the model. Pre-training shows raw text. Post-training shows pairs such as a request and a good reply, often with a ranking of replies. Fine-tuning usually shows your pairs: a claim, and the reply your best adjuster wrote. What the model learns most easily from pairs is the shape of the reply: its sections, register and length.

Step four is the alternative Geetika had to weigh. Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) leaves the weights alone: at question time the system searches the documents, pastes the best passages into the prompt, and the model answers from what is in front of it. The knowledge sits in a searchable index, where it can be replaced in minutes.

4. A worked example

Girish ran a 200-question evaluation, drawn from real claims with answers checked by the customer's senior adjusters. Each answer was scored twice: was the clause cited correct (the fact), and did the reply follow the customer's template (the format)? Four set-ups were tested.

Set-upFacts correct (of 200)Facts %Format correct (of 200)Format %
Base assistant, no documents6231%12060%
Fine-tuned on 40,000 documents11859%19296%
RAG only17487%13869%
Fine-tuned plus RAG18693%19497%
Percentages are counts divided by 200.

Read the lines. Fine-tuning lifted facts from 62 to 118, a gain of 56 questions or 28 percentage points, but lifted format from 120 to 192, a gain of 72 questions or 36 points. RAG lifted facts by 112 questions (56 points) but moved format only from 120 to 138, a gain of 18 questions or 9 points. Each tool did most for the thing it is suited to. The fine-tuned model's 59 per cent on facts was also uneven: it tended to be right on clauses that recur across many documents and wrong on one-off circulars.

Now the cost, at 200,000 queries a month. Fine-tuning: 40,000 documents of about 2,500 tokens is 100 million tokens; three passes is 300 million training tokens at ₹2,000 per million, or ₹6 lakh a run. Policies change quarterly, so four runs a year (4 × 6.00 = 24.00 lakh). A dedicated endpoint for the tuned model costs ₹2.4 lakh a month. RAG: embedding the corpus costs ₹10 per million tokens, or ₹1,000; each query carries six passages of 500 tokens, which is 3,000 extra input tokens at ₹250 per million, or ₹0.75 a query; a vector store costs ₹40,000 a month.

First-year cost (₹ lakh)Fine-tuningRAG
Training or indexing24.000.01
Hosting (12 months)28.804.80
Retrieved-passage tokens (600 million a month)0.0018.00
Total52.8022.81
Fine-tuning is 52.80 / 22.81, about 2.3 times RAG.

Second pass, one input changed. If the pilot sees only 50,000 queries a month, retrieved tokens fall to 150 million a month, which is ₹37,500, or 4.50 lakh over the year. RAG totals 0.01 + 4.80 + 4.50 = 9.31 lakh. Fine-tuning stays at 52.80, about 5.7 times as much. Volume would have to rise a long way before fine-tuning's fixed costs became competitive, and even then it would be buying the weaker factual result.

5. Nuances a learner must absorb

Knowledge versus behaviour

The table above is the whole lesson: stages are best judged by what they reliably change. Fine-tuning teaches how to answer (format, tone, a narrow task) far more reliably than what is true. The everyday slip, "it does not know our data, so fine-tune", treats the weights as a filing cabinet.

Scale is lopsided

Assume a pre-training corpus of 15 trillion tokens, which is the order of magnitude disclosed for recent open models. Gandiva's 100 million tokens are 1 part in 150,000 of that; the 300 million tokens of three passes are 0.002 per cent. A small dataset can shift style, because style is a low-dimensional habit. It cannot compete with the prior on facts.

Forgetting and distortion

Fine-tuning can degrade what the model already did well, an effect called catastrophic forgetting. Aggressive tuning on insurance replies can make the model worse at arithmetic or at declining unsafe requests, because post-training's safety behaviour sits in the same weights.

Hallucination is not cured

A fine-tuned model that has half-learned a clause will state it with full confidence. RAG narrows the error, because the source is in the prompt and can be shown to the user as a citation; it does not remove it.

Freshness and deletion

About 1,200 of the 40,000 documents (3 per cent) change each quarter. Re-indexing them costs roughly 3 million tokens at ₹10 per million, or ₹30. Retraining costs ₹6 lakh. Nor can a weight be told to forget one withdrawn circular, a serious matter where regulation requires that superseded rules not be applied.

Permissions

A fine-tuned model has absorbed every document. If junior staff should not see board circulars, the model cannot enforce it. A retrieval layer can filter by user before the prompt is built.

Where fine-tuning does win

Stable format, a house voice, classification at scale, or a cheaper small model imitating a larger one. The claim is not "never fine-tune"; it is "not for facts".

Questions before relying on it

How often does the content change? Who may see it? Is the failure a wrong fact or a wrong shape? What would the evaluation look like before, not after, the decision?

6. Consumer, B2B and marketplace; small and large

In consumer products, fine-tuning earns its place through voice and latency: a small tuned model that sounds like the brand, at low cost per conversation across millions of chats. Facts rarely matter as much. In B2B, as at Gandiva, facts are contractual, change often and carry permissions, so retrieval leads and fine-tuning polishes the output. In marketplaces the catalogue is the knowledge and it changes hourly; fine-tuning for listing quality or moderation tone is sensible, but prices and availability must be fetched live.

An early-stage company should almost never start with fine-tuning: it has little data, no evaluation set and no appetite for ₹2.4 lakh a month of fixed hosting. A large company with millions of examples, a stable task and a platform team may rationally fine-tune, and may even continue pre-training on its own corpus, a far more expensive undertaking with its own trade-offs.

7. Common mistakes

The filing-cabinet assumption. Symptom: a tuned model that answers fluently on your topic but cites outdated figures. Misunderstanding: weights as storage. Cheapest diagnostic: ask 20 questions whose answers exist in one document only and count the misses.

No evaluation before spending. Symptom: a launch announcement but no before-and-after numbers. Diagnostic: write 100 questions with checked answers first; Girish's 200 took two days.

Tuning to fix format that a prompt could fix. Symptom: a large training bill for tone. Diagnostic: try three worked examples in the prompt; if that yields most of the gain, tuning is premature.

Ignoring change and permissions. Symptom: a superseded circular appears in an answer. Diagnostic: plant one withdrawn clause and see whether the system can ever stop citing it.

8. What good looks like

A well-handled version of Geetika's decision begins with the evaluation, not the vendor quote. The team writes down which failures matter (wrong clause, wrong shape), measures the base assistant, tries retrieval, then tries a light format-only tuning, and compares on the same 200 questions with costs beside them. The customer is shown the table, not a promise. The documents stay in a permissioned index, every answer carries its citation, and the tuned component, if any, carries no facts at all.

9. What Geetika decided

On Friday 16 October she told the customer: "We will not store your documents in the model, because the model cannot reliably recall them and cannot forget them. We will retrieve them at question time with citations, and tune only the reply format." Fine-tuned plus RAG scored 93 per cent on facts and 97 per cent on format, against 87 and 69 for RAG alone. She accepted the extra run cost of tuning for format only, with a far smaller dataset of reply templates than the 100-million-token corpus. The tuned model was never asked to know a clause.

What to learn next: LoRA and parameter-efficient tuning, which explains why format tuning can be cheap; RLHF and alignment, for how post-training shapes refusal; and evaluation, which would have settled the argument before the meeting.

Two questions to sit with. First, which of your own "the model does not know our data" complaints are really complaints about format, and which about facts? Second, if a regulator withdrew one rule tomorrow, how many minutes would it take your system to stop applying it?
exp40v2-aivocab.training.stages:
Pre-training, post-training and fine-tuning: three operations on one set of weights, and why only one of them is yours

1. Two rooms, four days apart

On Thursday 8 October 2026, in Chennai, Harshada Venugopal took a printed email into her weekly review. She is vice-president of product at Harkara Freight Exchange, a truckload marketplace matching 41,000 fleet operators to shippers moving cement and textiles across the south. The email, from her second-largest shipper, held the sentence she had heard from four customers in six weeks: "Fine-tune your assistant on our rate circulars and contracts so it actually knows our business."

That knowledge sits in 61,000 documents — lane contracts, rate circulars, GST notes, desk memos — averaging about 1,800 tokens each, so 109.8 million tokens in all; about 4 per cent change every month. The assistant answers rate and detention questions for the inside-sales desk and, since June, for shippers directly. Harshada's answer was due at the board review on Friday 23 October, fifteen days later, against a ₹6.4 crore renewal. Quote a withdrawn circular and Harkara would be arguing about a freight bill it had mispriced itself. Hardik Motwani, her machine-learning platform lead, wanted to fine-tune.

Four days later, on Monday 12 October, in Pune, Hemangi Sathe used the same three words differently. She is chief product officer of Hitopadesh Learning Labs, whose tutor serves 8.6 lakh monthly active learners in CBSE classes eight to ten, mostly in Hindi–English and Marathi–English code-mixed speech. At 18 turns per learner per month that is 1.548 crore turns a month, or 18.576 crore a year, each a call to a large hosted model after the relevant NCERT passage is retrieved; the bill is ₹6.59 crore a year. Hrishikesh Kolhatkar, her head of applied machine learning, proposed tuning a 4-billion-parameter open model on 1.8 lakh dialogues written by the large one — not to teach it facts, but to make it sound like a patient Marathi-speaking tutor at a fraction of the cost per turn.

2. The idea, its history, and the four schools that disagree

A large language model is a function mapping a token sequence to a probability distribution over the next token, determined entirely by a weight vector — eight billion real numbers for an 8B model. Training means moving that vector by gradient descent. The three stages are three occasions on which somebody moves the same vector, differing in who acts, on what objective, with how much data, and to what effect.

Pre-training optimises next-token prediction over trillions of tokens of web text, books and code. Its lineage runs from n-gram models through word2vec (2013) to the transformer (2017), solving the scarcity of labels by letting text label itself. Kaplan and colleagues (2020) showed loss falling as a power law in compute, data and parameters; Chinchilla (2022) corrected the recipe towards roughly 20 tokens per parameter, and production runs pushed far past it, recent open models disclosing corpora of the order of 15 trillion tokens. The result is a base model: fluent, knowledgeable, unusable, because it continues documents rather than answering people.

Post-training is the developer's second pass: supervised tuning on curated demonstrations, then preference optimisation — reinforcement learning from human feedback (InstructGPT, 2022), successors such as DPO (2023), automated variants such as constitutional AI. Since 2024, reinforcement learning against verifiable rewards has mattered more, producing the reasoning models. Fine-tuning is the same operation done by the customer, on a released model, with the customer's data, almost always parameter-efficient: LoRA (2021) freezes the base weights and trains small low-rank matrices beside them.

Fifteen trillion divided by 219.6 million is 68,306: Harkara's whole document estate, seen twice, is one sixty-eight-thousandth of the gradient signal that built the model's picture of the world; the format-only tune, one part in 2.29 million. None of that stops a small dataset changing style, a low-dimensional habit. It does say what happens when one out-argues the prior about a fact.

Four schools read those numbers differently. The superficial-alignment school, named for LIMA (2023), where a thousand curated examples bought most of the instruction-following quality of far larger sets, signs: knowledge and capability are established in pre-training; post-training selects the style in which existing capability is expressed. It will not sign that post-training raises a capability ceiling. The domain-adaptive school, from continued-pre-training work (Gururangan and colleagues, 2020) and BloombergGPT (2023), signs: with billions of in-domain tokens, on the next-token objective, knowledge can genuinely be installed. It will not sign that 61,000 documents reshaped as question-answer pairs teaches facts — the claim vendors make while misquoting this school. The non-parametric school, from RAG (2020) and RETRO (2022), signs that facts belong outside the weights, in an index that can be updated, permissioned, deleted and cited, and denies that longer contexts make retrieval temporary. The elicitation-through-RL school, opposed to the first, signs that verifiable-reward training changes what a model can do, not merely how it says it, citing reasoning models whose mathematics scores moved tens of points with no new pre-training.

3. Mechanics: what moves, and by how much

Every stage runs one loop. Text is read, each next token predicted, a loss scores the probability given to the token that occurred, and every weight is nudged against its gradient. Two consequences go unstated.

The first is that nothing is written anywhere. One document leaves a faint tendency across millions of weights, surviving only if reinforced often and in varied phrasing. Harkara's 61,000 roughly equal documents make a one-off circular exactly 1 part in 61,000 of a pass, seen twice over two epochs. Allen-Zhu and Li (2024) found reliable recall required the same fact restated many times in different wordings, and put knowledge capacity at roughly 2 bits per parameter.

That makes the second consequence measurable. Hardik proposed a rank-16 LoRA adapter on the four attention projections of a 32-layer, 4,096-dimensional 8-billion-parameter model. Each adapted matrix trains rank × (input + output) parameters: 16 × (4,096 + 4,096) = 131,072, across 128 matrices (32 layers × 4), so 16,777,216 trainable parameters, or 0.21 per cent of 8 billion. At 2 bits each that is 33,554,432 bits of capacity, or 4.19 megabytes, against a corpus which at four characters per token is roughly 439 megabytes of text — a ceiling near 1 per cent of what it was asked to absorb, before any of it went on format and tone.

Three second-order effects follow. Interference with post-training: the developer's refusal behaviour lives in the weights the customer is about to move, and Hitopadesh lost 11.9 percentage points of correct off-syllabus refusal while gaining 32.1 points of register (section 8.2). Replay of 10 to 20 per cent general instruction data fixes most of it. Confident half-learning: Gekhman and colleagues (2024) found facts absent from pre-training are learned slowly and, as they are, raise the hallucination rate nearby. Irreversibility: a circular trained into weights can only be diluted by a later run.

4. The conditions, stated as testable claims

The usable form of this topic is four claims, each testable against a situation.

Testable claimHarkara Freight ExchangeHitopadesh Learning Labs
1. If the target is a format or register, a few thousand examples move it a long way.True: desk replies follow a fixed shape — rate, charges, clause reference.True, and it is the whole objective: a code-mixed, step-revealing tutor voice.
2. If the target is recall of facts, the data must be large, in the pre-training objective, and repeated in varied wording.Fails on all three: 109.8 M tokens, instruction pairs, one appearance each.Not applicable: facts come from the retrieved passage.
3. If facts change, or must be deleted, attributed or permissioned, they cannot live in weights.Fails hard: 4 per cent change monthly, and rates are confidential across sides.Passes: the syllabus changes yearly and is public.
4. If unit economics at volume dominate, a smaller tuned model imitating a larger one is the strongest lever.Weak: 3.2 lakh questions a month does not amortise a specialist model.Decisive: 18.576 crore turns a year turn a two-thirds cut into ₹4.13 crore.
Harkara passes one claim of four; Hitopadesh three, and the one it fails is irrelevant to its goal.

The idea misleads twice. "Fine-tuning does not teach facts" is false at the domain-adaptive school's scale, where ten billion tokens of in-domain text on the next-token objective is a different operation wearing the same word. The slogan can also dismiss tuning altogether, which is how a company pays three times too much per turn for a product whose problem was never factual.

5. Hard edge cases, and the organisational seams

Two-sided markets. Harkara's corpus holds shippers' negotiated rates and operators' cost structures. A leakage probe on a trial adapter asked 90 questions as a fleet operator, each seeking a figure only a shipper should see; 32 of the 90 (35.6 per cent) returned a contracted rate. A tuned model cannot hold an access-control list; retrieval filters by entitlement.

Regulated evidence. When a shipper disputes a bill, Harkara must show why the assistant said what it said. Weights produce no citation; an index produces the document, its version and timestamp.

Hardware. Hiranya Metering Industries ships smart water meters whose on-device 1.2-billion-parameter model reads its diagnostics offline. There is no retrieval in a basement pump room and no re-index, since firmware ships twice a year. Fine-tuning is the only option, and only stable facts may be baked in.

Multi-product seams. Four surfaces want four reply formats. The mature pattern is one base model, one permissioned index and four LoRA adapters of 16.78 million parameters each — 33.6 megabytes apiece at two bytes per parameter — swapped per request. Such firms say "we fine-tuned our own model"; what they run is one retrieval layer and an adapter library.

6. Eight distinctions that separate an expert from a competent practitioner

Knowledge and behaviour are not two ends of one dial. The expert asks which axis a failure sits on, because that picks the instrument. The tell is a request phrased as knowledge whose examples are all shape; Harkara's complaint log split 3 to 1 that way.

The objective matters more than the word. Next-token training on raw domain text and supervised training on pairs are both called fine-tuning; the first installs knowledge far better. The tell is a vendor citing BloombergGPT for an instruction-tuning job.

Fine-tuning can reduce factual accuracy. Harkara's adapter, trained on a corpus that still held superseded circulars, answered the traps correctly 5 times out of 90, worse than the base model's 12. The tell is an evaluation reporting one average rather than separating question families.

Capacity is finite and shared. A rank-16 adapter spends its parameters on everything asked of it, so format, tone and facts compete. The tell is a team that adds a second objective, watches the first decay, then blames the data.

Forgetting is quiet and lands on safety. Refusals, arithmetic and long-form coherence go first, and none appear in a domain evaluation. The tell is a model that improves on every metric the team wrote, then draws a complaint in week three.

Deletion is a product requirement, not an operational one. The expert asks what happens when a fact is withdrawn during design, not during an audit. The tell is no answer to "how many minutes until it stops saying that": retraining costs ₹3.07 lakh and days, deletion milliseconds.

Distillation is the honourable use of fine-tuning. Teaching a small model to imitate a large one on a narrow task pays best: the target is behaviour and the prize is unit economics. The tell is a team talking about cost per turn, not knowledge.

The prompt is the cheapest tuning method. Three worked examples in a system prompt often recover most of the format gain a run would buy, at no training cost, and an expert demands that comparison first. Hitopadesh's prompt route captured most of the register gain and none of the cost gain, which is why its tuning case survived.

7. Product types and company stages

In consumer products the differences favour tuning: volume amortises a specialist model, voice is the product, and facts are unimportant or retrievable. In business software they favour retrieval, because facts are contractual, versioned, permissioned and audited. In marketplaces the catalogue is the knowledge and changes hourly. In hardware, no network and slow firmware invert the default.

One asserted difference is not real: AI-native companies are not better at this — they tune earlier, so they meet forgetting and stale weights earlier too. Stage matters more. A seed-stage company with no data and no evaluation set should not fine-tune at all; its lever is the system prompt. A growth-stage company tunes for cost and voice once volume justifies a dedicated endpoint — Hitopadesh yes, Harkara no. Only a large enterprise with a platform team can maintain an adapter library, and only there is continued pre-training defensible.

8. Three worked examples

8.1 Harkara: the numbers that settled a fifteen-day argument

Hardik and Harshada priced three architectures over twelve months at 3.2 lakh questions a month, and scored them on 360 questions: 150 settled tariffs, 120 answerable from exactly one document, and 90 traps whose governing circular had been withdrawn.

8.3 Hastkala Looms: the failure and the recovery

Hastkala Looms Industries, a Jaipur marketplace for handloom textiles, fine-tuned a model on 2.6 lakh listings of about 340 tokens each — 88.4 million tokens, three epochs, 265.2 million training tokens at ₹1,400 per million, ₹3.71 lakh — so its buyer assistant would "know the catalogue". It went live on Monday 6 April 2026. By Monday 18 May, 42 days later, the operations lead, Hetal Panchmatia, sampled 1,500 conversations: 214 of the 1,500 (14.3 per cent) named a listing or dye lot that no longer existed. Those produced 63 orders, 29 of them returned — 46.0 per cent against a baseline of 11.4 per cent — at ₹1,160 each, ₹33,640 in all. Two cooperatives asked to be delisted.

A catalogue is the fastest-changing knowledge a marketplace holds, and it had been frozen into weights on 6 April. Recovery was decided on Wednesday 20 May and shipped 19 days later, on Monday 8 June: a live catalogue index queried at answer time, with a tune kept for reply format only — 9,000 examples of 300 tokens, ₹11,340 a run. Stale listings fell to 17 of 1,500 sampled conversations (1.1 per cent).

Four of the six are detectable within a week, and all four need an evaluation set stratified by failure type — which is why experienced teams treat that set, not the model, as the durable asset.

10. Where experts genuinely disagree

Does post-training add capability or only elicit it? The superficial-alignment position rests on evidence that very small demonstration sets reach most of the quality of large ones — hard to explain if post-training installed capability. The elicitation position rests on evidence just as hard: verifiable-reward training moved mathematics and coding scores by margins no prompt recovers. Settling it needs a problem class with no trace of the procedure in pre-training data, and measuring that is unsolved.

Will cheap long context make retrieval interim? One camp notes that windows grew from a few thousand tokens to a million while per-token prices keep falling, and concludes the end state is the corpus in the prompt. The other notes that accuracy degrades in long contexts, and that permissioning and citation are requirements no window size removes. Harkara's numbers sit oddly here: the 3,480-token input costs ₹0.87 a question, so a hundredfold larger context would cost ₹87. The first camp bets on prices, not architecture.

Is continued pre-training on a proprietary corpus worth it? The domain-adaptive school points to real in-domain gains; critics note that several such models were matched within a year by general models with no domain training — a temporary lead on a depreciating asset. The dispute is about how fast general capability keeps improving.

Should customers tune safety behaviour at all? One position holds that a customer accepting liability may remove refusals obstructing a legitimate workflow; the other that refusal behaviour is the thin layer between a capable model and predictable misuse. Regulation, not evidence, will settle it.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has studied this recites that fine-tuning teaches behaviour better than facts. Someone who has internalised it reclassifies the request first, turning "it does not know our business" into a count of format failures against fact failures; asks what the system does when a fact is withdrawn; insists on a stratified evaluation set before any technique is named; and tunes aggressively when the target is behaviour and the prize is unit economics — which is why Hemangi's decision and Harshada's point opposite ways, neither being inconsistent.

Pre-training supplies the world model, post-training the manners; fine-tuning adjusts the manners and, at ordinary scale, is a poor and irreversible way to add facts. Where facts change, keep them outside the weights.

12. What each of them decided

At the board review on Friday 23 October 2026, Harshada took option C. Her sentence to the shipper: "We will not put your contracts into the model's weights, because it cannot reliably recall them, cannot show where an answer came from, and cannot forget a circular you withdraw. We will retrieve them with a citation and a version, filtered by who is asking, and tune only the shape of the reply." The traps column persuaded; the cost table did not.

Hemangi approved the distilled tutor on Friday 30 October 2026 with three conditions: the 15 per cent replay mix in every run, the refusal measure on the weekly dashboard, and facts to keep coming from the retrieved NCERT passage. She accepted the fall from 92.1 to 85.6 per cent on shown working as the price of ₹4.13 crore, and wrote down that she had accepted it, so the next person to see the number would know it was a decision and not a defect.

Three questions. First, Harshada's options differed by 12 per cent in cost and by 81 percentage points on the traps (5.6 to 86.7): what does that say about how the fortnight should have been sequenced? Second, Hemangi traded 6.5 points of mathematical accuracy for ₹4.13 crore — at what number of points would you have refused, and who should own that threshold? Third, both companies ended with a tuned component and a retrieval layer for opposite reasons: if each had to give one up, which should go?

13. Going deeper

Inference versus training separates these operations from the serving cost that dominates the bill. What a large language model actually is supplies the next-token function all three stages modify. The transformer and attention explains why four projection matrices are the place to intervene. RLHF and alignment opens post-training proper. LoRA and parameter-efficient fine-tuning is the mechanics of those 16.78 million parameters. Distillation names what Hrishikesh did. System prompts and message roles is the free alternative to test first. Benchmarks, leaderboards and what SOTA means explains why vendor numbers rarely transfer to your own questions. Tokens and tokenisation produces the counts every figure rests on. The context window underlies the long-context disagreement. Embeddings and vector search and similarity are the machinery of Harkara's index. Quantisation squeezes a tuned model onto cheaper hardware. Small language models and when they win generalises Hitopadesh's case into a rule you can apply before the GPUs are ordered.
exp40v2-aivocab.vector.search:
Vector search and similarity

Retrieval is a chain of losses, and the threshold is only its last link

1. Two decisions, two cities

On Tuesday 8 September 2026, Mythili Raghavendra, Vice-President of Product at Mimansa Document Systems in Hyderabad, read a deviation report she had not expected. Mimansa sells a question-answering layer over manufacturing documentation — SOPs, deviation reports, cleaning-validation protocols — to Indian formulation manufacturers facing Schedule M and USFDA inspection. Its largest customer, Medhavi Formulations Industries, ran it at fourteen plants where some 2,400 staff asked about 62,000 questions a month. On Friday 4 September a supervisor asked the cleaning-validation acceptance limit of a molecule Medhavi dropped in 2023. The system returned a limit, with a citation, from another molecule's protocol; batch review caught the error four days later, on 8 September.

Mahesh Duraiswamy, who owns retrieval at Mimansa, had hand-labelled 600 logged questions with two reviewers from Medhavi's quality group. The shape of the corpus, not the cleverness of the model, sets how often the system is asked what it cannot answer.

Five hundred and seventy kilometres south, on Wednesday 16 September, Murad Hashmi, Head of Product at Mohalla Resale Exchange in Bengaluru, faced the opposite complaint. Mohalla is a consumer marketplace for second-hand furniture, appliances and baby goods in twenty-three cities, competing with OLX and Quikr, carrying 42,00,000 live listings against 2.4 crore searches a month. Malvika Ranadive, Mohalla's search scientist, traced one case: a buyer in Nagpur wanting a study desk under ₹5,000 got two results, both from Pune.

Mythili's system had to learn to refuse; Murad's had to learn that refusing destroys supply. Both found the similarity threshold — where most teams start and stop — the least interesting decision they made.

2. The idea, and the school that split over it

An embedding is a fixed-length list of numbers a trained model assigns to a text so that texts of similar meaning receive lists lying close together under some distance. Vector search embeds a query with that same model and returns the stored items whose embeddings are nearest, usually by cosine similarity. Nothing in that definition contains the word relevant, and nothing permits abstention: a ranking of bad candidates still has a first place.

The problem it solves is the vocabulary gap: keyword retrieval — Gerard Salton's SMART system at Cornell, made robust by Robertson and Spärck Jones's BM25 — scores documents on the query's own words. Latent semantic indexing (Deerwester, 1990) replaced words with a learned space, word2vec (Mikolov, 2013) made the vectors cheap, and dual-encoder retrievers such as DPR (Karpukhin, 2020) made passage retrieval learnable end to end. By 2020 the field had a schism that has not closed. The learned-retrieval school holds that relevance is a function to be learned and lexical matching a crude special case. It will sign that on natural-language questions a well-trained dense retriever beats BM25 by a wide margin; it will not sign that it beats BM25 on identifiers, part numbers or rare proper nouns. The lexical-first school, after Jimmy Lin's insistence on strong baselines, holds that BM25 is hard to beat out of distribution, that most reported dense wins come from benchmarks resembling their training data, and that the right architecture runs both. It will sign that a hybrid dominates either component alone, not that keyword search is obsolete, and it points at BEIR (Thakur, 2021), where dense models that beat BM25 in domain lost to it out of domain.

3. Mechanics: recall is a chain, not a number

The habit that most separates practice from vocabulary is refusing to treat "retrieval quality" as one number. Between a question and a correct answer sit six filters, each discarding some queries. Mahesh instrumented all six on the 402 single-passage questions.

Chunking decides what can be found at all

A chunk is the unit that gets embedded, so a fact split across a boundary has no embedding containing it. Mimansa's corpus was 9,480 documents averaging 2,000 tokens, or 1,89,60,000 tokens. In Exhibit 2, recall@10 is the share of the 402 questions whose correct passage appears in the top ten chunks under exact search.

4. When similarity is the right notion of relevance

State the conditions as testable claims. One: the corpus answers most real queries. Mimansa fails on 13.0 per cent and so needs abstention as a first-class feature; Mohalla fails far more often, a query being answerable only if some seller listed that item in that city this week. Two: relevance is about topic, not exact tokens. Mimansa half-fails — concepts are topical, molecule codes lexical, which is why Exhibit 4 looks as it does. Mohalla passes; a buyer wanting a study desk will take a writing table. Three: a wrong result is cheap. Mohalla passes; Mimansa fails outright, since a wrong acceptance limit enters a batch record. This claim, not model quality, is why the two pick different thresholds. Four: relevance is stable over time. Neither passes.

The idea is actively misleading on compositional queries. "Study desk under ₹5,000 in Nagpur, delivered this week" is three predicates and one similarity judgement, and embedding the whole sentence blends the predicates into the geometry, where they are barely enforced. Similarity is the wrong instrument for a constraint.

5. Hard edges: index structure, filters and the seams

Mohalla's 42,00,000 listings are embedded in 768 dimensions. At four bytes a number the raw vectors occupy 42,00,000 × 768 × 4 = 12,902,400,000 bytes, or 12.90 gigabytes. In Exhibit 5, recall@10 means something different from Exhibit 2: the average share of the exact top ten that the approximate index also returns, over 1,000 sampled queries. Two quantities share a name.

Product quantisation replaces each 768-number vector with 96 single-byte codes, so 3,072 bytes becomes 96 — a thirty-twofold reduction, taking Exhibit 5's vector payload from 12.90 gigabytes to 0.40 and the index onto smaller hardware. It pays in recall: 87.3 against 94.6 per cent. Doubling the HNSW graph from M = 16 to M = 32 buys 3.6 points of recall for 17 milliseconds — and no lever here is a model choice.

Now the filter. Mohalla has 61,000 Nagpur listings, or 1.45 per cent of 42,00,000, and 38 per cent of those are priced under ₹5,000, giving 23,180 eligible listings — 0.552 per cent of the corpus. Mohalla retrieved the top 100 by similarity and then applied the filter. If eligibility is independent of similarity, the expected number of survivors is 100 × 0.00552 = 0.55; to expect ten, it would have had to retrieve 10 ÷ 0.00552 ≈ 1,812 candidates first. That is the arithmetic behind the Nagpur buyer's two results. Filtered nearest-neighbour search is a different algorithm, not a WHERE clause.

At the organisational seam the pattern repeats. Mimansa's chunker belonged to data engineering, its embedding model to machine learning, its threshold to Mahesh and its fallback copy to design, so Figure 1 spanned four teams and nobody owned the number that mattered. Mature companies appoint one owner of end-to-end answer quality. What they say they do is invest in retrieval research; what they do is invest in labels.

6. Eight distinctions that separate the expert

The distribution matters more than the threshold. A competent practitioner asks what threshold to use; an expert plots the top-1 score distribution of in-scope and out-of-scope queries and reads the overlap, the irreducible error of any single cut-off. The tell is a team quoting a threshold but unable to draw Figure 3; the obvious reading, that a higher threshold is safer, is wrong, because in the overlap both errors move together.

Abstention is a classifier and deserves a classifier's metrics. Once refusal is a prediction — "nothing here answers this" — its recall and precision can be measured. The expert reports both middle columns of Exhibit 6; the amateur, only the bad answers blocked.

The score gap, a popular heuristic, is worst here: it refuses 47 answerable questions to catch 30 bad ones, because near-duplicate passages produce small gaps precisely where the corpus covers a topic well. Scaled monthly, the cross-encoder alone leaves 1,240 of 8,060 out-of-scope questions answered and refuses 1,550 answerable ones; the two-stage version, 723 and 2,687.

A cross-encoder is a different kind of model, which is why it helps. The retriever embeds query and passage separately and can never compare their words; a cross-encoder reads the pair together, far more accurately and far too slowly for 42,00,000 items. The architecture that follows is over-fetch, then re-rank, and the expert sets k by the re-ranker's ceiling: re-ranking cannot recover a passage retrieval never returned, so k belongs where recall flattens.

Query and passage are not symmetric. Queries are short and interrogative, passages long and declarative, and several modern encoders are trained asymmetrically, expecting a prefix — "query:" on one side, "passage:" on the other. Omitting it silently costs several points of recall. The tell is a recall jump on a one-line change nobody can explain: the model was used outside its contract.

Approximate search loses recall unevenly, and where you can least afford it. The 5.4 per cent HNSW at M = 16 misses concentrates on queries landing in sparse regions, where the graph has fewer links to traverse. Sparse regions are where the corpus is thin — where abstention already struggles — so two weaknesses stack on the same queries.

A threshold is a property of a model-and-corpus pair, not of a product. A cut-off calibrated on Medhavi's corpus is wrong for a Mimansa customer with a third of the documents, because a thinner corpus pushes every top-1 score down. Near-duplicates act the same way: Mimansa's SOPs exist in revisions, so a top-10 holding five copies of one passage is a top-6 in disguise. The tells are a shared constant in a configuration file and a recall curve flat from k = 5 to k = 20.

What you show below the line changes the cost of being wrong by an order of magnitude. Abstention is a product surface, not a model output: "I could not find this," with a handoff to a named quality officer, costs a minute, while the same non-answer as a blank page costs the relationship.

7. How this differs by product type and stage

The mechanism is identical everywhere; the economics are not. In consumer products volume dominates: Mohalla's 2.4 crore monthly searches make a one per cent error rate 2,40,000 bad moments, so cheap per-query techniques beat accurate expensive ones. In B2B and enterprise the calculus inverts — Mimansa can afford a cross-encoder on every question because 62,000 a month is nothing, and must, because a wrong answer becomes a regulatory observation. In marketplaces and platforms a third party is affected: when Mohalla refuses, a seller loses a view, so a missing match is both a retrieval failure and a demand signal — the difference most often missed. For hardware retrieval does not change; part numbers merely shift weight to the lexical half. For AI-native products the retriever feeds a generator that inherits every loss in Figure 1 and adds fluency. By stage, a pre-fit team should hand-label 200 queries and skip index work, exact search over 50,000 chunks being fast enough; at Mohalla's scale a standing evaluation set with a named owner is necessary.

8. Three worked examples, including one that failed

The chunking change that paid. Mimansa moved from 400-token chunks with no overlap to 800 with 160, lifting correct-passage recall from 341 to 362 of 402 — 84.8 to 90.0 per cent, a gain of 21 questions or 5.22 percentage points. Against 41,540 answerable questions a month that is 2,170 more answered correctly, for nine days of work.

The filter that hid the inventory. Post-filtering yielded 0.55 expected survivors from a top-100 retrieval on the Nagpur query. Pre-filtered graph traversal, walking only eligible nodes, restored results and raised p95 latency from 21 to 74 milliseconds. Views on listings outside the top eight cities rose — Murad's real number.

The fine-tune that went backwards. In May, Mimansa fine-tuned its embedding model on 4,100 query-click pairs harvested from the previous keyword system. On the evaluation set built from those same clicks, recall@10 rose from 356 to 376 of 402 — 88.6 to 93.5 per cent — and the team prepared to ship. Miroslav Havel, a retrieval consultant in Brno retained to review the method, asked for a set of separate provenance. On 210 questions hand-labelled by Medhavi's quality group, recall@10 fell from 185 to 170, that is 88.1 to 81.0 per cent, a loss of 7.1 percentage points. Clicks came from a keyword system, so the training signal rewarded lexical overlap and the evaluation set inherited the bias. The recovery, after seven weeks, was abandoning the fine-tune for chunking and re-ranking.

The queries drifted, not the listings, and dashboards built on a February label set showed nothing. Re-embedding cost little in compute: 42,00,000 listings at about 90 tokens each is 37.8 crore tokens, at ₹1.50 per lakh tokens ₹5,670. What it cost was a nine-day dual-run window and two reviewers re-labelling 200 queries.

10. Where experts genuinely disagree

Whether hybrid retrieval is permanent or transitional. Lexical-first, steelmanned: BM25 has no training distribution to fall outside of, so it degrades gracefully on new vocabulary, and Exhibit 9 is the case in point. Learned-retrieval, steelmanned: a hybrid adds a fusion parameter, a second index and a second failure surface, and the out-of-domain gap narrows yearly. The first is wrong if encoders become robust to unseen vocabulary; the second if drift proves permanent.

Whether abstention belongs to the retriever, the generator or the interface. Mei-Ling Chow, an information-retrieval researcher in Taipei whom Mythili consulted, argues the retriever must decide, because it alone sees the score distribution and a generator asked to judge sufficiency will rationalise whatever it was given. The opposing view is that a model reading the passages is better informed than any threshold, which Exhibit 6 supports at 84.6 against 52.6 per cent caught. A third camp says show the evidence and let the user judge — fine for Mohalla's buyers, useless for a supervisor.

Whether to fine-tune the embedding model. Mimansa is one data point against, but the honest statement is narrower: fine-tuning on provenance-contaminated labels failed, while practitioners with clean labels report gains. What would settle it is the experiment nobody runs — the same budget on labels versus fine-tuning, judged on a set built by people who saw neither.

Whether single-vector retrieval is the right primitive. Late-interaction models such as ColBERT store a vector per token and compare them pairwise, recovering much of a cross-encoder's accuracy at retrieval time; advocates point at the identifier-heavy queries of Exhibit 4. Critics point at storage: a per-token index is an order of magnitude larger, and Exhibit 5 shows memory binding already.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has merely studied this asks which embedding model is best. Someone who has internalised it asks to see the label set. They speak of recall at a stage rather than of a system, naming the stage a complaint belongs to before proposing a fix; they ask what happens below the threshold before asking what it is; and they distrust metrics whose labels came from the system measured.

12. What the protagonists decided

On 24 September Mythili shipped the last row of Exhibit 6: a cosine floor of 0.62, then a cross-encoder, refusing when either fails. It catches 71 of 78 out-of-scope questions and wrongly refuses 26 of 402 — a trade she accepted because a refusal in a plant costs a phone call while a wrong acceptance limit costs a batch. Below the line the product names a quality officer and logs the question. Murad went the other way: Mohalla pre-filters in the index, re-ranks only the 18 per cent in the ambiguous band at ₹12.68 per thousand searches, and never refuses outright, showing nearby cities and filing the query to supply operations. He also moved the drift review to a monthly 200-query resample, the cheapest line in his budget.

Discussion questions.

  1. Figure 1 loses 71 of 402 questions across six stages, none losing more than 6.5 percentage points. Which stage should Mimansa attack next, and on what evidence?
  2. Exhibit 7 shows selective re-ranking saving ₹8,85,600 a month. What would you measure about the other 82 per cent of queries before defending that saving to Mohalla's board?
  3. Mimansa's fine-tune improved one honestly labelled set by 5.0 points and worsened another by 7.1. What rule would you write so this is caught before seven weeks are spent, and what does it cost?

13. Going deeper

Embeddings supply the geometry every figure here depends on. Chunking and retrieval quality is the largest single link in Figure 1. Retrieval-augmented generation as an architecture puts a generator after this chain and inherits all seventy-one lost questions with added fluency. The context window caps the "tokens to model" column of Exhibit 2 and so caps k. Problem–model fit is the discipline behind Section 4's claims. Tokens and tokenisation explains why identifiers like MFI-0774 behave badly. What a large language model actually is, the transformer and attention and inference versus training explain the cost asymmetry between an encoder run 42,00,000 times and a cross-encoder run fifty times a query. Pre-training, post-training and fine-tuning names Section 8's failure; RLHF and alignment explains why a generator asked "is this enough?" says yes.
case20v1-aivocab.vector.search:
The Nearest Wrong Answer

Mrigaya Retail Network and the help-centre search that never said "I do not know"

1. Opening

On the morning of Monday, 5 October 2026, Mahima Lele opened a spreadsheet of fourteen customer complaints in her Mumbai office and read the first one twice. A buyer in Lucknow had asked the new help search whether she could cancel a custom-stitched blouse. The system answered, in a confident green card, with the policy for returning ready-to-wear clothes. She followed it, missed the cancellation window for her tailor, and lost ₹1,850.

Lele was Head of Product at Mrigaya Retail Network. She had until Friday, 9 October to freeze the search configuration, because the festive sale began on Monday, 19 October and engineering would not touch production during it. The question on her desk was a narrow one with wide consequences: what should the search do when it has nothing good to show?

2. Company background

Mrigaya is a Mumbai-headquartered online marketplace for ethnic wear and home textiles, founded in 2019. It lists about 41,000 sellers, mostly weavers, tailors and small boutiques in Surat, Jaipur, Kanchipuram and Varanasi, and sells to buyers in smaller cities that the larger platforms serve unevenly. Flipkart and Meesho dominate general fashion; Nykaa Fashion holds the premium end. Mrigaya competes on custom tailoring and regional crafts.

Its help centre holds 1,100 articles. Until August, search over them was keyword-based and poor. On Monday, 17 August 2026 the company replaced it with vector search: every article was converted into a list of numbers, an embedding, that captures its meaning. Each customer question is converted the same way, and the system returns the articles whose embeddings sit nearest to the question's.

3. The situation

On Monday, 21 September, the first complaints arrived about answers that were fluent, well formatted and wrong. By Mahima's count, fourteen in two weeks.

Naveen Pillai, who leads the retrieval engineers in Bengaluru, explained the pattern in one sentence: vector search returns the nearest stored item whether or not that item is near enough to matter. A question about custom blouses has no custom-cancellation article to land on, so it lands on the closest neighbour, and the closest neighbour is the ready-to-wear returns policy. The index has no concept of "nothing here". Unless the product defines one, it never says so.

The team had already measured this. Pallavi Mhatre's support analysts in Kolkata had labelled 2,000 real queries from August and September: 1,600 that the help centre could answer and 400 that it could not. Each result carries a similarity score between 0 and 1, and a threshold below which the system declines to answer is a product setting, not an engineering default. The team had tested three cutoffs. Exhibit 1 shows what each did.

Exhibit 1: Labelled test set of 2,000 queries, by similarity threshold
Threshold1,600 answerable queries400 unanswerable queriesBad share of answers shown
Correct shownWrong shownDeflectedAnswer shownDeflected
None1,3602400400032.0%
0.551,32816011228012024.9%
0.651,2408028013626414.8%
0.751,00024576243764.6%

"Correct shown" means the right article was among the top three results. "Bad share of answers shown" = (wrong shown + answer shown to unanswerable queries) ÷ all answers shown; for example, at 0.65 that is (80 + 136) ÷ (1,240 + 80 + 136) = 216 ÷ 1,456. Answers shown at each row: 2,000; 1,768; 1,456; 1,048. Source: Mrigaya support analytics, labelled sample, August to September 2026.

With no threshold all 2,000 queries get an answer, including the 400 that have none, and 640 of those answers are bad. At 0.75 the bad answers fall to 48, but 952 queries are deflected, and 576 of them were questions the help centre could have answered. At 0.65 the answerable queries answered correctly fall from 1,360 (85.0 per cent of 1,600) to 1,240 (77.5 per cent). The threshold does not remove error; it trades one kind for another.

Exhibit 2 shows four typical queries and the score of the top result. The 0.71 row is the uncomfortable one: a threshold cannot catch a result that is similar and still wrong.

Figure A: The timeline. The 14 days from 21 September to 5 October, and 14 more from 5 to 19 October, bracket the decision.

4. The people

Mahima Lele (Mumbai), Head of Product, owns the outcome. She wants a setting she can defend to the CEO and to customers in the same sentence.

Naveen Pillai (Bengaluru) leads retrieval engineering. He would raise accuracy by re-ranking results with a second, slower model and by splitting long articles into smaller chunks, but both take weeks and neither would be ready before 19 October.

Pallavi Mhatre (Kolkata) runs support operations and her 180 agents. Every deflected query lands in her queue, and her team is already stretched. She wants fewer deflections, but she is the person who answered the Lucknow complaint.

Omkar Mulay (Pune) manages seller relations. His sellers write the articles, and he sees a different benefit: every deflected query is evidence of a missing article, and he wants to see them.

5. The cost of each setting

Mrigaya's help search handles about 2,50,000 queries a month. Mhatre's team estimated that a bad answer costs ₹140 on average, in repeat contacts, goodwill refunds and the occasional lost order, and that a deflected query costs ₹60 in agent time. Exhibit 3 scales the Exhibit 1 rates to that volume (each test-set count multiplied by 125).

Exhibit 3: Monthly cost at 2,50,000 queries (₹ lakh)

None80,000112.000.0112.0
