Bad answers = (wrong shown + unanswerable shown) × 125 from Exhibit 1; deflected = (deflected, both groups) × 125. Example: 0.65 gives 216 × 125 = 27,000 and 544 × 125 = 68,000. ₹140 and ₹60 are support-operations estimates, not audited figures. 1 lakh = 1,00,000.

The monthly gap between no threshold and the best setting is ₹33.4 lakh. Between 0.65 and 0.75 it is only ₹1.2 lakh, in 0.65's favour, but the two settings feel very different to customers: one gives 27,000 bad answers, the other 6,000, and the second sends nearly twice as many people to a human.

6. The options

Option A: ship as is. Keep the search unfiltered and promise a re-ranker and better chunking in November. The upside is the highest apparent answer rate and no change before the sale. The cost is ₹112.0 lakh a month in modelled harm, from 80,000 bad answers, in the busiest weeks of the year.

Option B: a strict threshold of 0.75. Show only very close matches and send the rest to humans. The upside is trust: only 48 of every 2,000 queries produce a bad answer. The cost is 1,19,000 deflections a month, strain on Kolkata in sale season, and the loss of 576 of every 1,600 answerable questions.

Option C: a middle threshold of 0.65 with a designed "I am not sure" state. Below 0.65 the search says it could not find a confident answer, shows the three nearest articles as suggestions, offers chat, and logs the query to Mulay's team. The upside is the lowest modelled cost, ₹78.6 lakh, and a feedback loop that fills the gaps. The cost is design work in four working days, and the 0.71 problem in Exhibit 2 remains.

7. Questions for discussion

  1. Why did the search return the returns policy for the custom blouse, and why is that behaviour the default rather than a defect in the model?
  2. Using Exhibit 1, which kind of error does each threshold trade for which, and which matters more to Mrigaya's customers in a festive month?
  3. Exhibit 3 puts 0.65 and 0.75 within ₹1.2 lakh of each other. What other evidence would you want before relying on that cost estimate?
  4. What should the product say, and do, below the threshold, and who in the team should own that decision?

8. A note for the learner

Vector search finds the stored items whose embeddings sit nearest to the query's. "Nearest" is relative: the system always has a nearest item, so it will return something even when nothing relevant exists. It will not say "I do not know" until the product adds a threshold and decides what happens below it. That is why the decision belongs to a PM, not only to an engineer. The cutoff is a statement about how much wrong confidence the business will tolerate, and the below-threshold experience is a product design problem in its own right.

A well-reasoned answer starts from the labelled evidence and not from the score distribution alone. It names the two error types, wrong answers shown and good answers withheld, prices them in rupees, and notices that the cost estimate is soft.

One defensible path is Option C. Set the threshold at 0.65, freeze it on 9 October, and spend the four working days on the below-threshold state: honest wording, three suggested articles, a chat handoff, and a log of every deflected query. Keep Pillai's re-ranking and chunking on the November roadmap, since better retrieval lowers the cost at every threshold, and review the 0.65 setting weekly against fresh labels. The reasoning is not that 0.65 is optimal, since the ₹1.2 lakh gap to 0.75 is inside the noise, but that it is cheapest on current evidence, it generates the data that will improve the next decision, and it can be reversed.
exp20v2-aivocab.vector.search:
Vector search and similarity

Why semantic search sometimes confidently returns something completely unrelated

1. A search box that never said "I don't know"

On Monday 17 August 2026, Gayatri Subramanian, Head of Product at Grihini Appliance Services, opened a meeting with a screenshot. Grihini, based in Pune, sells maintenance contracts and on-call repairs for washing machines, refrigerators and air conditioners in eleven Indian cities. Six weeks earlier, on Monday 6 July, her team had replaced the help-centre keyword search with "semantic search", which matches queries to articles by meaning rather than shared words. The screenshot showed a restaurant owner in Nashik typing, "Do you service commercial chillers for restaurants?" The system had answered, in the same confident layout it used for every result, with the article "Warranty terms and what they cover."

Grihini did not service commercial equipment at all, and the article said nothing on the subject. The owner assumed commercial units were covered, booked a technician, saw the visit cancelled, and wrote a one-star review. Gopal Nambiar, who built the search, had since hand-labelled 240 real queries: did the help centre contain an article that actually answered each? Exhibit 1 gives the tally.

Exhibit 1. Hand-labelled audit of 240 help-centre queries, 6 July to 14 August 2026. Weekly figures scale to 1,20,000 searches.
Query typeIn sampleShare of sampleImplied per week
A relevant article exists20083.3%1,00,000
No article answers it4016.7%20,000
Total240100.0%1,20,000

The unsettling line is the second. The old keyword system returned an empty page when nothing matched, signalling a gap. The new system returned a result for all 40 unanswerable queries, and in 38 of them the top result scored above 0.50 on its similarity scale. Before the October renewal season, Gayatri had to decide whether to keep the system, add a guard, or retreat.

2. The idea

Begin with the vocabulary. An embedding is a list of numbers, typically several hundred to a few thousand, that a trained model assigns to a piece of text so that texts with similar meaning receive lists that are close together. A vector is simply that list, read as a point in a space with one dimension per number. Vector search is the operation of turning the user's query into a vector with the same model, then finding the stored items whose vectors lie nearest to it.

The problem it solves is the vocabulary gap. Keyword search, refined from the 1960s in Gerard Salton's SMART system at Cornell, matches the words typed, so "washer won't empty" finds nothing if the article says "drain pump fault." Latent semantic analysis (1990), then neural embeddings, popularised by Tomas Mikolov's word2vec at Google in 2013 and later extended to whole passages, turned meaning into geometry, so "nearby" could stand in for "about the same thing".

The query "commercial chillers" falls in a region where Grihini has written nothing, and the nearest stored point is "Warranty terms." The search does not ask whether that point is near. It asks only which point is nearest.

The sentence Gayatri could repeat in any meeting: vector search always returns the most similar thing it has, and "most similar" is not the same as "relevant".

3. How it actually works

The process has two phases. In preparation, each article is split into passages, each passage is embedded, and the vectors are stored in an index built to find near neighbours quickly. At query time the user's text passes through the same model, the index returns the closest vectors, and the system displays their passages.

Three steps usually stay implicit. First, the query and the stored items must come from the same embedding model; vectors from two models live in unrelated spaces. Second, a similarity measure, the formula that turns two vectors into one number, must be chosen; the most common is cosine similarity, which measures the angle between vectors and ignores length. Third, approximate nearest-neighbour search: comparing a query against every vector is exact but slow at scale, so indexes such as HNSW (Malkov and Yashunin, 2016) and libraries such as FAISS (Facebook, 2017) trade a little accuracy for speed, finding the true nearest items perhaps 95 times in 100.

The parameter k is how many neighbours to return. Grihini showed three passages of about 550 tokens each, so 1,650 tokens in all. If a language model reads them later, k is capped by the context window, the amount of text a model can read at once, and every extra result displaces something else.

4. A worked example, line by line

Shrink the space to three dimensions. Real embeddings have hundreds, with unlabelled axes, but read these three numbers as rough strengths of "repair", "money" and "hardware". The five articles receive the vectors in Exhibit 2; the chiller query becomes (0, 1, 6).

Cosine similarity is the dot product of two vectors divided by the product of their lengths. The dot product multiplies matching entries and adds them. The query's length is the square root of 0 + 1 + 36, which is 37, so about 6.083. For "Warranty terms" (2, 6, 3): the dot product is 0×2 + 1×6 + 6×3 = 24; its length is the square root of 4 + 36 + 9 = 49, which is exactly 7; so cosine = 24 ÷ (6.083 × 7) = 0.564. Repeating this for each article gives the table.

Exhibit 2. Query (0, 1, 6), length 6.083. Cosine = dot ÷ (6.083 × article length); Euclidean distance is straight-line.
ArticleVectorDotLengthCosineCosine rankEuclid. distanceEuclid. rank
Drain pump error(8, 0, 5)309.4340.52328.1244
Book a technician(6, 2, 3)207.0000.47036.7823
Warranty terms(2, 6, 3)247.0000.56416.1641
Refund for visit(1, 8, 1)148.1240.28348.6605
Change phone number(0, 3, 0)33.0000.16456.3252

"Warranty terms" wins at 0.564. Nothing compares 0.564 to anything; the procedure only orders the five numbers, so a query about a product Grihini has never mentioned produces a winner as surely as one it has answered a thousand times.

Now change one input. A customer types "Washing machine shows drain error E21", which embeds as (7, 1, 4), of length the square root of 66, about 8.124. Against "Drain pump error" the dot product is 7×8 + 1×0 + 4×5 = 76, and cosine = 76 ÷ (8.124 × 9.434) = 0.992. The score is near the ceiling of 1.0 and the answer is right. So the winner's score, not its rank, separates a good answer (0.992) from a bad one (0.564), and a threshold turns that into a rule. Exhibit 3 shows what each candidate costs.

Exhibit 3. Threshold sweep on the audit (200 answerable, 40 unanswerable). Refused = top score below threshold; wrongly answered = top score at or above it. Weekly figures scale to 20,000 unanswerable searches.
ThresholdAnswerable queries servedWrongly refusedRefused, % of 200Wrongly answered (of 40)Wrongly answered, %Wrong answers per week
0.5019642.0%3895.0%19,000
0.60188126.0%2767.5%13,500
0.701712914.5%922.5%4,500
0.751425829.0%37.5%1,500

Raising the threshold from 0.50 to 0.75 cuts weekly wrong answers from 19,000 to 1,500, but refuses 58 of every 200 good queries, 29,000 a week. Choosing a point on that trade-off is a product decision, not a modelling one.

5. Nuances a learner must not miss

Similar is not the same as relevant

Similarity is closeness in a space learned from general text; relevance belongs to the user's need. "Warranty terms" is close to a chiller question because both concern appliances; the model cannot know Grihini does not sell the thing asked about. Whether similarity is the right notion of relevance is a problem-fit judgement.

The system never abstains by itself

Nearest-neighbour lookup is a ranking; five poor items still have a first place. "I do not know" exists only if someone adds a threshold and decides what happens below it.

Scores are not probabilities

A cosine of 0.70 does not mean a 70 per cent chance of being right. The scale depends on the model, language, passage length and corpus, so a threshold must be recalibrated from labelled examples whenever any of them changes, as Exhibit 3 was.

The measure changes the ranking

In Exhibit 2, "Change phone number" is second by Euclidean distance and last by cosine: a short vector sits near the origin, close to everything in straight-line terms, yet points away from the query. Tripling the "Drain pump error" vector to (24, 0, 15) leaves its cosine at 0.523 while its Euclidean distance rises from 8.124 to 25.652. Use the measure the model was trained with.

Meaning is not exactness

Embeddings are weak on identifiers: error code "E21" may land near E12. Many systems therefore add keyword matching, called hybrid search.

Questions to ask before relying on it

What share of real queries have no answer in the corpus? What do top scores look like for them? Which model produced the scores, and what happens when it changes? Who decides what happens below the threshold?

6. Different products, different stakes

The same mechanism carries different risks depending on the product, as Exhibit 4 summarises.

Exhibit 4. Where the "always returns something" failure bites hardest.
SettingCost of a confident wrong resultUsual safeguard
Consumer help or product searchLost customer or bad review; cheap per error, high volumeThreshold plus "talk to us" fallback
B2B contracts, policies, manualsA wrong clause acted upon; rare but expensiveCitations, human review, conservative threshold
Marketplace listingsPoor match erodes trust; sparse categories have no good matchHide low scores; report supply gaps

In a consumer product the lever is volume: with 20,000 unanswerable searches a week, even a modest error rate yields thousands of bad moments, so a human fallback matters more than ranking polish. In B2B, queries are fewer but results are acted upon, so refusal is cheaper than a wrong clause. In a marketplace, absence is information: a category with no sellers should return nothing and be logged as unmet demand. An early company can hand-label fifty queries in an afternoon; a large one needs a standing evaluation set and a named owner, because a threshold calibrated in July is stale by December.

7. Common mistakes

Exhibit 5. Three recurring errors, how they show, and the cheapest test.
MistakeSymptom from outsideUnderlying misunderstandingCheapest diagnostic
Shipping with no thresholdFluent, off-topic answers to uncovered questionsBelief that the system knows when it has no answerAsk 20 uncovered questions; read the top result and score
Copying a threshold from a blog or another productGood demos, then too many refusals or wrong answersTreating similarity scores as universal unitsPlot top scores for 50 answerable and 50 unanswerable queries of your own
Judging quality on easy queriesDemo works, weekly complaints riseTesting with questions the content authors wroteSample real logged queries, including abandoned ones

Grihini made the third: its testers were content writers, so the unanswerable 16.7 per cent was invisible.

8. What good looks like

A well-run version has four features. A labelled evaluation set exists before launch, with answerable and deliberately unanswerable queries in realistic proportion. The threshold is chosen from measured trade-offs like Exhibit 3, with each error type's cost written down. Below the threshold the product is honest, offering a person, a form or closest topics labelled as only possibly related. And unanswered queries are logged and reviewed weekly, the cheapest market research the company owns. None of this requires a better model; it requires someone to own the question "what do we do when nothing is close?"

9. What Gayatri decided

She chose two tiers, not one line. At or above 0.70, the system shows the best article as before. Between 0.60 and 0.70 it shows "These might be related" with three titles and a prominent chat button, because this band held 17 answerable queries (188 less 171) and 18 unanswerable ones (27 less 9), nearly a coin flip. Below 0.60 it routes to a human and logs the query. At 0.70, wrong answers fall from 19,000 a week to 4,500, and the 14.5 per cent of good queries that lose an instant answer still reach a person. Gopal will rerun the audit whenever the embedding model changes, with Goncalo Teixeira, a retrieval consultant in Lisbon, reviewing the method.

Next come retrieval-augmented generation, which places a language model after this lookup and inherits every failure described here, and chunking, which governs what a "passage" is. Two questions to sit with. If 17 per cent of your product's searches had no answer, would you know, and what would you change? And where, in a product you know, is something being ranked first simply because it must rank somewhere?
case40v1-aivocab.vector.search:
Nearest Is Not Fitting

Yojak Industrial Exchange and the search that could not be silent — Pune, October 2026

1. The night before

At twenty minutes to midnight on Sunday, 11 October 2026, Yashodhara Kamat sat on the floor of her study in Baner, Pune, with three printouts before her and a fourth turned face down.

The first was a photograph. A maintenance supervisor at a textile mill in Ichalkaranji had searched Yojak Industrial Exchange for "bearing for the ring frame spindle, humming at 1400 rpm, outer race warm," taken the top result, and found that its bore was 30 mm where his shaft was 35 mm. The mill lost nine hours. The part cost ₹1,240; the credit note, the reverse pickup and two support calls cost rather more.

The second was Friday's retrieval benchmark, which said Yojak's search was both much better and much worse than anyone had assumed. The third was the sales forecast, which assumed the search would be ready for four client tenants by February. The fourth, face down, was Thursday's board page.

Engineering needed a direction on Monday morning — not because the problem had clarified, but because the index contract's amendment window closed on Saturday, 31 October, the Muscat storefront went live on Monday, 2 November, and the pre-Diwali procurement peak ran into both.

2. How Yojak came to be built this way

Yojak was founded in Pune in 2018 by Wamika Sule, a former plant-engineering manager, on one observation: a factory needing a gasket had an identification problem, not a procurement one. The buyer knew the symptom and the machine; the catalogue spoke in part numbers and standards.

The company aggregated spares and consumables from 9,400 sellers into a catalogue of 62,00,000 stock-keeping units, selling to manufacturers around Ludhiana, Rajkot, Coimbatore and Pune. In the year ended 31 March 2026 it recorded ₹2,850 crore of gross merchandise value, net revenue of 12.0 per cent of that figure — ₹342 crore — and an EBITDA loss of ₹58 crore. In September 2026, orders beginning with a search query accounted for ₹212.73 crore of the month's ₹246 crore of GMV, or 86.5 per cent.

What now constrained everything was decided on 18 March 2024, when Yojak signed a thirty-six-month managed-index agreement with Wistaar Retrieval Systems. Wistaar hosted the vector index, supplied the embedding model, and charged a tier fee of ₹9.60 lakh a month for up to 2,00,00,000 vectors and 1,200 peak queries per second, plus ₹6.40 lakh for each additional crore or part thereof. Yojak needed 62,00,000 vectors, one per SKU — 31.0 per cent of the cap.

Three clauses had become load-bearing. The embedding model was Wistaar's and could not be substituted mid-term. The fee was a floor rather than a usage charge, levied per index, so every isolated client tenant carried its own. And one re-pricing amendment was allowed, to be served by 31 October 2026.

3. The industry around it

Indian industrial MRO procurement was formalising fast. Moglix and IndiaMART had built scale on catalogue breadth, Zetwerk and Bizongo came at the same buyers from manufacturing, Amazon Business and Tata nexarc brought distribution, and ONDC promised portable catalogues. GST e-invoicing had made the paperwork tractable for a Udyam-registered buyer with eleven employees, the buyer Yojak was built for. The Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023, settled one argument before it began: an enterprise client's private catalogue could not share the index serving the public marketplace.

Wafa Technical Trading LLC, a Muscat distributor with 340 industrial accounts, had licensed Yojak's search as an embedded storefront for ₹2.40 crore a year, with a 900-millisecond p95 latency service level measured at Wafa's own edge. Yuvraj Deshpande, running enterprise sales for the Americas from Houston, had three North American OEM distributors in late-stage talks worth a combined ₹3.84 crore a year on the same model. Four tenants meant four private indexes and four floors: 4 × ₹9.60 lakh = ₹38.40 lakh a month, against tenant revenue of (₹2.40 crore + ₹3.84 crore) ÷ 12 = ₹52 lakh a month. The floors alone would take 73.8 per cent of it.

4. What happened, and what has since turned out to be wrong

On Monday, 6 July 2026, Yojak released "Describe It" to all of its traffic. A buyer could type what was in front of him — a noise, a leak, a machine model — and the system turned that text into an embedding, a list of numbers standing for its meaning, then returned the catalogue items whose embeddings sat nearest. Six weeks looked like a success: queries that had returned nothing now returned something, clicks rose, and the "cannot find the part" queue shortened. Yashodhara presented it to the board in August without qualification.

By early September the pattern had cohered. Waheeda Qureshi's catalogue-operations team in Coimbatore reported a sharp rise in items returned under the code "part does not fit," concentrated in the queries Describe It had been built for. In September, 4,122 of 1,15,614 search-originated orders came back as wrong-part returns — 3.57 per cent — but that average hid a five-fold spread across query types (Exhibit 1).

Zeeshan Tirmizi, who led retrieval engineering from Bengaluru, found the mechanism quickly. A vector index returns the nearest stored items to a query, and there is always a nearest item. If the catalogue holds no 35 mm bore bearing for that spindle, the index does not report absence; it offers the 30 mm bearing, almost indistinguishable in the geometry of the embedding, the descriptions differing in one number the model was never trained to treat as decisive. The system had no notion of "nothing here," and would acquire one only if the product set a threshold and designed a behaviour below it.

Worse, to Zeeshan, was the benchmark on part numbers. Embeddings smear exact identifiers: a buyer typing "6205 2RS" wanted one SKU and received a neighbourhood of plausible ones. The keyword index switched off in July as redundant had been far better at the 40.0 per cent of queries carrying a part number (Exhibit 3).

A test of a thresholded "no exact match" state ran from Monday, 14 September to Friday, 25 September, when a catalogue migration contaminated attribute data in one arm; the partial result has since been quoted in four meetings to support three conclusions (Exhibit 6). Fourteen weeks after launch, the search was better at understanding what buyers meant, worse at saying when it did not know, and running on a contract signed for a problem Yojak no longer had.

Figure A: 6 July to 12 October is 98 days, fourteen weeks exactly. The A/B ran 14–25 September inclusive, twelve days of a planned twenty-eight.

5. The people

Yashodhara Kamat, Chief Product Officer, Pune, owns the search roadmap, the Wistaar relationship and Thursday's board page, and knows a correction now reads as a reversal of her August presentation. Her stated position is that the threshold is the decision; she has not said she suspects it is not. Her co-founder Wamika Sule has told her to fix the returns and told Yuvraj not to slow the Houston pipeline, without acknowledging that the instructions conflict.

Zeeshan Tirmizi, Director of Search and Retrieval Engineering, Bengaluru, wants hybrid retrieval — keyword and vector candidates fused — with a cross-encoder re-ranking the top fifty, and his benchmark supports him. He also recommended retiring the keyword index in July, and has not volunteered that his preference partly restores what he removed.

Waheeda Qureshi, Head of Catalogue Operations, Coimbatore, has 210 associates enriching listings; only 12,00,000 of 62,00,000 SKUs carry verified attributes such as bore, thread and tolerance. She argues retrieval cannot resolve a distinction the catalogue does not record, and wants the Q4 budget moved to attribute coverage — her own line.

Yogesh Ambardekar, Head of Platform Infrastructure, Hyderabad, owns the Wistaar bill and the latency budget, and has measured 180 milliseconds of added p95 network and TLS time from Yojak's Mumbai region to Wafa's edge. He wants the amendment negotiated hard; privately he wants Yojak out of Wistaar altogether.

Zoya Mirchandani, Staff Data Scientist for relevance, Lisbon, built the labelled benchmark and is the only person who has read return reason codes individually. In a sample of 200 "part does not fit" returns she found a material share where the buyer had misidentified his own machine, and will not state a number from one week and one category. She will not call the returns a retrieval failure, nor say they are not.

Yuvraj Deshpande, Vice-President, Enterprise Sales (Americas), Houston, carries the ₹3.84 crore pipeline, is paid on signed contract value, and treats the per-tenant index floor as someone else's problem. He has not told Pune that two of his three prospects want a recall figure in the contract.

Zarin Fernandes, Director of Design, Kochi, designed the "no exact match" state used in the halted test, with its guided attribute picker. She argues the question is not whether to suppress uncertain results but how to make the buyer's machine part of the query at all. She has not mentioned that her state cost orders.

8. The options as Yashodhara currently frames them

Option 1: hold the search, fund the catalogue. Leave configuration A in production, move the Q4 engineering budget to attribute verification, and accept ₹58.53 lakh a month of return cost through the peak, on the argument that no retrieval change can separate parts on attributes the catalogue does not record.

Option 2: ship configuration D everywhere. Hybrid retrieval with a cross-encoder re-rank: 86.3 per cent recall@10 and 59.8 per cent precision@1 at ₹19.50 lakh a month. It breaches the Muscat service level at 940 ms and still has no concept of absence.

Option 3: set a threshold and design the silence. Resume Zarin's no-match state at a fused-score cutoff. The only evidence is Exhibit 6, which halved returns, cost 408 orders and finished ₹1.04 lakh behind — on a test contaminated, truncated and blind to everything past the first order.

Option 4: narrow the ground. Run configuration E, restricting Describe It to the 12,00,000 verified SKUs and keeping keyword search over the rest. Latency clears Muscat at 870 ms, recall@10 falls to 74.4 per cent against a ceiling of 77.6, and the saving is zero.

All four treat configuration as the variable and the query as given. Exhibit 3 suggests query type predicts more than configuration does; Zarin argues the query is what Yojak has never designed; Zoya argues nobody knows what share of the 4,122 returns the search caused. None is on the list.

9. The deadline and the hard constraints

Engineering needs a direction on Monday, 12 October, to have anything live before the pre-Diwali fortnight. The Wistaar amendment must be served by Saturday, 31 October, and whatever it asks fixes Yojak's index economics until 17 March 2027: a higher vector cap costs money she may not need, and not asking forecloses chunking. Wafa's storefront goes live on 2 November at a 900 ms p95 with service credits attached. The Q4 engineering budget is ₹1.9 crore and fully committed; headcount is frozen until the Series C closes. Catalogue operations can verify about 1,40,000 SKUs a quarter. The DPDP Act and the enterprise contracts require a separate index per private tenant, each at its own ₹9.60 lakh floor — ₹38.40 lakh a month against ₹52 lakh of tenant revenue once all four are live. Two of Yuvraj's three prospects want a recall figure in the contract that nobody has agreed to measure.

Wahini Industries: What Ingit Was Actually Doing

An ambiguous case for discussion. Pune, October 2026.

Wahini Industries is fictional; its market and regulators are real. The exhibits come from different parts of the company and do not agree.

1. Sunday night, 25 October 2026

A quarter past ten on the Sunday night before the board's technology sub-committee met. In Wahini Industries' product office on Mumbai–Pune Road, Iravati Deshmukh, Chief Product Officer, had three documents open that would not sit together.

The first, from Wimarsh Labs, the Bengaluru firm that built Ingit — the assistant Wahini's technicians carry on their phones — reported Ingit answering technical questions correctly 94.6 per cent of the time. The second, Wahini's own quality audit of 9 October, sampled 1,520 real answers and found 220 wrong: 14.5 per cent. The third, from Oloolua Process Works, a bottler outside Nairobi, claimed ₹38.5 lakh in damages after a wrong seal kit kept a filling line down sixty-one hours.

One transcript had lodged in her head. A Nashik technician had asked, in Marathi, which seal kit fitted a boiler-feed pump on chloride-bearing duty. Ingit replied WPX-280/4-SS304-K2: real, orderable, wrong metallurgy. The right answer, WPX-280/4-SS316-K2, differs by two characters.

Her engineering head had written that morning: "Ingit knows the 280 series cold. We will show it more of our own manuals and it will stop." She no longer believed anybody in the room could say what "knows" stood for. On Monday she had to recommend one of four paths to a sub-committee that had spent ₹7.2 crore.

2. The company, and a decision made in 2019

Waman Deshmukh — Iravati's father — founded Wahini in Pune in 1988, making bronze impellers for sugar mills. It now makes centrifugal pumps, screw compressors and water-treatment skids at Pune, Coimbatore and Nagpur. FY2026 revenue was ₹2,140 crore, spares and service ₹612 crore of it, or 28.6 per cent, and a far larger share of profit. Exports were ₹134.6 crore of that line, and Wahini works with 1,900 technicians, two-thirds on franchised rolls.

The constraining decision came in 2019, and was good. Project Ekroop consolidated fourteen catalogues into one ERP parts master of 1,42,000 codes, each with a metallurgy suffix, duty class and supersession chain. But Ekroop covered parts, not knowledge: bulletins and torque charts for machines sold before 2005 — roughly 8,400 photocopied pages — stayed in a document store as page images, never recognised into text. Eighteen per cent of the pumps Wahini services were sold before 2005.

In April 2023 Wahini signed a five-year, ₹12 crore agreement with Wimarsh Labs carrying exclusivity on "AI-assisted service tooling". ₹7.2 crore is paid; the remaining ₹4.8 crore carries a 30 per cent penalty, ₹1.44 crore, and legal reads the clause as blocking a second vendor to March 2028.

3. The industry

The market is unsentimental. Thermax, KSB, Grundfos, Shakti Pumps, Elgi Equipments and Atlas Copco India compete on first cost at tender, then earn, as Wahini does, on spares and maintenance. The Jal Jeevan Mission and AMRUT have put municipal pumping sets into districts where the nearest competent technician is ninety minutes away, while Bureau of Indian Standards and Bureau of Energy Efficiency labelling have tightened specification.

Two forces bear hardest on Ingit. Attrition ran at 31 per cent last year and a new technician takes fourteen months to become safe on the 280 series, so an assistant that compresses it is worth a great deal. And GST e-invoicing and supersession logic mean a wrongly ordered spare leaves a trail in three systems and, on exports, a customs record that an East African bottler on liquidated damages will cite.

4. What happened, and what has turned out to be wrong

Ingit was prototyped in November 2025, and the design was, on paper, conservative: the technician photographs a nameplate or types a question, Wahini's software identifies the machine, searches the digitised manuals, and sends what it finds with the question through Wimarsh Labs' gateway to a commercial large language model. Four things were believed: Ingit would answer only from Wahini's manuals; would say so when it did not know; would escalate hard cases; and its correctness was the model's property, improvable with more Wahini material.

The pilot opened on 1 July 2026 to 420 technicians in Pune, Nashik and Coimbatore, and to 30 September Ingit produced 38,000 answers. On 18 September, after the 12 August Nairobi incident, Ishrat Qureshi's quality team began a stratified audit of 1,520 of those answers, graded against the parts master, the manual, or a design engineer's ruling. It landed on 9 October; Wimarsh Labs' one-pager arrived on 20 October, eleven days later.

All four have since failed.

On the first and second: in 494 of the 1,520 audited answers the search layer returned no manual passage above threshold, mostly pre-2005 machines whose bulletins remain page images. Ingit declined in 38 of those 494, 7.7 per cent, and answered confidently in the other 456 — not from Wahini's manuals, none being in front of it, but from what the model absorbed in training about pumps generally. Nothing made declining likelier when evidence was absent, because nothing knew it was.

On the third: the sub-committee's dashboard reports "the model escalated to the expert desk in 8.2 per cent of answers" — 3,116 of 38,000. Reading the gateway code in October, Wasim Lodhi found escalation fired on a pattern match for phrases such as "I am not certain". The model cannot route anything; the 8.2 per cent counts a turn of phrase.

On the fourth, and most expensively: the implementation trimmed long conversations from the top of the message list to fit the cost tier's 8,000-token limit. The retrieved manual text sat at the top, so it went first — mid-conversation it quietly left the prompt while the answers went on sounding exactly as authoritative.

Not to scale. The vendor one-pager was circulated eleven days after the quality audit and does not cite it.

5. The people

Iravati Deshmukh, Chief Product Officer, Pune, owns the recommendation: no number in a technician's hand unchecked. Founder's daughter, Ingit's sponsor. Unsaid: she cannot yet explain the failure in one sentence, and fears tokens and probabilities will sound like excuses.

Ezhilarasan Subramanian, VP Engineering, Coimbatore: the problem is coverage, curable by fine-tuning on Wahini's manuals. His incentive is eleven engineers and eighteen months of work. Unsaid: he proposed a deterministic parts-code check in February and lost on cost; reopening it admits that.

Omana Velayudhan, President, Service and Spares, Nagpur, carries the service P&L. She wants Ingit live through the Diwali overhaul season, when volumes triple, and argues the audit over-sampled hard questions — rightly. Unsaid: her regional heads picked the pilot cohorts, and picked their three best regions.

Ishrat Qureshi, Quality and Product Compliance, Mumbai, ran the audit: no code or torque value unverified. Export damages claims land on her. Unsaid: eleven people graded 1,520 answers in three weeks and nobody measured inter-grader disagreement.

Eshwari Raghunathan, Chief Financial Officer, Pune, holds the ₹7.2 crore spent and the ₹1.44 crore penalty, and will fund whichever option carries a defensible benefit. Unsaid: she disbelieves the claimed benefit, and has not written that down.

Wasim Lodhi, Senior Data Scientist, Manchester, alone has read both the gateway code and the audit. The team grades the model, he says, when production is the model plus retrieval plus the trimming rule plus a pattern match. He joined after the architecture was set; his standing is low.

Ewa Lewandowska, Principal Designer, Kraków, designed the answer card and thinks it lies: a verified lookup and an unsourced sentence render in the same typeface, tone and card. Unsaid: she raised this in March and settled for a grey "based on service records" line.

Omondi Barasa, Regional Service Head, East Africa, Nairobi, holds the Oloolua relationship: switch Ingit off outside India, or give him a desk on his own hours. His incentive: the December renewals.

"A verified parts-master lookup and an invented sentence render in the same card, same size, same tone. The model is not lying to the technician. We are."Ewa Lewandowska, design review

"Switch it off for the overhaul season and I lose eleven working days a technician to calls the expert desk will not pick up. Give me the 85 per cent and I will manage."Omana Velayudhan, service review

8. The options, as Deshmukh currently frames them

Deshmukh has written four options on the whiteboard, costed by Raghunathan's office. Notice the framing: all four treat Ingit as one product with one accuracy number, and none separates "what part is this" from "explain this fault".

9. The deadline and the hard constraints

The sub-committee meets at 11 a.m. on Monday, 26 October. Four things bind it. Money: ₹7.2 crore of the ₹12 crore commitment is spent; the ₹1.44 crore penalty on the remaining ₹4.8 crore makes a clean break expensive, and exclusivity runs to March 2028. Raghunathan's FY2027 digital envelope is ₹400 lakh.

People and time. Nine expert-desk engineers serve 1,900 technicians, none on East African hours; four more for Barasa cost roughly ₹96 lakh a year and take four months. Overhaul season begins with the Diwali shutdowns on 8 November and runs to mid-January, tripling Velayudhan's volumes, so any change not live by 8 November is live in February.

Regulation and contract. The ₹38.5 lakh Oloolua claim is unresolved and four distributor contracts renew in December. Compliance has asked since July whether site photographs sent to a third-party endpoint fit Wahini's notice obligations under the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023.

10. Questions for discussion

  1. Rewrite "Ingit knows the 280 series cold" as what the system literally does on one request. Which of Subramanian's conclusions survive?
  2. Exhibits 1 and 2 report accuracies of 94.6 and 85.5 per cent on one product. What is each a property of, and what can each honestly answer?
  3. Exhibit 2's total states a weighted 14.5 per cent, the mean of its six rates is 12.6 per cent, and re-weighting to the period's mix gives 11.6 per cent. Which belongs in the board paper, and what does the choice commit Wahini to?
  4. Exhibits 3, 4 and 5 slice one audit three ways. Build the account that explains all three, say which option it argues for, and name what would falsify it.
  5. The dashboard says the model escalated 8.2 per cent of answers. Given what escalation turned out to be, what else there should Deshmukh distrust, and what rule catches such a metric first?
  6. Her four options assume Ingit is one product with one accuracy number. Is that defensible? What should she do on Monday morning, in what order, and what would she tell the sub-committee about the ₹7.2 crore?

11. A quarter past eleven

Deshmukh read the Nashik transcript once more. Khandare, nineteen years on pumps, had asked a reasonable question in Marathi, and Ingit had answered in a well-formed sentence containing a well-formed part code that resolved cleanly in the parts master and was wrong. Nothing had failed in the way that word is normally used. Somewhere the manual passage had left the prompt, and the machine had gone on producing the next plausible character, as built, with nothing in it to tell the part that fits from the one that merely reads so.

She wrote one line under the four options and left it for the morning: what did we think we were testing? Then she packed the documents away, undecided which she believed.
exp40v2-aivocab.llm.what:
What a Large Language Model Actually Is

A near-expert treatment: the function, the bits, the schools that disagree, and the tests the definition implies.

1. Two decisions, eleven days apart

On Thursday 3 September 2026, Sharvari Mhatre, vice-president of product at Vimarsh Support Systems in Bengaluru, opened a renewal file she had been avoiding. Vimarsh sells a support layer to thirty-eight Indian consumer brands: Vimarsh Uttar reads a ticket, retrieves the relevant passage of the brand's policy and drafts a reply, across 11,40,000 tickets monthly. Uttar Sahay drafts and an agent presses send; Uttar Swayam sends with no human in the loop, priced a third lower.

Yuvika Beauty Works, a Mumbai skincare brand and Vimarsh's largest client, wanted Uttar Swayam from its renewal date, Friday 16 October, forty-three days on. Its procurement note argued in one sentence: "Your model already knows our returns policy better than our agents do." Prateek Bhanushali, the engineering lead, had written much the same internally: "the model knew the right answer 73 per cent of the time and decided correctly on the edge cases." Kadri Mägi, Vimarsh's applied-science reviewer in Tallinn, returned the memo with one comment: knew and decided are not measurements. What did you measure?

Eleven days later, on Monday 14 September, the same argument ran in Coimbatore. Meenal Kanitkar ran connected products at Yantrik Pump Industries: about 2,40,000 fielded units carry a networked controller, and roughly 1,900 dealer technicians make about 60,000 service visits a quarter. Their assistant, Yantrik Nidan, answers a technician's spoken question. Nidan Onboard is a small model quantised into the controller's firmware, with no network call; Nidan Setu is hosted and first retrieves the relevant service bulletin. The ZX-series dealer rollout was fixed for Monday 2 November, forty-nine days out. Hariharan Ponnusamy, the embedded lead, preferred Onboard: no latency, no connectivity dependency, no per-call cost. Joris ten Kate, the firmware partner in Eindhoven, asked what happens to a specification living in the weights when the specification changes.

Both decisions turn on one piece of vocabulary. Each team had written a claim about what its model knows; neither was a measurement, and the accurate restatement implied a different test, architecture and contract.

2. The idea: a conditional distribution, and nothing else

A large language model is a deterministic function with fixed parameters. Its input is a sequence of tokens, the sub-word units into which text is cut. Its output is a score for every token in a fixed vocabulary, typically 50,000 to 2,00,000 entries, normalised by softmax into a probability distribution over what comes next: p(tokent | token1 … tokent−1). That is the whole of it.

Three negative statements follow, and holding all three at once is what this topic is for. There is no separate store of facts: nothing inside can be queried as a table, and the clause or torque figure in an answer was reconstructed, not looked up. There are no beliefs: the function holds no proposition that could be true or false. There is no execution step: software outside the model picks a token from the distribution, and the function is called again.

The history explains the shape. Shannon's 1948 information theory treated English as a stochastic source, and by the 1980s IBM's speech group was scoring transcription candidates with n-gram counts, which could not carry long-range conditioning. The transformer, published in 2017, replaced recurrence with attention and made conditioning length a matter of compute. Nobody set out to build a knowledge base.

That surprise is where the schools divide, and each signs a different proposition. Form-without-meaning, after Bender and Gebru in 2021: the model is a distribution over linguistic form with no communicative intent, and fluency is no evidence of accuracy. Emergent representation, arguing from interpretability work where probes recover board state from a model trained only on game moves: predicting tokens well enough forces internal structures that function as a model of whatever generated the text — but not beliefs. The simulator view: an apparent decision is the behaviour of a character the prompt conjured. Behaviourism, where most shipping teams sit: the ontology is undecidable from outside; specify the thing by measured behaviour on a stated input distribution.

The sentence Sharvari put into her renewal note: "Given the text we place in front of it, the model assigns high probability to the correct reply on a measured share of a stated ticket population."

3. Mechanics in depth: what "assigns probabilities" costs in bits

Experts do not argue about whether a model knows something; they measure how much probability it puts on the right continuation. The unit is the bit and the measure is cross-entropy: for each token that appeared, compute the surprisal, −log2 p. Average those for bits per token; two raised to that average is perplexity, the effective number of equally likely choices per step.

The correct tightening figure for the ZX-series impeller lock nut is 22 newton-metres; for the older VP-series it is 18. Kadri recorded the probability Nidan Onboard assigned to the token belonging at each of six positions, with nothing in the context but the technician's question.

The probability column is not summed: these are six conditional probabilities, not a distribution. Their product is the sentence's joint probability, 2−16, or 1 in 65,536.

Surprisals total 16.0 bits over six tokens, so cross-entropy is 16.0 ÷ 6 = 2.6667 bits per token and perplexity 22.6667 = 6.35, about a fair six-way choice. The average conceals the problem: 5.0 of the 16.0 bits sit on one token. Grammar was nearly free; the number cost more than all the rest.

She re-ran the same positions with the ZX-series bulletin retrieved into the context. The probability on " 22" rose from 0.03125 to 0.968, so its surprisal fell from 5.0 bits to 0.047. Two second-order effects are routinely missed. The failure is not noise but a systematic pull towards the commoner training pattern: VP-series pumps dominated fourteen years of service documents, and lowering temperature makes the answer more consistent, not more correct. And 11.4 per cent of the mass spreads across the rest of the vocabulary, the signature of an under-specified prompt.

4. When the definition bites, and when it is merely pedantic

Condition one: correctness depends on a fact the context may or may not determine. Test it by deleting the supplied text and re-running. At Yantrik this is decisive: remove the bulletin and accuracy on the newest family collapses. At Vimarsh too — a policy Yuvika revised in August cannot be in older weights.

Condition two: the same input will arrive twice and must not diverge. Test it by running one prompt twenty times and counting agreement. This bites hard at Vimarsh, where identical complaints may get different offers, and not at all on Yantrik's greedy-decoded answers, which are stably wrong.

Condition three: someone will ask the system to justify itself, and the justification will be read as evidence. Test whether the stated reason predicts the answer better than chance when the two are generated separately. This bites at Vimarsh, where a refund refusal may be contested, and at Yantrik, where a warranty claim may hinge on it.

Where the definition misleads is worth saying as plainly. Where deterministic code validates the output, checking three permitted labels or rejecting a malformed payload, insisting that the model has no beliefs produces anxiety without a test.

5. Hard edge cases: seams, firmware and regulators

In a multi-tenant platform like Vimarsh the weights are shared across thirty-eight clients and the context is client-specific, so a capability shown for one brand transfers only as far as that brand's retrieved text does the work. Vimarsh's sales engineers had been demonstrating on Yuvika's well-structured policy and quoting the result to clients whose policies live in email threads. In a two-sided setting the generated text becomes one party's words to another, so mature marketplaces narrow what may be emitted at all.

Regulated contexts expose the sharpest contradiction. India's Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 governs what may enter the context, and sectoral supervisors, such as the Reserve Bank of India for lending and the Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority for claims, expect a decision to be explainable and reproducible. A conditional distribution has no deliberation to disclose. So move the decision out: the model drafts, rules decide, and the trail records the retrieved text and the rule fired.

Hardware plus software adds a constraint software teams rarely feel. Onboard's weights are quantised to fit the controller's memory, which perturbs the distribution, and frozen in firmware across 2,40,000 units, so a specification change becomes a firmware campaign; Setu fetches the bulletin, so the same change is a document update. In an AI-native company the distinction becomes a warranty question.

6. Nine nuances that separate the expert from the competent practitioner

Knowing has a narrow honest meaning: frequency

Training made certain continuations more probable: that is all the word can legitimately mean. The tell is performance graded by frequency: from identical weights, Yantrik scored 81.25 per cent on the fourteen-year-old VP-series and 12.5 per cent on the six-month-old ZX-series.

Confidence is a property of the text, not the world

The 96.8 per cent on " 22" describes how strongly the context pushed towards that token, not a claim that 22 newton-metres is correct. The expert uses the number to route outputs to a human reviewer while refusing it as evidence of truth, and calibrates it against graded accuracy, as in Figure 3.

An explanation is more sampled text, not a readout

Ask why, and the same loop produces a plausible justification. The tell is a team that generates answer and reason in one pass and files the pair as an audit record: no process was executed to report on. Faithfulness is measurable — perturb the input, see whether the reason moves.

Greedy decoding has a failure mode of its own

Teams reach for temperature zero wanting determinism, and read determinism as safety. The tell is zero variance reported with no accuracy figure beside it. Where the weights hold a systematic bias, greedy decoding locks it in: Yantrik's least random setting gave its most reliably wrong answer.

Most "model problems" are retrieval problems

The tell is an incident review naming the model version and nothing else. When Vimarsh's replies degraded for one client in July, a chunking change had split a returns clause in two, so the retrieved half omitted the ninety-day limit. The context was wrong, not the model.

Tokenisation is not neutral across languages

The same 900-word science chapter occupied 1,980 tokens in Marathi and 4,140 in Telugu on Zubaan Learning Exchange's tokeniser, 2.09 times as many for identical content. A 1,28,000-token context holds 64 Marathi chapters but only 30 Telugu ones. The tell is quality reported by language without tokens reported by language.

Post-training changes the distribution, not the ontology

Instruction tuning and reinforcement learning from human feedback reshape which continuations are probable, which is why a modern model refuses, hedges and answers in the second person. An expert reads a refusal as a probable continuation; the tell is someone negotiating with it rather than changing the context.

The context window is a budget; truncation is silent

When the assembled prompt exceeds the window something is dropped, and the output gives no signal. The expert's tell is an alert on prompt length. Vimarsh's worst outputs clustered on long conversations, where the policy passage was appended last and cut first.

Aggregates hide the tokens carrying the money

The perplexity table makes this arithmetic: 5.0 of the 16.0 bits sat on one token, a 31.3 per cent share of total surprisal on a single number, while average perplexity looked unremarkable. The expert restricts the metric to the spans that matter: figures, amounts, dates.

7. Across product types, and across stages

In consumer products one wrong sentence costs little and volume is enormous, so the definition shows up as statistical discipline: sample outputs, track complaint rates, accept a known error floor. Zubaan could survive a wrong explanation, but not a wrong-explanation rate that differed by language. In B2B and enterprise settings each output feeds a professional's decision with money attached, so it becomes architectural: put the authoritative text in the context and keep a human or a rule between the distribution and the consequence. On a platform the issue is attribution. In hardware, weights are inventory. In AI-native products the definition becomes the contract.

By stage the differences are real but smaller than expected. An early-stage team calls a provider's model and tests a few dozen cases. A growth-stage team must pin a version, keep a standing golden set and own prompt changes, because a silent upgrade moves every distribution at once.

8. Three worked examples

9. Failure modes, their early warnings and the cost of catching them late

Crediting the weights with what the prompt supplied. Warning sign: a pilot succeeded where a colleague pasted the source document. Diagnostic: what is accuracy with the retrieved text removed? Caught late, it surfaces on the least-documented catalogue — Yantrik's 12.5 per cent, at rollout.

Treating a stated reason as an audit trail. Warning sign: compliance documentation quoting the model's explanation. Diagnostic: does the reason still track the answer when the input is perturbed? Caught late, the decision record records no decision.

Reading low variance as reliability. Warning sign: zero disagreement across repeated runs, with no accuracy figure beside it. Diagnostic: is the consistent answer correct on a graded set? Caught late, one systematic error has been repeated at volume.

Averaging over positions that do not matter equally. Warning sign: quality reported as one number. Diagnostic: what is accuracy on figures, amounts and clause references alone? Caught late, a settlement figure is wrong while the dashboard is green.

Blending populations that behave differently. Warning sign: one figure spanning languages, clients or product families. Diagnostic: what is the worst segment, and how large? Zubaan's 70.5 per cent blended figure concealed a 25.0-point language gap.

Assuming the model is a fixed asset. Warning sign: no pinned version and no alert on distribution shift. Diagnostic: if the provider changed the model tonight, which metric moves first, and who sees it? Caught late, a regression arrives with nothing of your own to blame.

10. Where experts genuinely disagree

Does next-token prediction produce understanding? The compression argument at its strongest: to predict text generated by a world, a system must implicitly represent that world's regularities, and interpretability results recovering internal structure are evidence of it. It would be wrong if those structures proved reliably shallow: present on toy domains, absent where they matter. The opposing position rests on fluent and correct output coming apart systematically.

Is "knows" a harmless shorthand? One camp holds that all engineering vocabulary is metaphorical — a database does not "remember" either — and that policing language wastes effort better spent on evals. The other holds that this metaphor makes teams test a handful of answers instead of a distribution, and survives into contracts. The first is wrong if loose vocabulary reliably produces worse tests.

Can chain-of-thought be trusted as a window? One position: intermediate tokens are real computation, since the model performs better when it produces them, so they carry information about how the answer was reached. The other: faithfulness measures poorly, the trace can be perturbed without changing the answer, and calling it introspection is a category error. The second is wrong if faithfulness proves an optimisable training target.

Is the distribution the product, or a component? The behaviourist view holds that a well-fenced system — schemas, validators, rules, humans — makes the model's nature an implementation detail. The opposing view holds that fencing moves the probabilistic character to the boundary rather than removing it, and the fence is specified by someone reasoning about what the model "understands".

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has merely studied this can recite that a model predicts the next token and has no fact store. Someone who has internalised it rewrites claims into tests as a reflex: "the model knows our policy" becomes "given the retrieved passage, accuracy on 200 graded tickets is X per cent". They ask where a fact lives, in weights or context, before asking whether the model is good, because that determines the fix and its cost. They read confidence as a routing signal. And they know when to stop: once the surrounding system constrains output to a validated set, the definition stops implying a test.

12. Closing: what Sharvari and Meenal decided

Sharvari renewed Yuvika Beauty Works on Uttar Sahay, not Uttar Swayam, and put the calibration table in the renewal note. Her reasoning was the ₹15.81 lakh monthly gap and, more importantly, Figure 3: a model overconfident at every band cannot have its own probability trusted as the auto-send gate. She offered a narrower alternative: auto-send on six ticket intents whose reply is a template with model-filled slots.

Meenal shipped Nidan Setu for the 2 November rollout and kept Nidan Onboard as connectivity-loss fallback, restricted to answers carrying no numeric specification. The ₹192.10 lakh quarterly warranty difference settled the architecture; Joris's question settled the principle: specifications live in documents Yantrik can revise.

Three questions. First: Vimarsh's top band is 95.5 per cent accurate, and reviewing it costs ₹15.81 lakh a month less than auto-sending it. At what measured accuracy would auto-sending become defensible, and what would you need to know about the 4.5 per cent? Second: Yantrik's retrieval build reaches 95.3 per cent overall but only 93.8 per cent on the newest family, where stakes are highest. Is the residual failure a model, retrieval or documentation problem? Third: name one segmentation in a product you own where a blended figure conceals a gap of Zubaan's kind, and state the test that would reveal it.

exp20v2-aivocab.llm.what:
What a Large Language Model Actually Is

A case-style explainer for product managers: when engineers say the model "knows" or "decided", what is literally happening?

1. A Tuesday meeting at Kritagya Claims Works

On Tuesday 29 September 2026, Mallika Soman, head of product at Kritagya Claims Works, a Pune insurer of small-business property, sat down with her engineering lead, Kaushik Anand, and a reviewer from the Lisbon data team, Mateus Ribeiro. Kritagya settles about 6,000 commercial property claims a month. Its adjusters, the staff who read a claim and decide what the policy pays, spend most of their day reading policy wording. The company had built an assistant called Lekhak Assist on top of a commercial large language model, and on Monday 12 October it was due to go live for 40 adjusters.

The status note Kaushik had circulated contained two sentences that troubled Mallika. "The model knows our policy wordings." And, about a test case: "The model decided the flood claim was excluded." Each sentence implied a test plan: if the model knows the wordings, check a handful of answers; if it decides, audit its reasoning.

The stakes were arithmetic. The average payout on a disputed claim was ₹1.8 lakh. If Lekhak Assist mis-summarised coverage on just 2 per cent of 6,000 monthly claims, that was 120 claims a month, and 120 × ₹1.8 lakh is ₹216 lakh of payouts misdirected every month: either wrongly paid, or wrongly refused and later litigated. She needed to know what kind of thing she was testing. This page follows her reasoning.

2. The idea

A large language model (LLM) is a mathematical function. Its input is a sequence of tokens, the small chunks of text (whole words, word fragments, punctuation) into which any text is first cut. Its output is a probability for every token in its vocabulary: how likely each is to come next, given everything before it. It was built to solve a long-standing problem: predicting language well enough to translate, transcribe and complete text. The transformer architecture was published by Google researchers in 2017, and labs such as OpenAI, Google and Anthropic then trained ever larger versions.

The definition has three negative consequences, and the learning objective of this topic is to hold all three. First, there is no separate store of facts: no database of policy clauses sits inside the model to be looked up. What the training produced is a very large set of numbers, called weights or parameters, which shape the probabilities. Second, there are no beliefs: the function does not hold a position that might be true or false; it produces a distribution. Third, there is no execution step: the model does not run a procedure called "decide"; it emits one token, then the next.

The sentence Mallika could repeat in a meeting: "The model is a function that, given all the text so far, assigns a probability to each possible next word-piece; everything it appears to know or decide is what falls out of repeating that one move."

3. How it actually works

Take the string Lekhak Assist received: "Claim 4471: flood damage to the stock is". The mechanics run in six steps, several of which practitioners leave unspoken.

Step one is tokenisation: the text is cut into tokens and each is replaced by an integer. Step two converts each integer to a long list of numbers (an embedding) that the rest of the function can manipulate. Step three is the body of the model: layers of arithmetic, using a mechanism called attention, let each position take account of every earlier position. Step four ends with one raw score, called a logit, for every token in the vocabulary. Step five converts scores to probabilities with a formula called softmax, which I show below. Step six, the one most often left implicit, is sampling: a separate, ordinary piece of software picks one token from the probabilities. It may pick the most likely one or draw at random in proportion to the probabilities. The chosen token is appended to the text and the function is called again.

Sampling is a setting the product team controls, and the only place in the loop where randomness enters. When Kaushik said the model "decided", what actually happened was that sampling software drew a token from a distribution, and the next call was conditioned on that draw. "Decision" is a description of the output, not of a process inside.

The phrase "everything before it" also deserves precision. The function sees only the text in front of it: the instructions, the retrieved policy excerpt if the product supplies one, the adjuster's question, and its own words so far. "Knows" therefore has a narrow honest meaning: the weights make certain continuations likelier. Whether Kritagya's Policy Form 12 was in the training text nobody could verify.

4. A worked example, with arithmetic

Mateus built a toy version of the key moment. After "Claim 4471: flood damage to the stock is", suppose the model has four candidate next tokens and assigns raw scores. Softmax turns scores into probabilities by computing e raised to each score (e ≈ 2.718), then dividing each by the sum of all four.

Check the first row: 20.0855 ÷ 31.1929 = 0.644, rounded to 64 per cent. The four exponentials sum to 31.1929, and the rounded percentages 64 + 24 + 9 + 3 sum to 100. Notice what this says about Kaushik's sentence. On this prompt the model leans towards "covered" but gives "excluded" about a one-in-four chance. Run the prompt 20 times with random sampling and one expects about 20 × 0.644 = 12.9 "covered" answers; the team saw 13, which is 65 per cent, consistent with the distribution.

Now the second pass, changing one input. The adjuster pastes the clause "Clause 7(b): loss caused by flood is excluded" into the prompt. The weights are unchanged, but the text before the next token is different, so the scores shift.

Note the residue: 14 per cent of the probability (7 + 4 + 3), about one draw in seven, still sits on other tokens. The figure below plots both passes.

5. Nuances a learner must become aware of

Knowing is not the same as continuing plausibly

A person who knows a clause can say where they learned it, and says "I do not know" when they do not. The model continues text in ways that resemble its training. Where the clause was common and consistent there, the continuation is usually right; where it was rare, the continuation is still fluent. Fluency is no evidence of accuracy.

The weights and the context are different things

What was learned in training sits in the weights and changes only when the provider retrains. What the model sees in a given call is the context. Table two shows the context doing the work: pasting Clause 7(b) moved "excluded" from 24 to 86 per cent. A product that supplies the clause is relying on the context; a product that does not is relying on whatever the weights retain.

A probability is not a measure of truth

The 86 per cent in the second pass describes how strongly the text pushes towards a token, not the chance that "excluded" is legally correct. A model can be sharply confident and wrong.

Temperature changes spread, not correctness

Temperature is a sampling setting that divides the logits before softmax. Dividing by 0.5 doubles them, which sharpens the distribution. Applied to the first pass, the scores become 6, 4, 2, 0; the exponentials are 403.4288, 54.5982, 7.3891 and 1.0000, totalling 466.416, so the probabilities become 86.5, 11.7, 1.6 and 0.2 per cent, which sum to 100.0. "Covered" is now far more consistent, and exactly as wrong as before if it was wrong. Lowering temperature buys consistency, not correctness.

An explanation is more text, not a view inside

If Mallika asks the assistant why it called the flood claim excluded, the reply is another sequence of tokens, generated by the same loop. It is not a readout of a hidden deliberation, because no deliberation was executed. Stated reasons cannot serve as an audit trail.

The model is not the product

Lekhak Assist is the model plus instructions, retrieved policy text, sampling settings and the screen the adjuster sees. A "model problem" is often a retrieval problem: the wrong clause was supplied.

Questions a newcomer should ask before relying on it

Which model version is this? What text was in the context? How often does the same input give a different answer? What would a wrong answer cost, and who would catch it? The last sets the testing budget.

6. How it looks in different products

In a consumer product, such as a shopping assistant in a retail app, a wrong sentence costs a moment of annoyance, and volume is high, so the working test is statistical: sample thousands of outputs and track the rate of complaints. In a B2B product like Lekhak Assist, each output feeds a professional's decision with money attached, so testing concentrates on the specific clauses and amounts, and human review remains in the loop. In a marketplace, where the model writes listings or replies between buyers and sellers, its text becomes one party's words to another.

Size changes the picture too. An early-stage company typically calls a provider's model directly, tests with a few dozen hand-picked cases. A large company adds version pinning, a standing evaluation set, and a named owner for changes. Kritagya sits between the two.

7. Common mistakes

Testing the answer once. The symptom: a demo works perfectly, then an adjuster reports a different answer to the same question. The misunderstanding is that the output is stored and retrieved. The cheapest diagnostic is to run the same prompt 20 times and count how many outputs agree.

Asking the model whether it is sure. The symptom: the team adds a line such as "answer only if confident" and declares the risk handled. The misunderstanding: a self-report reflects an internal state. The diagnostic is to compare its stated confidence against accuracy on 50 cases with known answers.

Crediting training with what the prompt supplied. The symptom: a pilot succeeds in a test where the clause was pasted, then fails in production where it was not. The misunderstanding is the weights-versus-context distinction. The diagnostic is to rerun the test with the supplied text removed.

Treating a low temperature as a safety setting. The symptom: outputs become identical and the team reads this as reliability. The diagnostic: check whether the consistent answer is correct.

8. What good looks like

Good handling starts with vocabulary. The status note would read: "Given the policy text we supply, the model assigns high probability to the correct coverage statement on a test set of 200 claims." Each phrase points to a test. "Given the text we supply" names the context; "assigns high probability" invites repetition; "a test set of 200" invites a count. The team records the model version and agrees in advance the error rate at which launch pauses.

9. Closing: what Mallika decided

Mallika kept the 12 October date but changed its terms. Every answer would be generated from the policy clause supplied in the prompt, never from the weights alone. Mateus would build a golden set of 200 claims, each run 20 times, which is 4,000 runs in all. The threshold was set by the exposure calculation: she could tolerate a mis-summary rate of 1 per cent, which on 6,000 claims is 60 claims and 60 × ₹1.8 lakh = ₹108 lakh of monthly exposure, half the ₹216 lakh she had feared at 2 per cent. Above that, the launch would slip. She also banned both phrases from status notes.

What to learn next: the context window, because it governs what text the model can see at once; then inference versus training, which separates what is fixed from what is supplied; and hallucination, which is what the distribution produces when the text before it is thin.

Two questions to sit with. First, think of a sentence in your own team's documents that says a model "knows" or "decides". What test does that sentence imply, and what test would the accurate sentence imply instead? Second, for one feature you own, which component would you examine first if an output were wrong, and why?
case20v1-aivocab.llm.what:
Upakar Services: The Assistant That "Knew" the Foreclosure Charge

A decision case on what a large language model actually is

1. Opening

On Thursday, 1 October 2026, Vaishali Nene sat in a glass-walled meeting room on the fourth floor of Upakar Services' headquarters in Hinjewadi, Pune, with a printed transcript in front of her. A customer had asked the company's new WhatsApp assistant what it would cost to close a fixed-rate two-wheeler loan early. The assistant had replied, politely and fluently, that there was no foreclosure charge. The loan agreement said 3 per cent of the outstanding principal.

Nene, the company's Chief Product Officer, had until Monday, 5 October to tell the management committee whether the assistant should go to all customers before the Diwali demand surge, which falls on 8 November this year. Her engineering lead, in a message sent at 7 a.m., had written: "The model knows our policy. It just got this one wrong. We will fix it by teaching it more." Nene was no longer sure that sentence meant anything.

2. Company background

Upakar Services was founded in 2011 by two former branch managers of a large public-sector bank. It lends small amounts, typically ₹40,000 to ₹6 lakh, to salaried and self-employed customers for two-wheelers, consumer durables and personal needs, mostly through dealers in Maharashtra, Karnataka and Gujarat. It serves about 14 lakh active loan customers. Larger rivals such as Bajaj Finance have built app-based servicing; Upakar's customers still mostly call, visit a branch or message on WhatsApp.

Servicing is the company's largest controllable cost. Every month, customers ask what they owe, whether they may part-pay, what closing early costs, and which documents they need. The Reserve Bank of India's fair-practices expectations require that charges be disclosed correctly and consistently, and that customers receive accurate information about their own loans. A wrong number is a conduct issue.

In June 2026 Upakar built an assistant on a commercial large language model accessed through an API. It was given a long instruction describing Upakar's tone and products. A pilot began on Tuesday, 1 September and ran for 21 days, to Monday, 21 September, with 12,000 customer conversations.

3. The situation

Exhibit 1 summarises the pilot. Conversations were sampled and checked line by line by Upakar's quality team against the loan system of record. The assistant performed well on factual lookups that arrived with the customer's own data attached, and badly where it had to state a rule. Foreclosure questions were wrong in 252 of 2,100 conversations, a rate of 12.0 per cent. Honouring wrong quotes cost an average of ₹6,500 each in goodwill adjustments, so the 252 wrong foreclosure answers carried a direct cost of ₹16.38 lakh over three weeks.

Wrong rate is wrong statements divided by conversations in that row. The overall rate is 402 divided by 12,000.

The team's reading of this result was divided, and its location mattered. In Bengaluru, Pranay Vedula's engineers had tested the assistant before launch with 40 foreclosure questions, each asked once; 38 came back correct, or 95.0 per cent. In Lisbon, the data scientist Urmila Prabhune had, a week earlier, asked those same 40 questions 25 times each, 1,000 runs in all. Exhibit 2 shows what she found.
