In the third row the share is 21 of 40 questions, not a share of runs. The single pass is one draw from the behaviour the 1,000 runs sample.

Prabhune's finding was the more important one. The same question, worded identically, produced the right charge on some runs and a wrong charge on others. Only 21 of the 40 questions were answered correctly every time. Navin Pereira, who leads customer success from Colombo, reported that wrong answers were hard to catch because they were as fluent and confident as the right ones.

Illustration: the pilot and decision calendar. Not to scale.

4. The people

Vaishali Nene (Pune), Chief Product Officer, owns the decision. She wants a servicing assistant that lowers cost without a single misquoted charge reaching the regulator's attention.

Pranay Vedula (Bengaluru), engineering lead, built the pilot. He believes the model holds Upakar's policies and that the remaining errors are gaps in what it has learned. He wants a launch before Diwali and a training project afterwards.

Urmila Prabhune (Lisbon), data scientist, designed the repeat test. She wants every release judged on distributions of answers, not single answers,.

Parthasarathy Vishwanath (Mumbai), head of compliance, wants no customer-facing statement of a charge that has not been verified.

Navin Pereira (Colombo) represents customers and branch staff, and wants the assistant to take routine volume off the phones before the festival peak.

5. What a large language model literally is

Nene asked Prabhune for a plain account. A large language model is a function. Given a sequence of text, broken into units called tokens, it returns a probability for every possible next token. The product then chooses one, appends it and repeats. That is all it does.

Three consequences followed, and First, the model has no separate store of facts that it looks up. What looks like a recalled policy is a pattern of probabilities shaped during training, which is why the answer varies from run to run. Second, it holds no beliefs, so "it knows our policy" and "it decided to waive the fee" describe nothing that happens inside it; a high-probability sentence was generated, and nothing checked it. Third, it has no execution step. It never consults the loan system unless the surrounding software puts the relevant text in front of it.

The vocabulary mattered because it determined the test. If the model "knows", a single pass of 40 questions is a reasonable exam, as it is for a trained employee. If it produces probabilities, the single pass is a sample, and Exhibit 2 is the honest picture: 87.2 per cent on average, and only 52.5 per cent of questions reliable. Money facts, which must be exactly right, cannot rest on that.

6. The options

Exhibit 3 sets out the three courses open to Nene, with twelve-month costs.

Exhibit 3: Twelve-month cost of each option (₹ lakh)
OptionOne-off buildTwelve-month running costTotal, 12 months
A. Fine-tune on policy documents4258100
B. Supply verified text per question, check outputs365187
C. Return to human agents0118118

Option C is 40 additional agents at ₹2.95 lakh a year each, 40 times 2.95 equals 118. All figures are Upakar's finance estimates.

Option A: teach the model more. Fine-tune the model on Upakar's policy documents and loan agreements, as Vedula proposes, and launch before Diwali. The upside is a more fluent, on-brand assistant. The cost is ₹100 lakh, and the weakness is that fine-tuning shifts probabilities; it does not install a table of charges. Errors will fall, but the same question can still produce a wrong figure on some runs, and the team could not prove otherwise.

Option B: change what the model is given and what is checked. Keep the model, but for every question that touches a charge or rule, have Upakar's software fetch the exact clause for that customer's loan and place it in the model's input, and send the quoted amounts through a deterministic check against the loan system before the customer sees them. Test by repeated runs on a fixed question set. The upside is control and an audit trail; the cost is ₹87 lakh.

Option C: stop and staff up. Withdraw the assistant and hire 40 agents. It is the safest option, costs ₹118 lakh, and surrenders the project's saving.

7. Questions for discussion

  1. Rewrite Vedula's sentence, "the model knows our policy", in terms of what the model literally does. What changes about how you would test it?
  2. Why does Exhibit 2 describe the system better than the 95.0 per cent single-pass result? What does the 52.5 per cent tell you that the average does not?
  3. Exhibit 1 shows errors concentrated in two topics. What do those topics have in common, and what does that imply for where a model should and should not be trusted?
  4. Which option would you take to the committee on 5 October, and what evidence would make you change it?

8. A note for the learner

This case frames the decision through one idea: a language model is a probabilistic next-token function, with no fact store, no beliefs and no execution step. Once students hold that definition, the wrong tests become visible. A single-pass exam, a fine-tuning plan to "make it know", and a hope that it "decides" correctly all assume a reasoner that does not exist.

A well-reasoned answer separates two jobs. Fluent language is what the model is good at. Exact money facts belong to the system of record. Option B respects that split, and Exhibit 1 supports it: the topics with errors were those where the assistant had to state a rule from learned patterns, not read a number given to it.

One defensible path is Option B, phased. Launch before Diwali only on the topics with the lowest wrong rates in Exhibit 1, EMI due, balance and documents, which run at 0.5 per cent; route foreclosure and part-payment questions to humans until verified clauses and the output check are in place and a repeated-run test shows no wrong quotes. At ₹87 lakh it costs ₹13 lakh less than Option A and ₹31 lakh less than Option C, and it is the only option whose correctness can be demonstrated to the regulator.

Tatsam Labs: Nine Thousand Tokens Before a Word Is Written

A catalogue-content company discovers that the unit it sells in and the unit it is billed in are not the same unit.

1. Sunday night, 29 November 2026

The generator outside the Tatsam Labs office in Madhapur, Hyderabad, had been running since eight, and Nupur Chaphekar had stopped noticing it. On her screen were two spreadsheets describing the same month of the same business, which disagreed about whether it made money.

The first was her applied-science lead's August model: a bottom-up estimate of what it costs to generate one marketplace listing, by language, showing a gross margin of ₹13.941 lakh a month on revenue of ₹79.65 lakh. The second was the reconciliation her platform engineer in Kraków had finished eleven days earlier, setting the provider's September invoice against the same month's billings. On that basis the business lost ₹4.313 lakh.

In the morning Nupur had to recommend what to do about Chaturang Retail Industries, the Mumbai house of brands that is 8.5 lakh of Tatsam's 17.7 lakh monthly listings — a little over 48 per cent — whose renewal terms had arrived on Friday. The board met on 11 December; the customer wanted an answer by 15 December; the new rate card took effect on 1 January, thirty-two days after Monday.

What she kept returning to was a line both spreadsheets accepted without argument: 10,200 input tokens per listing, of which 9,000 were the same instructions sent again, and again, for every one of 17.7 lakh listings. Tatsam charged for listings. It was billed for tokens. Nobody could say when those two had last been the same conversation.

2. Tatsam Labs, 2019 to 2026

Pranav Dharwadkar and Girija Seshadri founded Tatsam Labs in March 2019, Pranav from Infosys and Girija from a Chennai analytics firm. The business was unglamorous and useful: Indian sellers hold product data in supplier spreadsheets, PDFs and WhatsApp photographs, and marketplaces require structured titles, bullet points, attribute tables and long descriptions, in several languages, to a specification that changes without notice. Until 2023 Tatsam did that with people — a review bench in Coimbatore and Nagpur, still 94 of its 212 staff — and from 2024 with a large language model behind a product called Suchi Studio.

The decision that constrains everything today was taken in the festive season of 2024. Chaturang ran a five-week bake-off and Tatsam won on two promises. Price: a flat ₹4.50 per listing in every language, because Chaturang's finance team wanted one number it could budget. Completeness: a guarantee that 99.5 per cent of listings would arrive with every mandatory field populated and no English left in a vernacular listing.

To ship in five weeks, Kaushik Barve's team built the simplest thing that worked. Every call carries one assembled prompt: the brand's style guide, the marketplace's listing rules, and fourteen worked examples. To make the brand voice dominant, the brand block was placed first. That ordering is now the most expensive line of code in the company, because prompt caching — a tenth of the usual rate for instructions the provider has already seen — requires a stable prefix, and Tatsam's prefix changes with every seller.

3. The industry

Catalogue content sits in an awkward place in Indian e-commerce. Flipkart and Meesho both give sellers automated listing help, which caps what anyone can charge; Amazon India's seller tools do the same at the top of the market; Infosys and TCS bid for the enterprise end. Tatsam's differentiation is the vernacular long tail: a Nykaa-style brand launching in Telugu and Kannada wants a listing written for that marketplace in that language, carrying the country-of-origin and net-quantity declarations the Legal Metrology rules require on every one.

Three forces press on the product. ONDC has pulled thousands of smaller sellers into the catalogue problem below ₹2 a listing, where the rival Panna Catalogue Works sits. The DPDP Act obliges Tatsam to account for seller-contact data flowing to Kraków and Lisbon. And GST at 18 per cent on domestic software services means Chaturang compares Tatsam's invoice with an in-house salary bill, not another vendor's.

The exposure is no longer only Indian. Kurayama Retail Group, an Osaka buying house, has offered a term sheet for Japanese listings from April 2027 — 6.2 lakh a month at a flat ₹5.20, worth ₹32.24 lakh a month. Nirmal Chhabria quoted that price in October. Nobody has measured how many tokens a Japanese listing costs.

4. What happened, and what has since turned out to be wrong

In January 2026 Kaushik's team did fix the prefix problem — for some customers. Sellers on the standard template moved to a prompt whose first 9,000 tokens never change, and caching was switched on for them: 34 per cent of generation calls. Chaturang, with 1,100 brand-specific templates, is in the other 66 per cent. The change was recorded as "caching enabled" and nobody re-measured what share of spend it touched.

In the week of 10 August, Shalaka Nadgouda ran 2,000 real SKUs through the current model, Model A, and produced the two exhibits that have framed every conversation since: Exhibit 1, what a finished listing costs in tokens by language, and Exhibit 2, the unit economics at ₹4.50. Leadership took away that the business was thin but positive, with Telugu, Tamil and Kannada losing money per listing.

On 6 October the provider published a new rate card effective 1 January 2027: input 20 per cent cheaper, output 20 per cent dearer. On 8 October the September invoice arrived, and sat unexamined in the finance inbox for six weeks because the number was within the range Girija expected.

On Wednesday 18 November, Dominika Pawlak reconciled that invoice against the August model, and found the provider had billed 34.5 per cent more input tokens and 18.6 per cent more output than the model predicted. Her reconciliation, Exhibit 4, attributes the gap to two things the bench never included: a 9 per cent regeneration rate when the review bench rejects a listing, and a separate attribute-extraction call for every listing, which nobody had thought of as a model call because it returns JSON rather than prose.

Six days later, on Tuesday 24 November, Inês Caldeira sent an audit that complicated the other candidate solution. Shalaka's bench had shown Model B, a rival with an Indic-aware tokeniser, producing 1,780 output tokens for a Tamil listing against Model A's 3,150 — a fall of 43.5 per cent. Inês had read the listings. Model B wrote 1,490 characters of Tamil against 2,420, down 38.4 per cent, and 6.2 bullet points against 9.8. Per character the two were 1.195 and 1.302 tokens: Model B encodes Tamil about 8.2 per cent more efficiently, and the rest of the saving was a shorter listing, which Chaturang's specification does not permit.

5. The people

Nupur Chaphekar, vice-president of product, Hyderabad. Owns Monday's recommendation. Position: the unit of sale must be reconnected to the unit of cost first. Incentive: her 2027 plan is built on Kurayama. Not saying: she approved the January caching change without asking what share of spend it covered.

Pranav Dharwadkar, co-founder and chief executive, Hyderabad. Position: renew on terms the customer will sign, because 48 per cent of volume cannot be risked nine months before a Series B. Not saying: he has told two prospective investors that gross margin on the generation line is above 30 per cent.

Girija Seshadri, co-founder and chief financial officer, Hyderabad. Position: the invoice is the truth and the August model should be withdrawn. Incentive: she signed April's committed-spend agreement — a ₹60 lakh monthly minimum draw to 31 March 2027 for a 12 per cent discount. Not saying: a successful caching migration would take spend below that floor, and the shortfall is billed in full.

Kaushik Barve, head of engineering, Pune. Position: migrate the 1,100 Chaturang templates to a stable prefix — seven weeks, ₹26 lakh of his team's time — and the input problem largely disappears. Incentive: the fix he proposed in 2024 and was overruled on. Not saying: three of his fourteen engineers are already on Kurayama.

Shalaka Nadgouda, applied science lead, Bengaluru. Position: Model B is the structural answer; Indic tokenisers will keep improving. Incentive: four months spent on that evaluation. Not saying: she disputes Dominika's 9 per cent regeneration rate, believing it counts reviewer edits that never called the model — the gap real but misattributed — and has not said so in writing.

Inês Caldeira, localisation lead, Lisbon. Position: nothing moves to Model B until a blind read of 5,000 listings per language says the content is equivalent. Incentive: her team and the review bench carry the completeness guarantee. Not saying: her audit used the same Tamil reviewers who were overruled on the 2024 style guide.

Dominika Pawlak, platform engineer, Kraków. Position: measure before deciding; both disputed rates come from her instrumentation and both have gaps. Not saying: her cache figure counts calls, not tokens, and Chaturang's prompts are longer than average, so the share of spend caching touches is below 34 per cent.

Nirmal Chhabria, chief revenue officer, Mumbai. Position: hold the flat price everywhere; tiering will lose Chaturang and kill Kurayama. Incentive: the Kurayama term sheet is 60 per cent of his 2027 quota. Not saying: Chaturang's most-favoured-pricing clause means any discount to a new ONDC customer flows back to Chaturang automatically.

6. Exhibits

Exhibit 1 is the measurement every later argument rests on: the output side only, one finished listing averaged over Shalaka's bench, in each of the seven languages.

— Shalaka Nadgouda, chat, 25 November

"One correction before anyone quotes me. My 34 per cent is a share of calls, not of tokens or rupees. Chaturang's prompts are longer than average, so the share of spend caching touches is below 34 per cent and I do not yet know by how much."

— Dominika Pawlak, chat, 26 November

"Chaturang did not ask for ten bullet points because they love bullet points. They asked because that was the marketplace guidance in 2024. Has anyone been back to them?"

— Thandiwe Mokoena, customer success, Cape Town, 27 November

"Renewal at ₹4.50, three years, volume commitment up 15 per cent, completeness guarantee unchanged. We also want Japanese at the same unit price when Kurayama goes live, under the most-favoured clause."

— from Chaturang procurement's renewal terms, received Friday 27 November

8. The options as Nupur sees them on Sunday night

Option A — renew at ₹4.50 and migrate the prompts. Sign what Chaturang asked for, then spend ₹26 lakh and seven weeks moving 1,100 templates to a stable prefix, taking monthly model cost from ₹65.709 lakh to ₹35.601 lakh on the August basis. Against that: the migration must survive Inês's revalidation, it competes with Kurayama for the same three engineers, and Girija's ₹60 lakh floor means that on the invoice basis a fully cached month would spend ₹51.146 lakh and be billed the ₹8.854 lakh shortfall anyway until 31 March 2027.

Option B — re-price by language. ₹4.50 for English, ₹5.75 for Hindi, Marathi and Bengali, ₹6.50 for Telugu, Tamil and Kannada. Revenue rises from ₹79.65 lakh to ₹98.35 lakh, up 23.5 per cent, and margin at today's cost to ₹32.641 lakh. Chaturang's bill goes from ₹38.25 lakh to ₹48.35 lakh, up 26.4 per cent, and the most-favoured clause rules out tiering quietly for anyone else first.

Option C — move to Model B. Exhibit 6 says it costs ₹68.213 lakh, more than changing nothing; Inês says the saving is mostly a shorter listing; and it strands the committed-spend agreement.

Option D — shorten the listing. Nobody has written this one down. If ten bullet points became six, Tamil output would fall by roughly what Model B appears to deliver, on Model A, with no migration and no new vendor, and the truncations would largely disappear. It needs Chaturang to agree that the 2024 specification is not sacred, and it alone touches the guarantee rather than the price.

What the four share is the assumption that the per-listing unit is fixed. Chaturang does not buy listings; it buys conversion on four marketplaces. Tatsam has never priced a listing against what the listing earned.

9. The deadline and the hard constraints

Dates. Recommendation Monday 30 November; board 11 December; Chaturang's answer 15 December; new rate card 1 January 2027; Kurayama go-live April 2027.

Money. ₹9.2 crore of cash. Revenue of ₹31.76 crore annualised, the generation line ₹9.56 crore and the rest managed review. A ₹60 lakh monthly minimum draw to 31 March 2027. ₹26 lakh for the migration, not in the budget.

People. Fourteen engineers in Pune, three on Kurayama; nine localisation staff in Lisbon; a 94-person review bench whose rejection rate is itself one of the disputed numbers.

Regulation and contract. Legal Metrology declarations must appear on every listing, making Exhibit 5's 19,970 truncations a compliance exposure and not only an SLA one. DPDP obligations on seller data crossing to Kraków and Lisbon. A most-favoured-pricing clause coupling every discount back to Chaturang, and no pass-through for model price changes.

10. Questions for discussion

  1. Using Exhibit 1, say what a token is and why Tatsam's 2024 pricing conversation — conducted entirely in listings and words — could not have surfaced the Tamil problem.
  2. Exhibits 2 and 3 describe the same month and disagree by ₹18.254 lakh. Which is the right basis for Monday, and what does choosing it commit Nupur to?
  3. Exhibit 6 shows Model B costing more than changing nothing, while Shalaka's bench shows 43.5 per cent fewer Tamil output tokens. Reconcile those facts, and say what Inês's tokens-per-character figures add that token counts alone do not.
  4. ₹2.142 of the ₹3.712 blended cost per listing is input, and 9,000 of the 10,200 input tokens are the same text every time. Where does Tatsam's cost really come from, and what would you measure before authorising Kaushik's seven weeks?
  5. Exhibit 5 puts truncation at 1.13 per cent against a 99.5 per cent guarantee. Is that a pricing, engineering, contract or product-specification problem — and who is currently accountable for it?
  6. What should Nupur recommend on Monday morning, and what would she say to the board on 11 December about pricing a product whose cost Tatsam does not control, measure in the same unit, or fully understand?

Sunday night, continued

At a quarter to midnight Nupur typed one line at the top of a blank document: we sell listings and we buy tokens. Below it she wrote the four options, and beside Option D a question that did not belong in a pricing paper: who decided ten bullet points, and when did we last ask them?

Dominika's message about the 34 per cent being calls and not rupees was still open in another window. If the share of spend was lower, Option A's prize was larger than Exhibit 6 showed; if higher, January had already captured most of the gain. She did not have the number, and would not have it by nine. The generator cut out. Four options on the page, one unmeasured language in Osaka, two spreadsheets that could not both be right, and nine hours.
exp40v2-aivocab.tokens:
Tokens and tokenisation

AI & Data Products › AI Vocabulary and Primer for PMs · near-expert treatment

1. Two decisions, nine days apart

On Tuesday 8 September 2026, Deepshikha Ranade, vice-president of product at Darpan Retail Exchange, opened a spreadsheet she had been avoiding. Darpan is a marketplace where two lakh small sellers — tailoring units in Bhiwandi, handloom co-operatives in Nalgonda — list apparel for buyers arriving through Google and, increasingly, ONDC. A seller photographs a garment and types sixty words of description in whatever language they think in. Darpan's listing writer returns 110 words in English, so it is findable, and 110 in the seller's language, so the seller trusts it.

The feature handles 6,40,000 listings a month. The July budget said ₹2,23,718, built by measuring tokens on English listings and multiplying. Her engineer, Devdatta Pandhare, had re-measured by language: the true figure exceeded ₹2,93,000. Nothing in the product had changed; only the arithmetic had.

Nine days later, on Thursday 17 September 2026, Damayanti Iyengar faced the mirror image. She is product director at Dastak Insurance Services, which sells claims-adjudication software to health insurers; its largest client pushes 1,15,000 claims a month at ₹11 per claim. Dastak's model reads the discharge summary, the bills and the policy wording and drafts an adjudication note for a human assessor. Damayanti had not mis-measured; she did not control the measurement. The file is the client's, its length the hospital's, and IRDAI audit expectations forbid dropping material to save money.

Deepshikha priced her product in the wrong unit; Damayanti's unit is sized by someone else. Both are one problem, and this page argues one proposition through both: the token is the only unit in which a language model can be budgeted, bounded or timed, and a manager who cannot convert tokens into what the business sells will be surprised by an invoice, a latency complaint or a truncation — and will not know which.

2. The idea, and who disagrees about it

A token is an entry in a fixed list of text fragments — typically 32,000 to 2,56,000 of them — for which a model has learned a representation. A tokeniser is a deterministic program, shipped with the model but separate from it, converting text into positions in that list and back. The model reads and emits integers, never letters.

This solves the vocabulary problem. Whole-word units need a row per word, cannot spell an unseen name and waste capacity on inflections. Character units need a tiny list but long sequences, and attention cost grows faster than linearly in length. Sub-word units compromise.

Philip Gage published byte-pair encoding in 1994 as a file-compression trick; Rico Sennrich, Barry Haddow and Alexandra Birch repurposed it for machine translation in 2015–16, explicitly for rare words. Mike Schuster and Kaisuke Nakajima had built the related WordPiece for Japanese and Korean voice search in 2012; Taku Kudo added the unigram alternative in 2018 and, with John Richardson, released SentencePiece; GPT-2 moved to byte-level BPE in 2019. Then the critiques: Phillip Rust and colleagues in 2021 on multilingual tokenisers serving low-resource languages badly, Linting Xue and colleagues on token-free byte models, and Aleksandar Petrov and colleagues in 2023 quantifying the cost asymmetry between languages.

Four positions are genuinely held, differing on what a tokeniser is for. The compression school treats it as lossless compression under a vocabulary budget. It signs "fewer tokens is strictly better, because length costs money and attention," but not "boundaries should respect morphology": it sees no evidence that morpheme-aligned splits improve loss.

The linguistic school holds that boundaries carry meaning: splitting a morpheme or a Devanagari conjunct makes the model relearn composition it could have been handed. It signs "a split that cuts a morpheme costs accuracy, not merely tokens," but not "minimise token count."

The token-free school calls any learned vocabulary a frozen bet on one corpus, so a permanent bias and a robustness hole. It signs "a fixed vocabulary is a fairness bug," but not "length is the binding constraint forever" — exactly what its opponents believe.

The product-pragmatist school, where Deepshikha and Damayanti live, treats the tokeniser as an external constant, like a tax code. It signs "measure your own text, price per unit of work, re-measure on every upgrade," but not "choosing a tokeniser is a product decision": you choose a model, and the tokeniser comes attached.

3. Mechanics, worked through

Why tokenisation is not neutral is visible in miniature. Take four words: low five times, lower twice, lowest three times, slow four times — fourteen words, fifty-nine characters. Byte-pair encoding starts from characters and repeatedly merges the most frequent adjacent pair.

Two things matter more than the mechanism. Frequent words became single tokens; slowest, never seen, fragments into four. And nothing consulted a grammar — the procedure counted. Scale that to a corpus one per cent Devanagari and a fifth of one per cent Tamil: common English words survive whole, Tamil words shatter.

Devdatta's measurement on Darpan's listings, on the vendor's production tokeniser, quantified it: for a hundred-word passage, 130 tokens in English, 200 in romanised Hinglish, 340 in Devanagari Hindi, 400 in Bengali, 450 in Tamil. A Tamil seller's sixty-word description is therefore 270 tokens against an English seller's 78 — the same information at 3.46 times the length.

The second-order effect gets skipped. Vocabulary is not free: every entry needs a row in the input embedding matrix and, unless weights are tied, another in the output projection. At hidden width 4,096, 32,000 entries cost 13.11 crore parameters per matrix; 1,00,000 cost 40.96 crore; 2,56,000 cost 104.86 crore. Fairness for Indian scripts costs parameters that could have bought depth.

Third, asymmetry. Input tokens are read in parallel; output tokens arrive one at a time, each conditioned on its predecessors. Darpan's vendor charges ₹180 per million input tokens and ₹720 per million output, and output is what the seller waits through. Asking for more words pays twice.

5. When the frame applies, and when it misleads

Claim one: the token count of a unit of work is measurable in advance on your own text. Decisively true at Darpan — Devdatta sampled 500 listings per language in an afternoon. Partly true at Dastak, where the distribution is per-client and must be re-measured at every sale.

Claim two: the decision unit is cost per unit of work, not price per million tokens. True for both, and the most violated. Darpan's procurement team had ranked three vendors on headline rates.

Claim three: token cost is a controllable product input. Strongly true at Darpan, where 720 tokens of every input is prose her team wrote. Weakly true at Dastak, where the documents are the client's and the whole file must be considered.

Claim four: the tokens-per-word ratio is stable enough to plan with. True within a model version, false across them — Table 1 moves Devanagari from 2.97 times English to 1.68. Hard-coding a ratio into a pricing model hard-codes a model version into a contract.

The frame actively misleads in three situations. First, when the binding constraint is memory, not money. Dhaatu Instrument Works builds a handheld inspection unit for pump stations, running a small model on-device because the sites lack connectivity. Its key-value cache consumes 2 × 32 layers × 2,048 hidden units × 2 bytes = 2,62,144 bytes, or 256 KiB, per token, so 1.5 GiB free holds exactly 6,144 tokens. A 1,500-word Devanagari procedure at 3.4 tokens per word is 5,100 tokens, leaving 1,044 for instruction, question and answer. Here the token is a unit of RAM.

Second, when token reduction is traded against accuracy nobody measures — section 8's failure. Third, when hidden reasoning tokens are billed at the output rate but absent from the answer, so counting the visible response understates the bill.

But a band D claim costs ₹10.005, or 91.0 per cent of the fee, and band D is where an insurer most values a good note. Dastak's contract prices a mean while its costs have a long tail. That is the seam: commercial sold a per-claim price, engineering owns a per-token cost, and nobody owns the distribution between them.

The seams multiply. In a multi-product firm the prompt library is shared, so one team adding 400 tokens of instruction raises another's unit cost; firms that handle this well tag every call with a product code and review tokens per unit of work, not rupees, which move with renegotiation. In two-sided businesses the sides write differently — Darpan's sellers in Hinglish and Devanagari, its buyers in English queries — so cost attaches to whichever side the platform subsidises. In regulated settings prompts become records: Dastak stores full inputs for audit under the DPDP Act, so token volume is a storage liability too. In hardware, as at Dhaatu, tokens convert to milliseconds and megabytes. In multimodal products the unit extends — images billed as tokens from a patch grid, audio per second — so a photograph only moves the meter.

7. Eight distinctions an expert makes

The user's text is usually the minority of the bill

The tell is a cost per call that barely moves when the user's message halves. At Dastak the visible claim is 38.3 per cent of input; the rest is instruction, policy text and history. The obvious reading, that cost tracks user activity, picks the wrong driver.

Output is priced and felt differently from input

The tell is a latency dashboard whose p95 tracks response length, not prompt length. Being serial, output dominates rupees and seconds alike: Darpan pays four times per output token and sellers wait through every one.

Reasoning tokens are billed and invisible

The tell is a bill exceeding the sum of logged prompt and completion lengths. Models that deliberate internally charge for it at output rates, so auditing spend from transcripts fails silently.

There is no exchange rate between words and tokens

The tell is anyone quoting "about 750 words per 1,000 tokens" for a product serving Indian languages. The ratio belongs to a text-and-tokeniser pair: 1.3 for Darpan's English, 4.5 for its Tamil. It is no constant of nature or of language.

Numbers tokenise badly

The tell is a model that handles ₹1,00,000 correctly and ₹12,45,000 incorrectly. Digit groups split by corpus frequency, so a figure's boundaries depend on how it is written. Teams that care about arithmetic pass numbers as fields, not prose.

Whitespace lives inside the token

The tell is a prompt that worked in a playground and degraded in production after a template change. Most tokenisers absorb the leading space into the next fragment, so " the" and "the" differ, and a stray trailing space lands the model somewhere unintended.

Prompt caching is a token-prefix match, so prompt order is an economic decision

The tell is a cache-hit rate collapsing after a personalisation release. Providers discount input tokens repeating a previously seen prefix exactly, so a customer's name in line one destroys the match for everything after. Dastak's 11,100 fixed tokens are cacheable only because nothing client-specific precedes them.

Some vocabulary entries are barely trained

The tell is a rare string that reliably produces incoherence — the "glitch tokens" documented in 2023: fragments in the tokeniser's corpus but nearly absent from training data.

8. Three worked examples, including one that failed

The success: caching the constant. Darpan's 300-token style guide is byte-identical for every listing in a category. Its vendor bills cached input at 10 per cent of the standard rate, so those tokens fall from ₹0.054 to ₹0.0054 per listing — ₹0.0486 saved across all 6,40,000 listings, or ₹31,104 a month, with no output changed. This is the cheapest kind of saving: the reduction is in price, not information.

The failure: compression without evaluation. On Monday 4 May 2026 Darpan's growth team ran an experiment on the 4,99,200 monthly listings from non-English sellers. They deleted the style guide, cut the instruction block from 420 to 180 tokens and — the fateful part — stopped generating the English copy, reasoning that a seller writing in Tamil wanted a Tamil listing. The saving was real: 540 input tokens at ₹0.00018 is ₹0.0972, and 143 output tokens at ₹0.00072 is ₹0.10296, so ₹0.20016 per listing, or ₹99,919.87 a month.

Over five and a half weeks, to Friday 12 June 2026, conversion on those listings fell from 4.0 per cent to 2.5 per cent: buyers search in English, and a listing with no English text was invisible to the channel that brought them. Monthly sales on the cohort fell from 19,968 to 12,480 — 7,488 lost. At an average order value of ₹640 and 9 per cent commission, Darpan earns ₹57.60 per sale, so the loss was ₹4,31,308.80 a month against ₹99,919.87 saved: 4.32 times what the experiment earned. Compression was not the error; measuring the saving to five decimal places while not measuring discoverability was.

The recovery. Devdatta restored the English copy but generated it with a smaller model at ₹90 per million output tokens, cutting that line from ₹0.10296 to ₹0.01287 — ₹0.09009 across 4,99,200 listings, or ₹44,972.93 a month — and cached the style guide for the ₹31,104 above. Together ₹76,076.93 a month, a 25.9 per cent cut, taking the forecast from ₹2,93,241.60 to ₹2,17,164.67: below the naive July budget of ₹2,23,718.40, English copy intact.

9. Failure modes and their early warnings

Budgeting in words. Early sign: an invoice whose gap to forecast grows with the non-English share of traffic. Diagnostic: which tokeniser produced that number, on text in which script? Caught late, a mid-year re-forecast — at Darpan's scale, ₹8.34 lakh a year.

Ignoring the fixed block. Early sign: unit cost that will not fall however usage shifts. Diagnostic: log one call's full input and subtract the user's portion. Caught late, a gross-margin floor nobody can explain.

Pricing a mean over a fat tail. Early sign: a few accounts taking a disproportionate share of tokens. Diagnostic: plot cost per unit of work at the 50th, 90th and 99th percentile, not the mean. Dastak's band D is 3 per cent of claims and 91.0 per cent of the fee it earns. Caught late, a renegotiation with your largest customer.

Comparing vendors on headline rates. Early sign: a switch meant to save 17 per cent that saved nothing. Diagnostic: run 500 real units of work through both tokenisers. Caught late, a migration written off.

Compressing without an evaluation harness. Early sign: token spend falling while a downstream metric drifts the same week. Diagnostic: what must get worse for this saving to be a mistake, and are we measuring it? Caught late, it cost Darpan ₹4.32 of margin per rupee saved.

10. Where competent experts genuinely disagree

Is a larger multilingual vocabulary worth its parameters? For: Table 1's 50.0 per cent cut in Devanagari tokens reduces cost, latency and context pressure for hundreds of millions of users, and long sequences appear to hurt accuracy too. Against: the 91.75 crore extra embedding parameters between the 32,000 and 2,56,000 rows could have bought depth helping every language, and rare entries get too few gradient updates. The second fails if larger vocabularies also lift English benchmarks; the first fails if non-English quality does not improve with the reduction.

Will token-free models displace tokenisers? For: every fixed vocabulary is a frozen sample of one moment's internet, under-serving whoever was scarce in it, breaking on typos and unusual scripts, and byte-level models delete a non-differentiable stage. Against: length dominates attention cost, byte sequences are three to five times longer, and every attempt so far paid more in compute than it recovered in quality. A competitive byte-level model would re-price every forecast here.

Whose problem is the language asymmetry? One camp calls it a vendor defect to fix in the tokeniser, since Tamil users pay roughly three and a half times for the same service. The other calls it an ordinary input-cost difference to negotiate or engineer around, as Darpan did. The first fails if the asymmetry were cheap to remove; the second fails if regulators treated per-language differentials as discriminatory.

Should you transliterate input to cut tokens? For: romanising Devanagari takes 340 tokens per hundred words to 200, a 41.2 per cent cut, and most Indian users type in roman anyway. Against: transliteration is lossy, its errors silent, and converting a seller's Tamil to save ₹0.05 is an editorial decision about their language. Darpan has not settled it.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has merely studied tokens can define one. Someone who has internalised the unit differs in four observable ways. They never state a token figure without naming the tokeniser and the date of measurement. They convert every vendor quote into cost per unit of work — per listing, per claim, per ticket — before comparing anything, and keep that conversion where finance can open it. They treat the fixed part of the prompt as an asset with a recurring cost, and know its size to the token. And when someone proposes a token saving, their first question is not how much it saves but what it removes.

12. The decisions

On Monday 28 September 2026, twenty days after opening the spreadsheet, Deepshikha reset Darpan's budget at ₹2,17,164.67 a month, funded the caching and small-model work, and kept the bilingual listing for every seller. Her reason: the ₹0.20016 per listing the May experiment saved was a transfer from revenue to cost at 4.32 to one, and the only durable lever is paying less for the same information rather than buying less. She also instituted a re-measurement of tokens per word on every model upgrade, since her pricing depends on a number the vendor can change silently.

On Wednesday 30 September 2026, thirteen days after her first meeting, Damayanti changed neither model nor prompt. She took Table 6 to the client and proposed replacing the flat ₹11 with a banded price, arguing that a contract paying the same for a 14,300-token claim and a 57,100-token claim is not a price but a bet on the client's case mix. Her platform lead in Warsaw, Dorota Wisniewska, was meanwhile moving the 11,100 fixed tokens to the front of every prompt so they could be cached — cost cut without touching a word the insurer sees. Whether the client accepts banding is unresolved.

Discussion questions. First: Darpan's fixed block is 90.2 per cent of the input on an English listing. If 200 more tokens there improved listing quality, what would you have to believe about conversion to justify them, and how would you test that before shipping? Second: if cost is 91.0 per cent of fee on 3 per cent of claims, is the answer a banded price, a cheaper model for the tail, a refusal to serve it, or a different contract — and what does each say about what Dastak sells? Third: every number here uses a unit a vendor defines and can redefine. What contract clause would protect a business whose unit economics depend on someone else's tokeniser?

13. Going deeper

How LLMs work, for PMs: the pipeline makes sense only once its unit does. How AI is reshaping the PM role: converting tokens into business units is how a PM owns margin. What a large language model actually is: the tokeniser as the one non-learned component. The context window: the token as ceiling, not price — Dhaatu's 6,144. The transformer and attention: why length drives compute. Embeddings: the vector each token maps to, priced in Table 1. Temperature and sampling: the choice at each emitted token. Latency, throughput and the cost of a token: Table 2 in seconds. Multimodality: images and audio in the same unit. Vector search and similarity: chunk size costs twice. Inference versus training: per-token bill against one-time cost. Pre-training, post-training and fine-tuning: where the tokeniser freezes. RLHF and alignment: response length as trained, priced behaviour. LoRA and parameter-efficient fine-tuning: adapting without touching vocabulary. Quantisation: the other lever on Dhaatu's 256 KiB per token.

Companies, people and figures are fictional; Indian institutions appear only as market context. Token ratios illustrate production behaviour, not published vendor figures.
case20v1-aivocab.tokens:
Ekavali Services and the Price of a Tamil Sentence

1. Opening

On the evening of Thursday, 15 October 2026, Anuradha Pethe sat in the Pune office of Ekavali Services with a one-page term sheet and a spreadsheet she did not like. The term sheet came from Mritika Finance, a Mumbai lender with a large microfinance and vehicle-loan book. It offered Ekavali a three-year contract to run its customer messaging on WhatsApp and in its app, in four languages, at a flat ₹6 for every conversation handled. Mritika's board would approve the vendor panel on Friday, 30 October, and its procurement team had said plainly that it wanted the Diwali campaign, which begins soon after 8 November, to run on the new arrangement.

Anuradha was Ekavali's head of product. The spreadsheet, built that afternoon by her data scientist, showed that one of the four languages would lose money on every conversation, and the cause was a unit she had treated as a synonym for "word".

2. Company background

Ekavali Services was founded in Pune in 2019 by two former engineers from a large IT services firm. Its product, Sandesh Desk, is an assistant that answers customer questions, sends payment reminders and hands difficult cases to a human agent. About 140 staff work from Pune, Bengaluru and Chennai.

The market is crowded. Haptik and Yellow.ai sell similar assistants; Freshworks and Zoho bundle bots into their helpdesk suites; large banks build in-house. Ekavali's edge was Indian languages. Lenders speak to borrowers who are often more comfortable in Hindi, Marathi or Tamil than in English, and the Reserve Bank of India expects regulated lenders to communicate in language a borrower understands. Ekavali's total billing across all clients was ₹4.56 crore a month, and Mritika would be exactly half of that.

Ekavali does not train its own language model. It calls a commercial model through an API and pays by the token. Its pricing to customers, however, has always been simple and flat, because that is what procurement teams prefer: a rupee figure per conversation, the same in every language.

3. The situation

Until September, Anuradha's team described every limit in words. The model provider, however, counts and bills in tokens, which are fragments of text, typically a whole short word, a piece of a longer one, or a few characters of punctuation and script. The model never sees words. It sees a sequence of fragment identifiers, and it produces its answer one fragment at a time. Every price, every limit on how much text may be sent, and every delay a customer feels is a function of that count (Figure 1 sketches the idea).

The reason this matters to Ekavali is that tokenisers are built mostly from English-heavy text. English words are often one token. Hindi, Marathi and especially Tamil words are frequently split into many small pieces, so the same meaning costs more fragments. Meghana Raut, Ekavali's data scientist in Melbourne, ran the same 40-word loan-reminder message through the current model's tokeniser in each language. Exhibit 1 shows the result.

Exhibit 1. A 40-word reminder message, tokens by language (current model)

Tokens per word = tokens divided by words. Source: Ekavali internal test, October 2026.

A Tamil message therefore consumes about 4.5 times the tokens of its English twin (236 against 52), although it says exactly the same thing. Conversations are heavier still, since each turn re-sends the long English system prompt and earlier chat. Meghana measured typical conversations and priced them at the rates Ekavali pays: ₹250 per million input tokens and ₹1,250 per million output tokens. Exhibit 2 projects the monthly position for Mritika's full scope at the flat ₹6.

The picture is stark. English earns a 75 per cent margin on revenue. Hindi, the largest language by volume, earns 25 per cent of revenue. Tamil costs ₹6.50 per conversation against ₹6.00 of revenue and loses ₹3 lakh a month, and At twelve lakh Tamil conversations a month the loss would double to ₹6 lakh.

There was one more fact. In September, a second model became available to Ekavali, priced higher per token at ₹300 per million input and ₹1,500 per million output, but with a tokeniser trained on far more Indian-language text. On the same 40-word test, it produced 96 tokens for Hindi, 92 for Marathi and 140 for Tamil. On Exhibit 3's numbers, the same traffic would leave a margin of ₹119.7 lakh, which is 52.5 per cent of ₹228 lakh, and Tamil would earn ₹1.80 per conversation instead of losing ₹0.50. What the table could not show was quality. Meghana had checked only 300 Hindi replies by hand, and none yet in Tamil.

4. The people

Anuradha Pethe (Pune), head of product, owns the recommendation. She wants a contract that Ekavali can keep honouring without subsidising it.

Shreyas Kuppuswamy (Bengaluru), engineering lead, estimates that moving three languages to the second model, with prompt changes and a test suite, would take six weeks and ₹18 lakh of engineers' time. He is wary of a rushed migration before Diwali volume arrives.

Dhruv Anchan (Austin), sales head, fears that any request to change the price will push Mritika toward a rival.

Meghana Raut (Melbourne), data scientist, wants quality tested properly in Tamil before anything is promised. And on the client side, Jayesh Kolhatkar (Mumbai), Mritika's head of customer experience, wants one simple rate his finance team can budget.

5. The options

Option A: sign the flat ₹6 as offered. The cost is that Ekavali earns ₹77 lakh a month on Mritika, a 33.8 per cent margin on revenue, after model cost alone, and Tamil growth erodes it, with no protection if token prices or customer behaviour shift over three years.

Option B: price by language. Ekavali would offer ₹6 for English, ₹9 for Hindi and Marathi, and ₹11 for Tamil, reflecting their token weight. Revenue would be 60 + 198 + 66 = ₹324 lakh a month, a margin of ₹173 lakh on the ₹151 lakh model cost. The price is 42.1 per cent above the ₹228 lakh Mritika expects, and a procurement team may well choose Haptik instead.

Option C: keep the flat ₹6, but move the Indic traffic to the second model. Ekavali's model cost falls to ₹108.3 lakh. The cost is the ₹18 lakh and six weeks of effort, an unproven Tamil quality record, and a contract signed before the work is finished.

6. Questions for discussion

1. Why did Ekavali's team see the Tamil problem only after counting tokens, and what would "800 words" have told them? (Use Exhibit 1.)

2. In Exhibit 2, which single column explains why margin differs by language, and which would a flat-price contract hide from the customer?

3. In Exhibit 3, the second model has higher rates per token yet a lower cost per conversation. Why? What evidence would you still demand before relying on it?

4. Which option would you take to Mritika, and which contract terms would you attach?

7. A note for the learner

This case turns on a definition. A token is the fragment of text a model actually reads and writes, and every limit and price is quoted in it. Words and characters are what a human sees; tokens are what the invoice sees. The ratio between them varies by language and by tokeniser, so a product that serves several languages has several cost structures, whether or not the price list admits it.

One defensible path is Option C, taken with conditions. Sign the flat ₹6, which gives Mritika the simplicity it asked for and does not endanger a deal worth half of Ekavali's billing. Before the Diwali campaign, run a Hindi and Tamil quality test on the second model, with Meghana's checks widened to a few thousand replies. Make a go or no-go call on that evidence. If the model passes, the saving of ₹42.7 lakh a month repays the ₹18 lakh migration in under two weeks of full volume. If it fails, Ekavali still has a fallback: renegotiate language tiers before signing, using Exhibit 2 as evidence. Add a clause allowing a price review at month 12 if token rates or conversation lengths move materially.

Option C attacks the cause, which is token weight, instead of the symptom, which is price, and it keeps the commercial story simple.
exp20v2-aivocab.tokens:
Tokens and tokenisation

AI & Data Products, AI Vocabulary and Primer for PMs

1. The budget that was built on words

On Monday 14 September 2026, Bhuvan Ranganathan, head of product at Bhavana Dispatch Labs, sat down with Bharti Lokhande, the company's finance lead. Bhavana sells customer-support software to Indian retailers and lenders. Its newest feature drafts a first reply to every incoming support ticket, which a human agent then edits and sends. The feature was live in English. The board wanted Hindi switched on for all customers from 1 November.

The budget Bharti had received from the product team was tidy. It assumed 4,00,000 tickets a month, a typical ticket of 150 words and a typical reply of 100 words, and it priced every ticket as though the language did not matter. Bharti had one question: the model vendor invoiced by something called a token, not by a word, so what exactly was being counted?

Bhuvan could not answer with confidence. He had said "tokens" in meetings for a year, usually meaning "words, roughly". If the roughly was wrong by a factor of two for Hindi, the feature would cost far more than the budget allowed, and he would learn this from an invoice in December rather than from a spreadsheet in September. The rest of this page follows him as he works out what a token is, because every limit, price and speed figure he would be quoted for the next year was denominated in that unit.

2. The idea

A token is the fragment of text that a language model actually reads and writes. It is usually a piece of a word, sometimes a whole word, sometimes a single character or a space with a letter attached. A language model, for this page, is software that takes a sequence of text and predicts what should come next; a tokeniser is the separate, simple program that chops text into tokens before the model sees it and stitches tokens back into text afterwards.

The problem tokens solve is one of vocabulary size. A model needs a fixed list of units it knows. A list of whole words would be enormous, would miss names, typos and new coinages, and would waste capacity on rare forms. A list of single characters is small but makes every sentence very long. The compromise is a list of a few tens of thousands of fragments, chosen so that common words are one piece and rare words are assembled from several.

The method most tokenisers use, byte-pair encoding, was described by Philip Gage in 1994 as a way to compress files. Rico Sennrich and colleagues adapted it for machine translation in 2015 and 2016. It starts from single characters, repeatedly merges the pair of neighbouring units that occurs most often in a large body of text, and stops when the list reaches the desired size.

The sentence Bhuvan could repeat without sounding glib: a token is the unit the model is priced, limited and timed in, and how many tokens your text needs depends on the language and the tokeniser, not on how many words it has.

3. How it actually works

Figure 1 shows the sequence. First, the tokeniser matches the text against its fixed list, taking the longest fragments it can. "unhappiness" is not in the list as a whole, but "un", "happi" and "ness" are, so three tokens result. Second, each fragment is replaced by its position in the list, a number. The model never sees letters at all. Third, the model processes the numbers and produces, one token at a time, the numbers of the fragments it predicts should follow. Finally the tokeniser converts those numbers back into text.

Two steps that practitioners leave implicit deserve stating. Spaces are usually absorbed into the following fragment, so " the" with a leading space is a different token from "the" without one. And a model emits its answer one token at a time, each new token depending on everything before it. That is why output is slower and dearer than input: input tokens can be read together, while output tokens must be produced in sequence.

The important consequence is that the list was built from a particular body of text. Where that text was mostly English, English words became single tokens. Where a language was thin in the training text, its words were never merged into long fragments, and they fall apart into many short ones, sometimes into individual bytes of the character encoding.

4. A worked example

Bhuvan asked Badri Kulkarni, the engineer who built the feature, to measure rather than guess. On a sample of real tickets, Badri found that English text averaged 1.3 tokens per word and Devanagari Hindi text averaged 3.5 tokens per word on the vendor's tokeniser. Every call also carried a fixed instruction block of 500 tokens, written in English. The vendor charged ₹250 per million input tokens and ₹1,000 per million output tokens, so one input token cost ₹0.00025 and one output token ₹0.001. Ticket and reply lengths were as in the budget: 150 and 100 words.

Table 1. Cost of one drafted reply (prices per token: input ₹0.00025, output ₹0.001)

The same 250 words of content cost 825 tokens in English and 1,375 in Hindi, a ratio of 1.67. Cost, however, rose by 1.996 times, almost exactly double, because the Hindi reply is the part that grew most (130 to 350 tokens, a factor of 2.7) and output tokens are four times dearer than input tokens.

Now the monthly view. Of the 4,00,000 monthly tickets, 60 per cent, or 2,40,000, arrive in English and 40 per cent, or 1,60,000, in Hindi. The word-based budget priced all 4,00,000 at the English figure.

Second pass, one input changed. Badri observed that the 500-token instruction block was carrying examples nobody needed. Cutting it to 200 tokens reduces every ticket's input by 300 tokens, worth ₹0.075 per ticket. English falls to ₹0.22875 and Hindi to ₹0.53125. Monthly, English becomes 2,40,000 × 0.22875 = ₹54,900 and Hindi 1,60,000 × 0.53125 = ₹85,000, a total of ₹1,39,900. That saves ₹30,000, or 17.7 per cent, against ₹1,69,900, and it still leaves the feature ₹18,400 above the word-based budget.

5. Nuances a learner must become aware of

A token is not a word, and there is no fixed exchange rate

For English prose on a typical tokeniser, a rule of thumb of roughly 1.3 tokens per word is serviceable. The figure is not a law. It moves with vocabulary, with punctuation and with the tokeniser, and Badri's 3.5 for Hindi shows how far it can travel. Always measure on your own text.

Tokenisers differ between vendors, and between versions of one vendor

Each model family ships with its own list. The same paragraph can be 400 tokens on one and 520 on another. A price per million tokens is therefore not comparable across vendors until you have converted it to a price per unit of your own content, such as cost per ticket.

Languages pay unequally

Because the lists were built mostly from English text, scripts such as Devanagari, Tamil, Telugu and Bengali tend to need more tokens for the same meaning.

Output tokens and input tokens are priced and felt differently

Table 1 showed output at four times the input rate. Output is also what the user waits for, since it arrives one token at a time. A design that asks for long answers pays twice, in rupees and in seconds.

The limit is in tokens as well, and it is shared

A model's context window, the maximum number of tokens it can consider in one call, covers instructions, history, retrieved documents and the answer together. Every token spent on instructions is unavailable for the customer's text.

Token counts do not measure quality

More tokens do not mean a better answer, and fewer tokens do not mean a worse one. A token count tells you what a call costs and whether it fits. It cannot tell you whether the reply is correct, polite or safe; that requires evaluation.

Questions to ask before relying on a token figure

Which tokeniser produced it? On what kind of text? Does it include the instructions and history, or only the visible message? Does it count input and output separately?

6. How this looks in different products and companies

In consumer products, volume is high and revenue per user is low, so a few hundred extra tokens per interaction compound into a margin problem. In B2B products, the customer's own data fills the window: contracts, tickets, records. The token count is set by the client's documents, not by your design, so it must be estimated per client during sales, and pricing contracts should say what happens when a client's text runs long. Bhavana sits here.

In marketplace products, two sides generate text in different languages and registers, buyers writing in Hinglish and sellers in formal English. Token counts then vary by side, and cost attaches to whichever side the platform chooses to subsidise. The per-language cost should be known before a fee structure is set.

An early-stage company can reasonably spend attention on the bill once a month and accept a loose estimate; its risk is running out of runway on a surprise. A large company has negotiated rates, internal chargeback between teams and dashboards by feature, so its risk is different: token consumption becomes invisible overhead that no one owns, until a finance review finds a feature that costs more than it earns.

7. Common mistakes

Budgeting in words

Symptom: an invoice higher than the forecast by a margin that grows with the share of non-English traffic. Misunderstanding: words and tokens are assumed interchangeable. Cheapest diagnostic: run fifty real tickets per language through the vendor's token counter and compare tokens per word.

Forgetting the hidden tokens

Symptom: calls that cost more than the visible message explains. Misunderstanding: only the user's text is counted, whereas instructions, conversation history and retrieved passages are counted too. Diagnostic: log the full input token count of one real call and subtract the user's part.

Comparing vendors on price per million tokens

Symptom: a cheaper vendor that produces a dearer bill. Misunderstanding: tokens are taken as a common unit. Diagnostic: price the same fifty tickets on each vendor and compare cost per ticket.

8. What good looks like

Suppose Bhuvan had handled the decision well from the outset. The forecast would have been built from tokens per language measured on real tickets, with separate lines for instructions, input and output. It would have shown the cost per ticket by language, the monthly total at the expected language mix, and the same total at an adverse mix, say 60 per cent Hindi. It would have named the tokeniser and the date of measurement.

9. The decision

On Friday 25 September, eleven days after the first meeting, Bhuvan took a revised plan to Bharti. He did not postpone Hindi. He trimmed the instruction block to 200 tokens, which took the monthly forecast from ₹1,69,900 to ₹1,39,900, asked Badri to shorten Hindi replies where the ticket allowed it, and reset the budget at ₹1,39,900 with a review in December. His reasoning was that the extra ₹18,400 a month over the original figure was a known and bounded cost of serving 1,60,000 Hindi tickets that customers had asked for, while a delay would have cost the goodwill of those customers. The thing he refused was the original budget line, because it had been built on the wrong unit.

What to learn next: the context window, because it turns the token into a hard ceiling rather than a price; then embeddings and latency, because both are also denominated in tokens.

Two questions to sit with. First, if your product served users in three languages and you could measure only one of them, which would you choose to measure, and what would you assume about the other two? Second, where in your own organisation does a number currently travel as "words" or "users" that is really billed in tokens, and who would notice if it was wrong by a factor of two?
exp40v2-aivocab.transformer:
The transformer and attention: a cost shape, not a quality claim

AI & Data Products › AI Vocabulary & Primer for PMs

1. Two decisions, five weeks apart

On Thursday 3 September 2026, Prerana Patwardhan, chief product officer of Parinaam Assessment Labs in Pune, received two quotations for the same job. Parinaam scores descriptive answer scripts for university examination boards: a digitised answer goes to a language model, which applies the board's rubric and proposes a mark an examiner confirms. The coming cycle carries 6,00,000 scripts. The model already in use accepts 8,000 tokens at a time — a token being roughly three-quarters of an English word — at ₹180 per million input tokens; the alternative accepts 1,28,000 tokens, at ₹320 per million.

Pushkar Pendse, Parinaam's head of machine learning, cut each script into six chunks of about 2,000 tokens. The rubric ran to 1,500 tokens and had to be repeated in every chunk, so chunking consumed 6 × (2,000 + 1,500) = 21,000 input tokens per script against 12,000 + 1,500 = 13,500 for one whole-script call: 55.6 per cent more tokens, not fewer. What chunking cost, he suspected, was consistency: a marker who cannot see the whole argument cannot tell confusion from an answer finished overleaf. Prerana had until the board meeting on Thursday 8 October, five weeks later.

Four days later, on Monday 7 September 2026, Preeti Paranjape, vice-president of product at Pankti Retail Exchange in Bengaluru, read a different memorandum. Pankti is a marketplace for refurbished household appliances, with some 41,000 refurbishers on the seller side. Its buyer assistant, launched in June, handled 4,20,000 conversations a month at about eight turns each. Piyush Padhi, principal engineer for serving, wrote that the infrastructure bill was growing faster than usage because of conversation length, not count. Prakash Pendharkar, the chief financial officer, asked whether that was a bug or a property.

Both decisions turn on one mechanism, and neither is helped by knowing what a transformer is in a researcher's sense. Both are helped by knowing the shape of its cost. Architecture almost never decides whether a model is good; its cost curve almost always decides whether a product is viable.

2. The idea, its history, and who disagrees about what

A transformer is an architecture whose central operation is attention: every token's representation is recomputed as a weighted average of the representations of all tokens it may see, the weights themselves computed from the tokens. Nothing carries forward in a running summary; every position reaches every other directly, in parallel, in one step.

It was invented against sequential reading. Machine translation in 2014 ran on recurrent networks that compressed a sentence, word by word, into one fixed vector: long inputs degraded, and training could not be parallelised, because word forty waited on word thirty-nine. Attention arrived that year, in work by Bahdanau, Cho and Bengio, letting the decoder look back over all encoder states. The 2017 paper by Vaswani and colleagues at Google, “Attention Is All You Need”, removed recurrence altogether. All positions could then be computed at once, so training spread across thousands of accelerators, and that scalability produced today's models.

Four schools disagree about what follows, and about what each would sign.

The scale-and-data school holds architecture close to incidental, and would sign: two models of equal size trained on the same data with different attention variants differ less than two models of identical architecture trained on different data. It rests on the scaling-law literature from 2020 and on frontier-model convergence. It would not sign that architecture never matters, conceding that it changes serving economics at equal quality.

The sub-quadratic school — linear attention, and the state-space line from S4 in 2021 to Mamba in 2023 — treats the squared cost as a tax to be engineered away, and would sign that dominant long-context products will not long rest on full quadratic attention. It would not sign that today's state-space models match transformers on recall-heavy tasks; its own benchmarks say otherwise.

The systems school, emblems FlashAttention in 2022 and grouped-query attention in 2023, would sign that the binding constraint is memory bandwidth and key–value cache footprint, not arithmetic. It would not sign that asymptotic complexity is irrelevant, only that you measure the machine.

The interpretability school argues over whether attention weights explain anything: Jain and Wallace said in 2019 that they do not, Wiegreffe and Pinter that the claim was too strong. Both agree: an attention map is not an audit trail.

3. Mechanics, worked through

Parinaam's long-window candidate has 48 layers, an internal width of 4,096 numbers and 64 heads, so each head works in a 4,096 ÷ 64 = 64-dimensional slice. Take one token attending to four earlier. Each token's vector becomes a query (what I seek), a key (what I offer) and a value (what I contribute if chosen); the query is dotted with each key, giving raw scores of 8.4, 6.0, 4.8 and 2.4.

Here is the step practitioners leave implicit. Scores are divided by the square root of head width before the softmax: √64 = 8, giving 1.05, 0.75, 0.60 and 0.30. Softmax exponentiates, turning score differences into weight ratios, so without the divisor a wide head's gaps are large merely because more terms were summed, and softmax saturates. The scaled exponentials 2.8577, 2.1170, 1.8221 and 1.3499 sum to 8.1466, giving 0.3508, 0.2599, 0.2237 and 0.1656. Unscaled, 4,447.07, 403.43, 121.51 and 11.02 sum to 4,983.03, giving 0.8924, 0.0810, 0.0244 and 0.0022.

Attach one-number values of 12, 8, 5 and 2. The scaled blend is 0.3508×12 + 0.2599×8 + 0.2237×5 + 0.1656×2 = 7.7385; the unscaled weights give 11.4832. One omitted divisor moves the output from 7.74 to 11.48, a 48.4 per cent shift. “It is all just weighted averaging” is true and useless: the behaviour lives in the weights.

This runs for every token at once, in each of 64 heads and 48 layers, and the cost follows from counting. Per layer, the work linear in length — projections plus the feed-forward block — is about 24 d² operations per token: 24 × 4,096² = 402,653,184. The quadratic work, scoring every token against every token and blending the values, is about 4 n d: 4 × 4,096 × n = 16,384 n. Multiplying the sum by n tokens and 48 layers gives prefill.

Prefill is half the machine; the other half is Pankti's problem. Reading the window is arithmetic-bound and happens at once; generating happens one token at a time, each token re-reading a stored key–value cache, so decoding is bandwidth-bound and the cache occupies the accelerator. Its size is 2 × layers × key-value width × bytes per number, per token: with 64 heads each keeping its own, 2 × 48 × 4,096 × 2 = 786,432 bytes, or 768 KiB. Grouped-query attention shares one set across eight query heads, cutting the width to 512 and the footprint to 96 KiB.

4. When the idea applies, stated as testable claims

The quadratic term matters only above roughly six times the model width. Test it by computing the composition, as in Exhibit 1. For Parinaam at 13,500 tokens the quadratic share is 13,500 ÷ (13,500 + 24,576) = 35.5 per cent: real, not dominant. For Pankti at 6,140 tokens it is 20.0 per cent, so Pankti's costs are not a quadratic problem.

Architecture does not predict quality, so do not buy it. Test it by demanding results on your own evaluation set and refusing architectural adjectives as evidence. True for both protagonists, and the claim this topic's learning objective insists on.

Architecture does predict serving economics, so do price it. Test it by asking for key-value head count, layer count, and whether cache reuse is billed. Exhibit 2 shows an eightfold concurrency difference between models scoring identically on any benchmark. Decisive for Pankti; nearly irrelevant for Parinaam's nightly batch.

The idea turns misleading in three situations. Where the bill follows a linear price list, reasoning from the squared term yields forecasts wrong in the direction of panic. Where the model sits behind a sparse mixture-of-experts router, arithmetic per token decouples from parameter count. And where accuracy is the question, the mechanism is silent.

5. Hard edge cases, and the organisational seams

In multi-product companies the window becomes a shared budget nobody owns. A prompt change made for Parinaam's essay product in July lengthened the preamble shared by all three products by 900 tokens, raising the cost of the other two with no decision recorded. Mature companies make that preamble a versioned asset with a token budget and a named owner; what they say they do is review prompts in design review.

Two-sided products meet the mechanism twice with opposite economics. Pankti's buyer assistant is latency-sensitive and short; the tool helping refurbishers draft listings from photographs is neither and can run overnight on a long window. One platform team owns the fleet for both, so capacity planning follows buyer-side concurrency while the unit-cost dashboard follows seller-side token volume. Averaging them describes no workload.

Regulated products meet the cache in an unexpected place. Paatra Payments Network, which reconciles for co-operative banks, found that the prompt caching making shared preambles cheap also leaves a tenant's tokens in a provider's memory for a retention period — which its auditors read as a data-handling question under India's Digital Personal Data Protection Act. The resolution was contractual: per-tenant cache namespaces and a written retention term.

Hardware-plus-software products inherit a window they cannot widen: Palash Field Services ships a tablet assistant whose on-device model has a 4,000-token window fixed at manufacture, so its long-context strategy is permanently retrieval. AI-native companies hit the opposite trap, treating a widenable window as the answer to everything.

6. Eight nuances that separate an expert from a competent practitioner

FlashAttention is exact, not approximate

Competent practitioners file FlashAttention beside Linformer and Performer and assume all trade accuracy for speed. The approximations change what is computed; FlashAttention returns the identical result by never writing the full n × n score matrix to slow memory. The tell is a team disbelieving “four times faster, no quality loss”; the saving is in data movement.

Position is not in attention

Attention is indifferent to order: shuffle the tokens and the weights follow them unchanged. Order enters through a separate positional encoding, so a window can be pushed past the lengths a model was trained on, degrading while the arithmetic stays valid. The tell is a model advertising 2,00,000 tokens whose accuracy collapses at 40,000.

Softmax makes tokens compete

Because weights must sum to one, every token added takes weight from the others, so padding a prompt dilutes attention on what matters and accuracy can fall before the window limit. The tell is an evaluation score peaking at a middling context length.

Capacity is not reliability

A model that accepts 1,28,000 tokens is not one that uses them evenly; a fact planted mid-input is found less reliably than at either end. The tell is a vendor quoting a window length and a benchmark average who will not supply accuracy by answer depth.

Prefill and decode are different businesses

Prefill is arithmetic-bound and parallel; decode is bandwidth-bound and serial, and they answer to opposite interventions. A bigger batch helps decode and barely touches prefill; a shorter prompt helps prefill and does nothing for a long answer. The tell is one latency number.

The cache, not the arithmetic, sets unit cost

Exhibit 2's eightfold concurrency difference comes from a head-sharing choice that appears on no model card a buyer normally reads. The tell is a team that can quote the parameter count but not the key-value head count. Ask which appears in the capacity plan.

Attention weights are not explanations

A heat-map showing that a scoring model attended to “therefore the market clears” describes one head in one of 48 layers; it is not a reason for a mark. The tell is a slide titled “why the model decided”; the substitute is measured agreement with examiners.

Equal architecture, unequal shape

Two vendors both selling a transformer may differ by an order of magnitude in serving cost through layer count, head sharing, expert routing and precision. The tell is a procurement note comparing architectures rather than measured cost per thousand tokens at your own length.

7. How the practice differs by product type and stage

In consumer products the mechanism is felt as waiting: each turn re-reads a growing history, so time-to-first-token rises through a session and the instrument is cache reuse, not a wider window. In business-to-business products like Parinaam's it is felt as unit cost per document and accuracy on long inputs, and the instrument is a chunking decision. In enterprise deployments the constraint is usually the retention and residency of cached tokens, as Paatra found. For platforms and marketplaces there is no distinct attention story; two workloads with opposite cost shapes simply share one fleet. In hardware the window is frozen by the memory on the board, and in AI-native products the risk is announcing window length as a feature.

Stage changes the arithmetic, not the mechanism. A seed-stage company running 4,000 assistant conversations a month would spend ₹25,286 a month on the stateless design in Exhibit 4b, and should not spend an engineer-month fixing it. Pankti, at 4,20,000 conversations — 105 times the volume — spends ₹26.55 lakh a month.
