Exhibit 2 complicates the first. A from-scratch model is cheaper to run than the hosted API, yet it resolves seven points fewer conversations, and the lost resolutions cost almost what the cheaper inference saves: ₹116.4 lakh a month all-in against ₹115.2 lakh. Option C, even with a three-point quality gap against the vendor, comes out ₹23.6 lakh a month ahead of A.

6. The options

Option A: stay on the hosted API and negotiate. It carries no training risk and the highest measured quality, 91 per cent. The cost stays per-request, so it grows linearly with every new client, the 2.8-second wait remains, and the bank's data-residency question stays a contract clause.

Option B: train Madhyam's own model. It delivers the independence Gaurav wants. It costs ₹18 crore up front and months before anything ships. It would be cheap to run per request yet the most expensive all-in, because quality would suffer; the training outlay is a sunk bet on quality not yet demonstrated.

Option C: fine-tune a small open-weights model. It spends ₹1.2 crore once to adjust an existing network's weights on Madhyam's archive, then serves it from Indian data centres. It gives the lowest all-in monthly cost, the quickest replies, and data that stays in India. Its weaknesses are quality, three points below the vendor, and a duty to monitor and retrain the model.

7. Questions for discussion

  1. Classify every cost in Exhibit 1 as one-off or recurring. Which move with request volume?
  2. Why does Option B have the lowest per-request cost among the owned options yet fail to beat Option A all-in? What assumption in Exhibit 2 would you test first?
  3. If monthly requests fell to 60 lakh, would Option C still beat Option A on running cost alone? What if they doubled?
  4. What must a two-week pilot show before you recommend anything, and what would make you choose Option A?

8. A note for the learner

The topic frames the decision by forcing one question onto every proposal: does this cost arrive once, or with every request? Training is a capital item. It buys weights, and the bill does not rise when Diwali traffic does. Inference is an operating cost, charged per request and felt by the customer as waiting time. A proposal that says "own model" is really two bets: a one-off training bet, and a recurring serving commitment that never goes away. Every option's sheet should show both columns, plus the quality consequence, so that a cheap-to-run model that fails customers is not mistaken for a saving.

A well-reasoned answer separates the ₹18 crore from the monthly lines, computes payback in months rather than intuiting moats, and prices quality in the business's currency, here handoff cost.

One defensible path. Recommend Option C, with Option A kept as a fallback. The fine-tuning outlay of ₹120 lakh is repaid in about five months of the all-in saving of ₹23.6 lakh against A (120 ÷ 23.6). It also answers the bank's two complaints, speed and data residency. Gate it on the pilot: ship only if resolution on a larger, Marathi- and Tamil-heavy test set stays at 88 per cent or more, routing low-confidence conversations to the hosted API. Decline Option B for now. It may be right later, but today it commits ₹18 crore to a quality result Madhyam has not seen.
case40v1-aivocab.inference.vs.training:
Chhavi Vision Systems: The Bill That Arrives Every Six Seconds

An unresolved case on inference, training and a take-or-pay contract

1. Sunday night, 1 November 2026

At a quarter past eleven on Sunday night, 1 November 2026, Harshada Tilak was still at the dining table of her flat in Hinjawadi, Pune, with three versions of one slide in front of her. The board of Chhavi Vision Systems met at nine the next morning. The slide was titled Where inspection runs.

In her twenty-six months as Vice-President, Product, Chhavi's inspection platform had gone from nine plants to thirty-eight. It now inspected 5.35 crore auto components a month across 214 camera stations, at four images a part: 21.40 crore images a month, about ten parts a minute at each station, one every six seconds.

Inside Chhavi the decision was described as cloud against edge. Harshada had stopped believing that description. Three things were tangled: a February 2025 contract committing Chhavi to a minimum monthly payment to its GPU supplier until 31 January 2028; that supplier's offer, open until Friday 13 November, to cut the per-image rate by 22.7 per cent for a larger minimum and a term to 2031; and her engineers' proposal to spend ₹3.10 crore once — on distillation, qualification and rollout, the appliances themselves costed separately — so the model would run on a box bolted to the station instead of a data centre in Navi Mumbai.

Chandrakant Risbud, the chief executive, had written on Friday: "Let us stop renting the arithmetic." Hemangi Sule, the chief financial officer, replied: "I need to know which part of this we pay once and which arrives with every part down the line." Harshada thought Hemangi's was the only sentence in the thread about the decision.

2. Chhavi Vision Systems, 2018 to 2026

Chhavi was founded in Pune in 2018 by Chandrakant Risbud, a quality engineer from a Chakan component maker, and Raghavendra Nerurkar, a computer-vision researcher. Its first product, shipped in January 2021, used hand-tuned filters to find surface porosity on aluminium castings. It worked and it did not travel: each new part family took six to ten weeks to retune, so Chhavi grew only as fast as it could hire.

In March 2023 Raghavendra persuaded the board to replace that stack with one trained vision-language model of about 14 billion parameters, fine-tuned on Chhavi's labelled images, with a single classification head for every customer and part family. The decision was commercially right, and it is what constrains the company today: a new family now took eleven days, but the model was too large for anything except rented accelerators, and because one network served every family, Chhavi had never maintained two sets of weights.

Those accelerators came from Himgiri Compute Services, a GPU provider with data centres in Navi Mumbai and Hyderabad, billed at first by usage. On 1 February 2025 Chhavi signed a thirty-six-month agreement expiring 31 January 2028, cutting the effective rate to ₹0.011 an image against a take-or-pay minimum of ₹1.20 crore a year, ₹10 lakh a month. The 2026 forecast was then 34 crore images a month; actual volume is 21.40 crore, so a floor chosen to look generous is within sight of the usage.

A ₹62 crore Series B closed in October 2025; revenue for the year ended 31 March 2026 was ₹13.8 crore. The subscription line runs at ₹12.2 crore annualised: ₹190 per thousand parts inspected against ₹71.23 of delivery cost, a contribution margin of 62.5 per cent. Cash at 30 September 2026 was ₹41 crore against ₹1.35 crore a month of burn, about thirty months of runway.

3. The industry

Indian automotive component manufacturing is large and unforgiving. Members of the Automotive Component Manufacturers Association supply Tata Motors, Mahindra, Bajaj Auto, TVS and Hero MotoCorp. The production-linked incentive scheme has pushed capital into new lines, specified by customers who expect defect escapes in parts per million and who audit their suppliers.

Inspection has been automated for decades by Cognex, Keyence and Omron, whose fixed-function systems are trusted, expensive and narrow; Bosch and Tata Elxsi sell integration around them. Chhavi's claim is that a trained model handles variation a threshold cannot: changing light, a new alloy, a different angle. Rohtas Inspection Labs, of Hyderabad, makes the opposite claim about delivery, selling an edge-only appliance at a flat ₹1.45 lakh a station with no platform fee, and has won two accounts Chhavi expected to close.

Two other currents matter. Camera frames capture operators' hands and sometimes their faces, so under the Digital Personal Data Protection Act third-party processing of that imagery is now a question Chhavi's larger customers put in writing. And export exposure cuts against the cost sheet: Hanazono Kiko, an Osaka brake-component group whose Indian supplier network Chhavi serves, has made it a condition of expansion that imagery not leave the plant.

4. How the question arrived

Exhibit 1 sets out the sequence. The pilot that began on 13 April 2026 at eleven stations — six at Chandrabhaga Metal Works near Pune, five at Hemkund Precision Industries in Coimbatore — was not about cost but availability: when a plant's link to Navi Mumbai degraded, the reject gate timed out, and the plant either stopped the line or passed parts unverified.

On 18 June 2026, at Hemkund's Hosur unit, brake-bracket castings with hairline weld porosity reached a customer. That defect class, which Chhavi labels D3, had been added to the model only in February. Ninety-five days later, on 21 September, Charumathi Sundararajan's team finished a seeded-defect audit at the pilot plants, comparing the distilled edge model with the cloud teacher on physical parts; Exhibit 6 reports it. Raghavendra's benchmark, Exhibit 5, was run the same month on held-out images and reads far better. Nobody on the call of 24 September could explain the gap, and Harshada had not resolved it.

Three beliefs of February 2025 have proved wrong. Volume would reach 34 crore images a month: it reached 21.40 crore. Part families would stay few: there are six, and the pipeline adds two. And one model would remain sufficient: a model small enough for an appliance cannot carry six families in one set of weights, so the edge proposal needs six distillation runs, repeated quarterly as the teacher is retrained. Training therefore does not fall to zero after a project; under that proposal it doubles, from ₹12 lakh a month to ₹24 lakh.

5. The people

Chandrakant Risbud, chief executive, Pune. Approve the edge programme: a unit cost that falls with growth is worth more than a linear one, and Rohtas is winning on that ground. Unsaid: he has told two Series C prospects the appliance ships by March 2027.

Hemangi Sule, chief financial officer, Mumbai. Sign the renegotiation, defer the rest. Exhibit 4 is the only paper comparing options on one number; she has promised the board a 70 per cent margin by March 2028. Unsaid: her sheet amortises the ₹3.10 crore over sixty months and omits the minimum, both of which flatter the option she opposes.

Raghavendra Nerurkar, co-founder and Head of Machine Learning, Bengaluru. Distil six family-specific models onto the appliance; the 2023 architecture was his and its ceiling is visible. Unsaid: quarterly re-distillation needs two engineers who are not in the ₹3.10 crore.

Charumathi Sundararajan, Director of Deployments, Chennai. She will not sign off a configuration scoring worse on D3 than today's, and her team absorbs every escape. Unsaid: five of her nine SLA plants breached availability in September, the strongest argument for the appliance she opposes.

Rupinder Sahota, Head of Edge Engineering, Coimbatore. The appliance is ready, and her group exists only if the programme is approved. Unsaid: her ₹24 lakh store-and-forward design, about ₹11,200 a station, would buffer frames through an outage and remove most breaches without moving inference.

Chege Mwangi, data scientist, Nairobi. No decision until drift is instrumented: the D3 rate in live traffic has risen from 0.4 per cent of inspected parts in January to about 6 per cent. Unsaid: his dashboard runs on the audit sample — the only cloud traffic left under full edge.

Chiaki Morisawa, Regional Director, Osaka. On-premise inference, or Hanazono Kiko will not expand; her 2027 target assumes forty-two new Hanazono stations. Unsaid: the condition is that imagery not leave the plant, which the audit sample violates.

Holly Rasmussen, Vice-President, Sales, Chicago. Sell the appliance as the customer's capital expenditure: her pipeline closes faster against capex than a per-part fee. Unsaid: it cuts the subscription from ₹190 to ₹135 per thousand parts, ₹29.4 lakh a month at 214 stations.

7. Voices

"Read the offer again. At 214 stations we would pay ₹22.50 lakh for ₹18.19 lakh of use. That is ₹0.0105 an image against the ₹0.011 we pay now. We are being sold a 22.7 per cent rate cut that saves ₹1.04 lakh a month, and paying for it with a commitment to January 2031." — Harshada Tilak, board thread, 27 October

"Eighty-one point seven per cent on D3. On brake brackets. I will not put my name on that configuration whatever it saves, and the board should notice that the benchmark they were shown was frozen in January." — Charumathi Sundararajan, same call

8. The options as Harshada frames them

Option A: do nothing. Keep the present contract to 31 January 2028: ₹38.11 lakh a month today, ₹49.82 lakh at 310 stations, ₹1.50 crore of minimum still to run. The inference line grows with every station sold — the shape Chandrakant objects to and Hemangi can forecast.

Option A′: sign the renegotiation by 13 November. The rate falls from ₹0.011 to ₹0.0085 an image against a minimum of ₹2.70 crore a year to 31 January 2031: fifty months at ₹22.50 lakh, ₹11.25 crore committed, ₹3.375 crore of it beyond Exhibit 3's window. The minimum binds until about 265 stations, so at today's volume the cut is largely notional. It is the cheapest row on Exhibit 4, and it turns a variable cost into a fixed one.

Option B: full edge. ₹3.10 crore once, six distilled models, an appliance at every station: inference becomes nearly free at the margin and training doubles. It is the only option that satisfies Hanazono if the audit sample is dropped — and dropping it removes Chege's drift instrumentation.

Option C: cascade. ₹1.95 crore once; the appliance decides the easy 78 per cent and escalates the rest. It recovers most of the benchmark quality at a cost between the other two, and beats neither on any column.

Two things sit outside the frame. Holly's proposal is not an architecture: sell the appliance at ₹2.35 lakh a station plus GST, book ₹117.70 lakh of hardware margin on the present estate, and cut the subscription to ₹135 per thousand parts — ₹29.4 lakh a month given up for a one-off. And Rupinder's ₹24 lakh buffer answers the availability problem that started the pilot without moving one inference. On her pad Harshada had written, and crossed out: the question may not be where the model runs.

9. The deadline and the hard constraints

The board meets at nine on Monday 2 November. Himgiri's offer lapses on Friday 13 November, eleven days later, and the account manager says it will not be re-quoted before the contract expires. Charumathi has a veto in practice: nothing ships to an SLA plant without her sign-off, and she has withheld it on D3. Hanazono decides on expansion when its financial year opens in April 2027; Chiaki needs a written answer on imagery before February. Capital is not the binding constraint, with ₹41 crore of cash against a ₹3.10 crore programme; engineers are, since distillation needs two hires Raghavendra has not requested and Rupinder's group is five people. Against all of it sits the ₹27.50 lakh of credits paid in the September quarter, which appears in no cost exhibit and alone exceeds the three-year operating saving Exhibit 3 attributes to Option B.

10. Questions for discussion

  1. Classify every line of Exhibit 2 as a cost arriving once, with each image, with each station, or with each part family. Which is Chhavi's real growth constraint?
  2. Exhibit 4 ranks Option B above A; Exhibit 2 ranks it last. Identify the three assumptions behind the reversal, and say which you would defend to a board.
  3. Under Option B the training line doubles to ₹24 lakh a month while inference falls to almost nothing. Is Chhavi's training spend capital or operating expenditure, and what follows for how the programme is financed and approved?
  4. Reconcile Exhibit 5 with Exhibit 6. What would you measure, and for how long, before quoting either recall figure to Hanazono Kiko or Charumathi's nine plants?
  5. Does the renegotiation reduce Chhavi's cost of inference, or only change its shape? What would have to be true about the 310-station pipeline, and about Rohtas, for signing it to be a decision rather than the cheapest row on a sheet?
  6. It is Monday morning. What does Harshada do, in what order, and with whose consent? Write the three sentences she says to the board about the ₹3.10 crore, the ₹11.25 crore and the ₹27.50 lakh — and say which comes first.

At midnight Harshada closed the three slides and opened an empty fourth. She typed a title: What we pay once, and what we pay every six seconds. Under it she wrote two column headings and stopped, because the ₹12 lakh a month of teacher retraining belonged in neither, and because she could not decide whether the service credits were a cost of inference, a cost of the customers' networks, or a cost of a sales promise made in 2024. The board met in nine hours.

Sugam Bima Services: The Fourteen-Second Answer

A teaching case on latency, throughput and the cost of a token

1. Opening

On the evening of Tuesday, 6 October 2026, Aishwarya Srinivasan sat in the Pune office of Sugam Bima Services with two numbers on her screen that did not belong together. The first was 2.4 seconds, the time her team's claims assistant had taken to answer a question during testing in July. The second was 14.1 seconds, the median time it was taking in production. The bill told the same story: ₹13.8 lakh a month had been projected, and ₹79.2 lakh was arriving.

Aishwarya, the head of product, had until Friday, 9 October to tell the executive team how she proposed to fix it. The board review was on Monday, 12 October; Diwali on 8 November would bring more policyholders to the helpdesks.

2. Company background

Sugam Bima Services, founded in 2019, sells a claims helpdesk to insurers and hospital networks: policyholders type a question about cashless approval, a rejected claim or a waiting period, and Sugam answers from the insurer's policy documents. Fourteen insurers and three hospital networks were on the platform by September 2026; 180 people work in Pune and Bengaluru.

Large insurers such as Star Health and HDFC Ergo run their own digital channels, and aggregators like Policybazaar have taught customers to expect instant replies. The Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority of India (IRDAI) expects clear communication of claim decisions, and the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023, governs every conversation. Sugam's differentiator was accuracy on policy wording, not speed.

3. The situation

In July, Sugam rebuilt its assistant around a hosted large language model. Pricing is metered per token, in two directions: ₹0.25 per 1,000 input tokens (the words sent to the model) and ₹1.00 per 1,000 output tokens (the words it writes back). Output costs four times as much because the model writes one token at a time, each needing a pass through the network, while input is processed in parallel.

The typical test request carried 600 input tokens and produced 80 output tokens. In production each request carried 3,200 input tokens: 700 for the standing instructions, 1,900 for the retrieved policy clauses and 600 for the running conversation. The prompt asked for explanation and clause citations, so answers ran to 520 tokens. Exhibit 1 sets the two side by side.

Prices: ₹0.25 per 1,000 input tokens, ₹1.00 per 1,000 output tokens. Sugam handles 2,00,000 requests a day, taken as 60 lakh (6,000,000) a month. Generation speed is 40 output tokens per second in both columns. Total latency is time to first token plus generation time.

Input grew by a factor of about five (3,200 against 600) and output by a factor of 6.5 (520 against 80). Yet input accounts for 86 per cent of tokens in production (3,200 of 3,720) and only about 61 per cent of the cost (₹0.80 of ₹1.32). Output is 14 per cent of tokens and about 39 per cent of the cost. Time tells a sharper story still. The long input raised the wait for the first token from 0.4 to 1.1 seconds, a delay of 0.7 seconds. The long output added 11 seconds of generation, which is 13.0 seconds of the 14.1 in total, about 92 per cent of the wait. A longer answer is slow in a way a longer question is not.

Throughput compounded the problem. In the busiest hour of a weekday, about 24,000 requests arrived, or 400 a minute. Requests in progress at once equal the arrival rate multiplied by the time each takes: at 14.1 seconds, 400 × 14.1 ÷ 60 = 94 simultaneous streams. Sugam's contract with its model provider allowed 80. Fourteen requests at any moment therefore waited for a slot.

Anwesha Dasgupta in Kolkata evaluated 500 real claims questions. The current model answered 470 correctly, or 94 per cent. Sagar Kamble in Hyderabad relayed that two insurers had written to say the helpdesk felt slow, one quoting a six-second target in its service agreement.

4. The people

Aishwarya Srinivasan, head of product, based in Pune. She must bring one recommendation to the executive team.

Kabir Dhillon, chief technology officer, based in Bengaluru. He favours an infrastructure fix, has a quotation for reserved capacity.

Anwesha Dasgupta, data scientist, based in Kolkata. She trusts only measured accuracy and warns that cheaper models fail silently on rare, high-stakes questions such as pre-existing disease exclusions.

Sagar Kamble, claims operations head, based in Hyderabad. He speaks for the insurers and the human agents who take over when the assistant stalls, and wants shorter answers.

5. Exhibits and the economics

Sugam charges insurers ₹1.80 per request handled. At 60 lakh requests a month, revenue is ₹1.08 crore, or ₹108 lakh. Against a model cost of ₹79.2 lakh, the contribution before staff and hosting costs is ₹28.8 lakh, a margin of 26.7 per cent. July's spreadsheet had shown only ₹13.8 lakh of model cost. Exhibit 2 compares the three courses open to her.

6. The options

Option A: shorten the output. Rewrite the prompt so that the assistant gives a direct answer of about 180 tokens and one cited clause, with detail available on request. Output cost falls to ₹0.18 a request, total cost to ₹0.98, and the model's 180 tokens take 4.5 seconds, so latency drops to 5.6 seconds, inside the six-second target. Simultaneous streams fall to 37, comfortably under the limit of 80. The cost is one point of accuracy (465 correct answers, not 470) and some policyholders wanting the full explanation.

Option B: move to a smaller model. A cheaper model priced at ₹0.06 and ₹0.24 per 1,000 tokens, and generating 110 tokens a second, would cut the monthly cost to about ₹19 lakh and latency to 5.2 seconds. Its cost is accuracy: 86 per cent in Anwesha's test, so about one answer in seven is wrong, and a wrong answer on a policy exclusion is a regulatory matter.

Option C: buy reserved capacity. Kabir's quotation of ₹12 lakh a month would guarantee enough streams for the peak hour and remove queueing. Nothing about the product changes, but latency stays at 14.1 seconds, because reserved capacity does not make each token arrive faster. It also takes the margin down to ₹16.8 lakh, or 15.6 per cent of revenue.

7. Questions for discussion

1. Using Exhibit 1, explain in your own words why the request was fast and cheap in testing but slow and expensive in production. Which share of the delay came from output?

2. The contract allows 80 simultaneous streams and the peak hour needs 94. Why would faster responses reduce this need, and why would reserved capacity not reduce latency?

3. In Exhibit 2, Option B has the best margin and Option A the second best. What would you want to know about the 70 questions that Option B answers incorrectly before deciding that its margin is worth having?

4. Which option, or combination, would you take to the board on 12 October, and what measure would confirm it within a fortnight?

8. A note for the learner

This topic separates three questions that the word "slow" blurs. First, which meter is running: input tokens, output tokens, or both? Second, which delay is the user feeling: the wait for the first token, which grows with the input, or the generation time, which grows with the output? Third, is the problem one request or the whole system: per-request latency, or throughput, which is the number of requests the capacity can carry at once? Option C answers only the third question, and Option B trades quality for the first two. Option A addresses all three, because output tokens dominate the wait.

One defensible path is therefore to adopt Option A first. Aishwarya should rewrite the prompt for a 180-token answer, keep detail behind a "show more" control, and stream the reply. She should re-run Anwesha's 500 questions before release and publish the budget: 1.1 seconds to first token, 4.5 seconds of generation. The saving is ₹20.4 lakh a month (₹79.2 lakh less ₹58.8 lakh), lifting margin from 26.7 to 45.6 per cent, and the 37 streams make Option C unnecessary. After the festive season she can test the smaller model on routine intents such as status checks, keep the larger one for exclusions, and examine whether the 3,200 input tokens can be cached.

Lipyantar Media Works: The Hour of Twenty-Nine Units

A case on latency, throughput and the cost of a token

1. The night before

At a quarter past eleven on the night of Tuesday, 17 November 2026, Jayanti Raghavendra was still at her desk in Madhapur, Hyderabad, looking at a bar chart she had understood for a week and could not accept. It showed, hour by hour, how many serving units Lipyantar Media Works' workload had demanded on a Saturday in October. For twenty-three hours the answer was comfortable. For the hour between ten and eleven at night it was twenty-nine. The company owned eighteen.

Jayanti, Vice-President of Product, had until Friday, 20 November to tell Yashoganga Sports Network whether Lipyantar would take the expansion offered on 6 November: live captions and translation for two further sporting properties, worth ₹38 lakh a month from 1 December on top of the ₹56 lakh already billed. Her board met on 26 November. And on 30 November the amendment window closed on the contract that mattered more — the thirty-six-month take-or-pay signed with Jyotirmay Compute Labs on 1 April 2025, either Lipyantar's largest waste or the only reason it could promise a broadcaster anything.

On her second monitor sat Yashoganga's October audit. Of eleven matches sampled, nine had breached the caption latency threshold — 81.8 per cent. At ₹2.50 lakh per breaching match that was ₹22.50 lakh against a monthly fee of ₹56 lakh, or 40.2 per cent of the month's revenue. Her own dashboard reported 1.1 per cent and called the product inside budget.

2. The company, and the contract that still binds it

Lipyantar was founded in Hyderabad in 2017 by two dubbing-studio managers who had noticed that India's regional television libraries were worth more than their owners could afford to localise. For seven years it was a factory of 260 translators and voice artists in Hyderabad, Kochi and Guwahati. It did not scale.

In late 2024 the pipeline was rebuilt around a large language model. A source hour now passed through six machine stages — cleanup, segmentation, translation, timing, critique and revision — and reached a human reviewer only as a sample. By October 2026 Lipyantar processed 13,500 source hours a month into nine languages, almost all for Jharna Entertainment Industries, whose catalogue migration had to finish by 31 December 2026.

The decision that constrains everything today was made on 1 April 2025. Inference prices were high and rising, and the forecast showed 24,000 source hours a month by mid-2026. Lokesh Vaidyanathan, the Chief Technology Officer, reserved eighteen serving units from Jyotirmay Compute Labs at ₹7 lakh per unit per month — ₹1.26 crore a month, ₹45.36 crore over thirty-six months, take-or-pay, expiring 31 March 2028. At April 2025 prices it modelled as a saving of three-fifths against metered usage.

Two things then went wrong, both good news on their own. Jyotirmay's metered output price fell from ₹2.60 per thousand tokens in April 2025 to ₹0.88 by September 2026 — 66.2 per cent. And the volume did not arrive: 13,500 of the 24,000 source hours assumed, or 56.3 per cent. Lipyantar pays ₹1.26 crore a month for capacity it could rent, at October volumes, for ₹83.03 lakh.

3. The industry

Indian sports streaming is a business of enormous audiences and thin patience. The consolidation of JioCinema and Disney+ Hotstar into JioHotstar established that a cricket feed in eight or nine languages is table stakes, not a premium feature; Sony LIV, Zee5 and Amazon Prime Video all carry multilingual commentary. A viewer in Nanded does not distinguish a late caption from a wrong one, but notices a wicket announced after the neighbours have.

Regulation sits lightly on captions and heavily on data. The Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023, governs the viewer telemetry Lipyantar's clients collect, which is why Yashoganga requires caption traffic to stay inside Indian data centres — removing roughly half of Jyotirmay's capacity from reach. Bhashini and AI4Bharat's open models have pushed the floor price of a passable Indian-language translation towards zero. Lipyantar cannot sell translation, only translation on time.

Lachlan Verhoeven, who sells internationally from Melbourne, holds a letter of intent from a diaspora broadcaster for Hindi and Tamil captions on matches in Australian evening hours — Indian pre-dawn, the window batch owns.

4. How the latency budget came to be the way it is

Yashoganga's playout chain holds the broadcast feed for 7.0 seconds. Inside that window the commentary must be captured, transcribed, segmented, translated into eight languages and packaged in time to reach the frame. Exhibit 1 gives the division, agreed in August 2026 and never revisited.

Commentary is dense. The segmenter cuts a segment every 2.5 seconds — 24 a minute — and across eight languages that is 192 calls a minute, 3.2 a second, per feed. A feed runs 3.5 hours: 40,320 calls a match.

Each call carries far more input than it returns: 780 tokens of standing instructions, 1,460 of glossary, 640 of rolling match summary, about 120 for the transcript segment — 3,000 input tokens for a mean of 118 out. Exhibit 2 prices one call four ways.

Two features took Jayanti weeks to absorb. The money is almost all in the input: ₹0.660 of the ₹0.764 as built. The asymmetry has a twin in the machine. A serving unit has no speed; it has a trade. Configured for throughput — large batches, deep queues — it emits 630 output tokens a second in aggregate while each stream crawls at 10. What has since turned out to be wrong

Three August beliefs have not survived October. That mean latency was 3.1 seconds; Exhibit 5 shows the two clocks. That four simultaneous feeds was the peak worth planning for; the expansion makes it eight. And that spare capacity was fungible: a unit-hour at four in the morning cannot be spent at half past ten.

The 1.5 per cent line falls between the readings: the dashboard's 1.1 per cent under it, the audit's 6.2 per cent four times over. And the tail is where the money is. A wicket produces a burst of dense commentary in every language at once, and the segmenter does not smooth it. Calls queue behind the four streams a latency-mode unit holds, and a queued call spends its wait inside the 4.90-second allowance generating nothing: sized for the mean, not the burst.

One: burst to metered capacity. Keep the eighteen reserved units on batch and meter what the fleet cannot hold. At eight feeds the peak needs 100 streams and the fleet holds 72, so 28 of the 100 streams burst out — 28 per cent. December's slate of 86 feeds is 3,467,520 calls; metered at ₹0.764 a call it costs ₹26.49 lakh against ₹94 lakh of December revenue. Comfortable arithmetic. Data residency, the lack of a concurrency guarantee and tail latency when two providers serve one match are not in it.

Two: cache the prompt. Of the 3,000 input tokens, 2,240 are identical for every call within a match. Caching them cuts cost per call from ₹0.764 to ₹0.320 — 58.1 per cent — and halves time to first token. Column D adds a 110-token cap and reaches 2.89 seconds, which at eight feeds needs 19 units: one more than the fleet. Yashica's objection stands.

Four: batch the languages. One call returning eight captions. Calls per second fall eightfold, but output tokens per call rise eightfold and generation time with them — against an allowance of 4.90 seconds. Three months' work, and the engineer may go.

Five: shrink the commitment. Take Jigisha's reduction to twelve units, a cut of six, pay ₹2.10 crore, save ₹42 lakh a month from January and meter all live capacity — making Lipyantar a reseller of someone else's latency.

Nobody has costed a product whose segmenter fires only on a scoring event, which would cut calls per second by perhaps three-quarters and change every number in Exhibits 3b and 4.

Yashoganga wants an answer by Friday, 20 November; the expansion starts 1 December. The Jyotirmay amendment window closes 30 November, after which the eighteen units run to 31 March 2028 at ₹1.26 crore a month whatever Lipyantar does with them. The Jharna migration must deliver its remaining 27,000 source hours by 31 December, and its delay clause is stated in finished hours, not unit-hours. Caption traffic must stay in Indian data centres, and the Kochi desk needs output by 08:00. Three matches above the 1.5 per cent threshold in any month give Yashoganga a termination right.

  1. Using Exhibit 2, explain why a longer glossary and a longer caption have such different consequences. Which configuration buys seconds, which rupees, which both?
  2. Exhibit 4 reports 41.9 per cent utilisation and Figure 1 demand of 29 units against 18. Both are correct. What is each answering, and which should a board see first?

  5. Exhibit 6's aggregates are averages across equal samples. If Yashoganga's audience is 40 per cent Hindi and 4 per cent Malayalam, is the exhibit more or less alarming, and should routing be per language, segment or property?

Jayanti closed the laptop at twenty to twelve and did not get up. The bar chart was still behind her eyes: twenty-three hours of slack and one hour of famine. In Guwahati, Lalitesh had sent a line she had not answered — the segmenter is the product, not the fleet — and in Kochi, Yashica's desk would start at nine with whatever the night had produced. The eighteen units were already running, as every hour since April 2025, mostly waiting.
exp20v2-aivocab.latency.cost:
Latency, Throughput and the Cost of a Token

Why one request is fast and cheap in testing but slow and expensive in production.

1. A forecast that was off by a factor of eight

On Tuesday 6 October 2026, Harleen Sodhi, head of product at Hamrahi Travel Exchange, a Pune-based holiday-package platform, opened a spreadsheet that her finance partner, Farhan Mistry, had built the night before. The company was three weeks from launching Hamrahi Assist, a chat feature that drafts day-by-day itineraries for customers. The launch was set for Monday 26 October, two weeks ahead of Diwali on 8 November, when bookings traditionally double. The model bill had been approved at ₹5 lakh a month.

In testing, an average request had cost ₹0.30. The team expected 50,000 requests a day, or 1,500,000 over a 30-day month. Multiplying gave ₹4,50,000, comfortably inside the approval. Then Hemalatha Rangan, the chief technology officer, replayed a week of realistic multi-turn staging traffic. The average request cost ₹2.40. The same multiplication gave ₹36,00,000, which is ₹36 lakh, more than seven times the approved figure. Worse, the typical answer took 19 seconds to finish, against under 3 in the demonstrations.

Nothing was broken; the model behaved identically. What had changed was the shape of the request: how many tokens went in, and how many came out. Harleen had to decide within the week whether to launch, delay, or redesign.

2. The idea

A token is the unit of text a language model reads and writes: a whole short word, a fragment of a long one, a punctuation mark. A provider charges per token and spends time per token, so money and seconds are metered in the same currency. Latency is the delay a user experiences for one request. Throughput is how much work the whole system completes per unit time across all users. Cost per token is the price the provider sets, quoted per million tokens, and it differs for tokens going in (input or prompt tokens) and tokens coming out (output or completion tokens).

The vocabulary exists because a model call is not a database query: a query costs roughly the same whatever it returns, while a model call costs in proportion to the text it consumes and produces. The asymmetry traces to the transformer architecture of Vaswani and colleagues at Google in 2017, which generates text one token at a time. Commercial model interfaces, spreading from about 2020, adopted per-token metering because it mirrors the cost of serving, and iteration-level batching, described in the Orca paper of 2022, let servers interleave many users' requests token by token.

The sentence Harleen could repeat in a meeting: "We pay for every token we send, we pay more for every token we receive, and the user waits for every token we receive, one after another."

3. How it actually works

A request passes through two phases that behave very differently. In the first, prefill, the server reads the entire input, every token of the instructions, the customer's trip details and the conversation so far, and processes it in parallel. Parallel work is fast, which is why long inputs are comparatively forgiving. Prefill ends when the first output token appears, and the wait up to that point is the time to first token (TTFT).

In the second phase, decode, the model produces the answer. Each token depends on the one before, so the tokens emerge one at a time, at a rate called tokens per second (TPS) for that stream. The only way to a shorter wait is fewer output tokens or a faster stream. Three steps usually stay implicit. Network and queue add a fixed overhead before prefill. The full conversation history is sent again on every call, because the model holds no memory between calls. And the server batches many streams, so the per-stream rate drops as the batch fills.

For Hamrahi Assist, the team measured this simple model of one request:

End-to-end latency = 0.25 s overhead + (input tokens ÷ 8,000 per second) + (output tokens ÷ stream rate).
Cost per request = (input tokens × ₹250 + output tokens × ₹1,000) ÷ 1,000,000.

Prices are ₹250 per million input tokens and ₹1,000 per million output tokens: output costs four times as much. The stream rate was 60 tokens per second in quiet testing and 50 under production load.

Production input was ten times the test input, yet the amber prefill segment grew by under one second. The teal segment, driven by output, grew from 2.5 to 18 seconds.

4. A worked example, line by line

The test request held 600 input tokens and produced 150 output tokens. A production request carried 6,000 input tokens: a 1,400-token instruction block, about 2,600 tokens of matched packages and policies, and about 2,000 tokens of conversation history. It produced a 900-token itinerary, because customers planning a week in Kerala want seven days of detail.

5. Nuances a learner must become aware of

Input tokens and output tokens are different commodities

Input is processed in parallel and priced lower; output is produced serially and priced higher. A blended "cost per token" hides that two requests with identical total tokens can cost and feel entirely different.

Time to first token is not end-to-end latency

TTFT measures how soon the user sees anything; end-to-end latency measures when the answer is complete. With streaming, where tokens display as they arrive, a 19-second answer can feel acceptable because reading begins after one second. Streaming changes perception, not the work or the bill.

Latency is not throughput

Latency is one user's wait; throughput is the system's output per second. They trade against each other: batching more streams raises throughput and slows each stream. Hamrahi's serving slice sustained 2,400 output tokens per second in aggregate. A peak hour holds 12 per cent of the day's 50,000 requests: 6,000, or 1.667 per second. At 900 tokens each that is 1,500 tokens per second, 62.5 per cent of capacity. At double volume in Diwali week it is 3,000, or 125 per cent: requests queue and latency rises for everyone.

Averages conceal the users who leave

Latency is reported as percentiles. The p50 is the wait that half of requests beat; p95 and p99 are the waits that 95 and 99 per cent beat. Output length varies, so the tail is long:

p95: 0.25 + 0.875 + 38 = 39.125 s; cost 1.75 + 1.90 = ₹3.65. p99: 0.25 + 1.0 + 75 = 76.25 s; cost 2.00 + 3.00 = ₹5.00. These are illustrative tail profiles, not a measured distribution.

The p99 request costs roughly twice the p50 and takes four times as long. The unhappiest customers are also the costliest.

Hidden tokens are still billed

Some models generate internal reasoning first. They are billed at the output rate and delay the first visible word, so a bill sized from the visible answer alone will undercount.

Cost and latency say nothing about quality

Capping output at 400 tokens helps only if itineraries stay usable. These metrics give the price of an answer, not its worth.

6. How it looks across products and stages

In a consumer product the user is waiting on a screen, so TTFT and streaming dominate, and the cost is a subsidy against later revenue; Hamrahi Assist sits here. In a B2B product calls are often batch jobs, such as overnight claim summaries, where nobody waits and throughput and price per token matter most. In a marketplace there are two audiences, and cost must be split: a seller-side listing assistant is an expense the platform can recover through commission, while a buyer-side helper is usually a pure cost of conversion.

Stage changes the stakes. An early-stage company at 500 requests a day pays ₹1,200 daily for a ₹2.40 request, which is noise beside learning. At 50,000 a day the same request costs ₹1,20,000 daily, and a 10 per cent cut pays for engineering time. Large firms also negotiate committed-volume prices and reserve capacity.

7. Common mistakes

Forecasting from demonstration prompts. The symptom is a first-week bill several times the plan. The misunderstanding is that a request has a fixed cost. The diagnostic is to replay a week of realistic traffic and log tokens per request before launch.

Reporting the average latency. The symptom is a healthy dashboard beside support tickets saying "it hangs". The misunderstanding is that the mean represents the experience. Plot p50, p95 and p99.

Shortening the prompt to fix a slow answer. The symptom is a sprint spent trimming instructions with latency barely moving, as in the table where 2,500 fewer input tokens saved 0.3125 seconds. The misunderstanding is that input and output drive time equally. The diagnostic is to split latency into TTFT and decode time before choosing a lever.

Ignoring history growth. The symptom is cost per request creeping up through a long conversation. The misunderstanding is that each turn adds only the new message; each resends everything before it. The diagnostic is to chart input tokens against turn number.

8. What good looks like

A well-handled version begins with a token budget written beside the feature specification: target input and output tokens per request, the price per request derived from them, and a latency target stated as p95, not average. The team logs tokens for every call. Streaming is on. Output is capped by design: itineraries arrive as a short draft with an invitation to expand any one day. History is summarised, not replayed in full. The finance partner sees cost at peak and at double peak, not one monthly figure.

Checks: (2.40 − 1.275) ÷ 2.40 = 0.46875; (19.0 − 8.6875) ÷ 19.0 = 0.5428. Throughput improves too: peak demand falls to about 667 tokens per second (27.8 per cent of the 2,400 capacity), and at double volume to about 1,333 (55.6 per cent), so the festival surge fits.

9. The decision, and what to learn next

Harleen chose to launch on 26 October with the redesign, not the original design and not a delay. The original version would cost ₹36 lakh a month against a ₹5 lakh approval and would push the Diwali-week peak past capacity. The redesign would cost ₹19.125 lakh, still 3.8 times the approval. She asked Farhan for a ₹20 lakh monthly ceiling, reviewed after the first full month, and asked Hemalatha to report p95 latency and tokens per request weekly. She would test whether customers given short drafts booked at the same rate as those given long ones.

The natural next topic is prompt caching: the 1,400-token instruction block is identical across thousands of calls, and some providers charge less for input they have seen recently.

Two questions to sit with. First, if your product's requests were replayed from real logs today, which would surprise you more, the input count or the output count? Second, what is the longest answer a customer of yours will tolerate waiting for, and is that a number you have measured or one you assumed?
exp40v2-aivocab.latency.cost:
Latency, Throughput and the Cost of a Token

Why a request is fast and cheap in testing and slow and expensive in production — and why the answer is always a question about how full the machine is.

1. Two decisions, twenty days apart

On Thursday 8 October 2026, above a tyre showroom in Bengaluru, Mrinalini Kanade, chief product officer of Tarjuma Voice Network, boxed one number on a whiteboard: 1,200. Tarjuma's voice agent, Tarjuma Vaani, answers inbound service calls in nine Indian languages for lenders and insurers, and 1,200 was the milliseconds a caller would tolerate between ending a sentence and hearing a reply. Beyond that, callers talk over the agent.

The board wanted an answer by Monday 2 November, twenty-five days later. Tarjuma bills ₹6.50 per handled call minute; the average call runs 4.5 minutes across nine agent turns, so revenue is ₹29.25 a call. At 42,00,000 handled calls a month — from 58,00,000 dial attempts, a connect rate of 72.4 per cent — that is ₹12.285 crore of monthly revenue. On a large frontier model the launch configuration returned a gross margin of 22.89 per cent against a promise of 55. Sudarshan Hebbar, who runs platform engineering, wanted to buy machines rather than rent inference; Naushad Kanjariya, who sets pricing, thought the model bill was never the problem.

On Tuesday 13 October, in Gurugram, Shreyasi Mahanta of Ullekh Contract Systems faced the mirror image. Ullekh Samiksha reviews loan agreements and vendor contracts overnight for banks, lenders and insurers; clients care only that the file enters the queue at 22:00 and the flagged clauses reach the reviewer by 06:30. Three clients send 55,700 documents a night, averaging 14,800 input tokens each. At ₹11.50 a document that is ₹192.165 lakh of monthly revenue on 16,71,000 documents, and on the hosted API the margin was 36.61 per cent against a target of 60; Prithviraj Ahluwalia, her infrastructure lead, wanted to reserve four machines. Both firms were about to learn that the cost of a token is a price divided by a utilisation rate — and theirs differed by a factor of four.

2. The idea: a token is a unit of time and of money at once

A token is the unit into which a model chops text — a short word, a fragment of a longer one, a mark. Providers meter money and time in tokens: input tokens the model reads, output tokens it writes. Latency is one user's wait; throughput is what the system completes per second across all users. Time to first token (TTFT) is the wait until the first output token appears; tokens per second must be quoted per stream or in aggregate, because the two diverge sharply.

The vocabulary exists because of one architectural fact. The transformer, published by Vaswani and colleagues at Google in 2017, reads its input in parallel but writes its output one token at a time, each conditioned on all before it. Reading saturates an accelerator's arithmetic units; writing drags the weights and the growing key–value cache past idle arithmetic. Prefill is compute-bound, decode is bandwidth-bound, and that asymmetry explains nearly everything here: why long inputs are cheap in seconds and long outputs are not; why servers interleave requests, as in the Orca paper of 2022; and why per-token pricing, adopted from about 2020, is a lossy summary of serving cost.

Three schools disagree. The capability school signs that prices for a fixed capability fall by roughly an order of magnitude a year, so design for the best model and let deflation fix the economics; it will not sign that a margin may rest on an unpromised price cut. The unit-economics school signs that a product with negative contribution margin today is not a product; it will not sign that you should ship the weakest model that passes evaluation. The capacity school signs that per-token prices wrap accelerator-seconds, so the only question is what fraction of them you fill; it will not sign that self-hosting is therefore cheaper, because the fraction is usually embarrassing.

Both protagonists ended up able to say: "We pay for tokens, but we buy machine-seconds."

3. Mechanics: prefill, decode, the batch and the node-second

Take Tarjuma's turn. Five things happen in series after a caller stops speaking: transcription finalises the utterance, the request crosses the network, the model prefills the prompt, it decodes enough tokens for the synthesiser to start — about 18, a first clause — and audio begins. Only the middle two depend on the model, and in opposite ways. The large model prefills at about 4,200 tokens a second and decodes at 45 per stream at the provider's batch size; the small model prefills at 25,000 and decodes at 110. The launch configuration's longest turn, its ninth, puts 3,440 tokens in flight.

Little's law, L = λW, sizes the system. Tarjuma's peak hour carries 18 per cent of the day's 1,40,000 calls, so 25,200 calls arrive in an hour at 4.5 minutes each, giving 1,890 concurrent calls and 63 agent turns a second. At 1,900 input tokens a turn that is 1,19,700 input tokens a second to prefill, against 3,780 output tokens decoded.

The unit that makes this comparable is the node-second: the share of one node's time a request consumes. Tarjuma's redesigned call takes 17,100 ÷ 25,000 = 0.6840 node-seconds of prefill and, at 48 small-model streams of 110 tokens a second, 540 ÷ 5,280 = 0.1023 of decode, 0.7863 in all, 87.0 per cent of it prefill. An Ullekh document with a 1,150-token coded review takes 3.5238 and 0.6911, or 4.2149, of which 83.6 per cent is prefill. Input dominates the machine while output dominates the price. A reserved large-model node costs ₹16,80,000 a month and holds 30 × 86,400 = 25,92,000 node-seconds, so a node-second is ₹0.648148; a small-model node at ₹8,40,000 a month gives ₹0.324074. Multiply by node-seconds per request, divide by utilisation.

Effective cost per request = (node-seconds per request × cost per node-second) ÷ utilisation. A hosted price is therefore an implied utilisation: the fraction you would have to fill your own fleet to match it.

4. When the framing applies, and when it misleads

Four testable claims. Output tokens dominate the wait, input tokens dominate the bill and the machine. True for Ullekh, where prefill is 83.6 per cent of node-seconds and input is 72.0 per cent of the hosted price of a coded review, ₹4.44 of ₹6.165. Half true for Tarjuma, whose wait ends at first audio: on the small model, prefill and the first 18 decoded tokens are comparable. Latency and throughput trade against each other. True for both. Reserved capacity beats metered tokens above a break-even utilisation. True as an identity; only the side of the line differs. The token bill dominates an AI feature's cost. False for Tarjuma: its redesigned call costs ₹1.4445 of tokens, ₹10.80 of speech recognition and synthesis and ₹3.60 of telephony, ₹15.8445 in all, so the model is 9.12 per cent. Halving the token bill wins 4.56 per cent of cost; the speech layer at 68.16 per cent is where the money is.

5. Hard edges: seams, regulation, two sides and silicon

The interesting failures happen at seams. Ullekh sells two things from one cluster: the nightly batch, and Ullekh Sawaal, a pane where a reviewer questions the contract on screen. A question sends the contract (14,800 tokens), instructions (900) and the query (60), so TTFT is 15,760 ÷ 4,200 + 0.18 = 3.9324 seconds.

Mature firms handle this with a capacity contract, not good intentions — a floor of node-seconds the batch scheduler may not borrow. They say autoscaling handles it: reserved accelerators do not autoscale on a Tuesday morning.

Regulation adds a second edge: Ullekh's bank clients require that contract text not leave named jurisdictions, which removes the cheapest serving regions and raises its node price, while India's rules on outbound calling shape when Tarjuma's traffic may occur — what makes its demand spiky. In two-sided products the question is ownership: a marketplace recovers a seller-side listing assistant through commission, while the same tokens on a buyer's assistant are pure subsidy. Hardware adds the on-device option, where a token costs electricity but cannot be updated weekly. For AI-native firms inference is cost of goods sold, so 22.89 per cent is existential.

6. Eight nuances that separate the expert

Prefill and decode are different businesses sharing a building. The tell is one tokens-per-second figure quoted for a whole system. An expert asks which phase and at what batch size: the small model's 25,000 and 110 differ by a factor of 227. A faster model is not faster at everything.

A long prompt is a capacity lever, not a latency lever. The tell is a team trimming its system prompt to fix a slow answer. Trimming input barely moves a completion-bound wait, yet it is the largest lever on capacity: prefill is 83 to 87 per cent of node-seconds here. The obvious reading reverses the two.

Per-stream rate is a scheduling decision. The tell is a benchmark at batch size one. Tarjuma's provider quotes 96 tokens a second for one stream; the product gets 45, because the provider runs a profitable batch. Read every published latency figure as a claim about a batch size.

Averages hide the users who leave, and they are the expensive ones. The tell is a dashboard with one latency line. Ullekh's p99 takes 42.6308 seconds against a p50 of 9.0937 — 4.69 times as long — and costs ₹11.088 against ₹5.208. Streaming does not fix that: it moves when reading begins, leaving tokens and rupees untouched.

Hidden tokens are billed tokens. The tell is a bill exceeding a forecast built from visible output. Reasoning models emit internal thinking tokens at the output rate, which also delay the first visible word. An expert reads the usage fields and caps reasoning effort before launch.

Conversation cost is quadratic, not linear. The tell is cost per request drifting upward with no change in traffic mix. Because each turn resends the prior turns, Tarjuma's twelve-turn call costs ₹1.974 a minute against ₹1.65 for a six-turn call. Assuming a turn adds only its own message is the commonest error.

A list price is an implied utilisation. The tell is a build-versus-buy argument conducted in rupees per million tokens. Ullekh's coded review costs 4.2149 × ₹0.648148 = ₹2.7319 at full utilisation against a hosted ₹6.165, an implied 44.31 per cent; Tarjuma's call costs ₹0.254811 against a hosted ₹1.4445, an implied 17.64 per cent.

Achievable utilisation is a property of demand, not of engineering. The tell is a capacity plan with no diurnal curve. Batch work is schedulable, so Ullekh reaches 67.93 per cent; voice arrives when callers call, and after peak and failover Tarjuma tops out at 15.93 per cent — why one identity gives two firms opposite answers.

7. Across product types and company stages

In consumer products the user is on a screen, so TTFT and streaming dominate and tokens are a subsidy against later revenue. In business-to-business products the work is largely asynchronous, so throughput and price per unit of work dominate — why Ullekh runs at a batch size of 64 and Tarjuma cannot. In enterprise deals residency and audit clauses can flip build-versus-buy alone; in platforms and marketplaces the live question is attribution. In hardware the on-device option changes the unit to milliamp-hours. Stage changes the stakes, not the mechanics: at 500 requests a day an ₹8 request costs ₹4,000; at 1,40,000 calls a day it is ₹11.2 lakh.

8. Three worked examples, one of them a failure

Tarjuma's quality upgrade, which cost quality

For the four weeks from Monday 24 August to Sunday 20 September 2026, Tarjuma ran the large model on one client's traffic — 4,60,000 calls — expecting better understanding to raise containment, the share resolved without a transfer. The budget went to 1,599.0 milliseconds, 33.25 per cent over the ceiling. Callers talked over the agent, interrupted turns were repeated, and the average call grew from nine turns and 4.5 minutes to eleven and 5.5. At eleven turns the prompt sum is 31,900 input and 660 output tokens, so tokens cost ₹10.56 a call against ₹8.154, and speech plus telephony at ₹3.20 a minute ₹17.60 against ₹14.40. Cost per call was ₹28.16 against revenue of ₹35.75 — a margin of 21.23 per cent, worse than the 22.89 per cent the same model gave at nine turns, because the longer call raised cost faster than revenue. Containment fell from 70 per cent to 61 per cent, so of the 4,60,000 pilot calls 2,80,600 were resolved rather than 3,22,000, and the client absorbed 41,400 extra transfers at about ₹34 each, ₹14.076 lakh.

Sopaan's reasoning tokens

Sopaan Learning Network, a Chennai exam-preparation company with 1,86,000 subscribers paying ₹399 a month, shipped a doubt-solving tutor on Monday 6 July 2026 and read the bill nine days later. The budget assumed 2,400 input and 700 visible output tokens a doubt: ₹0.72 plus ₹1.05, or ₹1.77. The model also emitted about 2,600 internal reasoning tokens at the output rate, so the real figure was ₹0.72 plus ₹4.95, or ₹5.67 — 3.20 times the plan. At 23 doubts a subscriber the token bill was ₹242.5626 lakh a month against ₹742.14 lakh of revenue, 32.68 per cent where 10.20 per cent was planned; for the heaviest decile at 62 doubts, ₹351.54 of a ₹399 subscription, 88.11 per cent. Bhargavi Natarajan and Irfan Mulla capped reasoning effort near 600 tokens and routed 71 per cent of doubts to the small model: ₹0.57 there against ₹2.67, a blend of ₹1.179, or ₹50.4376 lakh a month — 6.80 per cent of revenue.

9. Failure modes, early warnings and diagnostics

Forecasting from demonstration prompts. Sign: a first-week bill several times the plan, as at Sopaan. Diagnostic: replay a week of production traffic, logging input, output and reasoning tokens. Late cost: a third of revenue, against a published price.

Reporting the mean latency. Sign: a healthy dashboard beside tickets saying "it hangs". Diagnostic: plot p50, p95 and p99 on one axis, split by phase. Late cost: churn among the customers with the largest documents.

Letting batch and interactive share a pool. Sign: latency correlating with the clock, not with traffic. Diagnostic: overlay interactive p50 on the batch scheduler's start times. Late cost: four sprints of misdirected investigation.

Reserving capacity on a demand curve you do not control. Sign: one utilisation figure and no churn scenario. Diagnostic: recompute cost per unit with your largest client removed. Late cost: a fixed commitment whose unit cost worsens as revenue does.

Buying latency with quality, or the reverse, without measuring the other. Sign: a migration justified on a single metric. Diagnostic: require a paired measurement — containment, task success, reviewer trust — on every change. Late cost: Tarjuma's pilot, where a better model made a worse product.

10. Where experts genuinely disagree

The capability school, steelmanned: the price of a fixed capability has fallen roughly tenfold a year for three years, providers are racing to cut it further, and a team shipping a weaker model to protect a margin will be beaten by one that ships the strong model and waits. It is wrong if that deflation is mostly investor subsidy, or if your bottleneck is memory bandwidth on hardware no longer improving that fast.

The unit-economics school: Tarjuma's 22.89 per cent margin is not a forecast problem but a fact about a signed contract, and a company building its costs on an unpromised price cut has outsourced its survival. Its evidence is the AI features quietly repriced when the first bill arrived. It is wrong if the gap is temporary and fundable — and wrong more subtly whenever the token bill is 9.12 per cent of cost and the argument has anchored attention wrongly.

The capacity school: per-token prices wrap accelerator-seconds, and once demand is schedulable you should own the machines, as Ullekh's 65.03 per cent margin shows. It is wrong where demand is spiky, where the on-call burden of a serving stack exceeds the saving — a cost these node prices exclude — or where model upgrades outpace a twelve-month reservation.

Two narrower disputes stay live. Whether tail latency matters: the streaming camp holds p99 to be a perception problem, the queueing camp that p99 determines capacity. And whether to route: one tuned model is simpler to evaluate, while Sopaan's cascade doubles the surface to test.

11. What mastery looks like

Four visible differences. Such a person asks how many input and output tokens, at what percentile, before asking about the model. They put a token budget and a p95 target beside the acceptance criteria. They convert every price into node-seconds and every quoted latency into a batch size, making build-versus-buy arithmetic rather than temperament. And they never take a cost or latency win without a paired quality measurement.

12. The decisions, and three questions

Mrinalini Kanade took the small model, the rolling summary and a 700-millisecond speaking rule to the board on 2 November, and refused Sudarshan Hebbar's cluster: at eight nodes — six for the peak, two for failover — Tarjuma would fill 15.93 per cent of what it bought, ₹1.60 a call against a hosted ₹1.4445. She refused Naushad Kanjariya's repricing too, since the speech layer at 68.16 per cent of cost was untouched: recognition and synthesis renegotiated from ₹2.40 to ₹1.05 a minute take the call to ₹9.7695 and the margin to 66.60 per cent.

Shreyasi Mahanta reserved four nodes and shipped the coded review, taking Ullekh from 36.61 per cent to 65.03 per cent, with two conditions Prithviraj Ahluwalia had not asked for: a reserved floor of node-seconds for Ullekh Sawaal, and a monthly exhibit recomputing cost per document with each client removed.

Three questions. First, Tarjuma's achievable 15.93 per cent sits 1.71 percentage points below the 17.64 per cent the hosted price implies: what would flip that decision? Second, Ullekh's four nodes run at 96.42 per cent inside the bank's window — what breaks first, and what would you price in? Third, who at Sopaan owns the evidence that students routed to the weaker model are as well served?

13. Going deeper

Tokens and tokenisation is the foundation: clock and bill are metered in this unit, and Indian-language text tokenises less efficiently than English. Inference versus training separates making a model from running it; this page is the second. The context window bites hardest: all of it is prefilled and paid for on every call. AI infrastructure basics for PMs supplies the node-second. Prompt caching is the next move: if cached input prefills ten times faster, caching Ullekh's contract takes the pane's time to first token from 3.9324 seconds to about 0.7610. What a large language model actually is and the transformer and attention explain why decode is serial and prefill parallel. Embeddings and vector search and similarity decide how many input tokens you send, and so your capacity. Pre-training, post-training and fine-tuning offers Tarjuma's other route, a small model taught one job well. RLHF and alignment closes the loop: answer length and style are trained behaviours.
